The Grand L&dge of California has again convened. Hearty rreetings have
been exchanged between old-time friends and brethren; the warm Masonic hand
has been extended to our new members; the Grand Lodge has been •pened in
Ample Form ; and we ar11 now ready to proceed with the annual busineBB.
Before calling your attention to the various subjects which it is both a duty
and a pleasure to present for your consideration, pennit me to remind you of our
increased obligation to the Suprem1> Grand Architect, who, in mercy and loving
kindnesa, enumerates and watches over every living soul, although in the world's
vast aggregate we count no more than the falling leaves.
The year just clo"6d has been especially marked by great proaperity. A beneficent Providence has vouchsafed to the Fraternity-indeed, to the whole people of
the State-the blessings of health and happines·s, with an overf!owinR' mea.sure of
the necessaries and comforts of life. We ought to be indeed thankful that our
"lot has been cast upon such pleasant times and in such favored places." While
many other peoples, whose intelligence, virtue'and morality would suffer little fo
comparison with our own, have struggled with the horrors of pestilence and famine,
we have basked in the genial sunshine of peace, health and plenty; ind011d, it might
almflst be said that earth and sea have thrust their treasures upon us, while
. "Every ray from yonder blue, and every drop of falling dew,
Seems to bring down to human woes, from Heaven, a message of repose."
A source of additional gratitude to the Great Giver of All Goodie found in the
presence here to-day of that large number of members who for so many years have
been spared to punctually fill their places at the sound of the gavel, ready to share
the burdens and enjoy the pleasures incide11t to each Annual Communication.
But, alas I our joy is freighted down with the sombre reflection that the heads of
th~se grand old Masonic servants are rapidly whitening for the grave, while the
presence of an increasing list of new members, whom we now greet with a most
cordial welcome, warns us that al{e is upon us, and that we should clasp more
firmly to ; our hearts the sacred tenets and pure principle& of our beloved Order,
and be ever ready to respond tO the closely approaching summons of our Supreme
Grand Maater. In this coo1;1ection, beiflg in perfect accord with my own sentiments, I hope to be justified in appropriatin11 a few paragraphs from the eloquent
Addrees of the Gmnd M aster of Maine for the present year i LookinJf at the large number present to-day, it is a pleasure io recognize
eo wanv tamiliar faces. I see the co:untenances of those who have labored gladly
and faithfully, year after yrJar, in the cause of Freemasonry. When first they
came into these halls their steps were firm and their eyee flashed with the glew of
youth, but Time has smitten them with his heavy hand, and many are now bend·

ing with the burden of care and years. Yet, alt~ough grown old i!l fa!thf"!ll se.rvice, their presence here to-day tells me that their love for the Institution ls still
young and unabated.
I, too, see before me many new faces which have come to increase our numbers and learn the mysteriea and duties of a new career. They come in the strength
and glory of young manhooli to assume the burdens and honors of active' Masonic
life. Destined, as they are, to succeed soon to honors and responsibilities which
older ones now ahare, may I not hope and trust that they will merit the greatness
of their opportunity and obligation. It affords me great pleasure thus to note the
auspicious reunion of the old and the young, and I gladly welcome each and all
to our thirty-sixth Annual Communication. I am thankful that I can age.in
welcome the old members to this familiar shrine of devotion, and to a renewal of
friendships as sacred as they have been lasting. I rejoice, too, that I can gladly
and cordially welcome the new memoors, who now meet in this hall for the
first time, to a sphere of usefulness and dignity and friendship which, as they
may be worthy, shall end only with their lives.
I now bell' lMve to direct your attention to a brief report of my official acts for
the paet year, and to such other matters of interest to the Craft as custom and our
fEli'Ulatlone require the Grand Master to present.
During the year I have visited several Districts and quite a number of Lodges-some officially, others informally-but, in deference to your time and patience, I
forbear any detailed account of the interesting incidents and pleasant courtesies
attending these meetings. Your Grand Lecturer generally accompanied me ill
these visits, and it is needless to say to California Masons that we were everywhere
received and entertained in the most graceful and agreeable manner. I feel justified in saying that much good resulted from these personal inspections. The work
was everywhere carefully exemplified, difficulties were healed, and the methods of
transacting Masonic business were CGrrected. As a result of these visits, to.ken in
connection with the information furnished by the Inspectors, I am led to the conclusion that Masonry in this jurisdiction was never more vigorous and prosperous than
now. No work has been done in thirty-three Lodges during the year, although the
returns show a small general increase in membership. Eight Lodges have conferred
no degrees during the last twe years; three Lodges have conferred none during the
last three years; and Lodge No. 28 has conferred no degrees during the last four years.
It is a question worthy of consideration whether some of these should not surrender their charters. Affiliati(ms have been numerous. The books and papers,
including even the much a.bused black-book, are, generally, correctly and neatly
kept ; business is transacted in accordance with the orders of the Grand Lodge; and
you wlll learn from the able and interesting report of the Grand Lecturer tha.t,
with few exceptions, the ritual is rendered with accuracy and uniformity. I am
especially pleased to be able to report that the practice ef the cardinal virtues,
especially temperance, is steadily gaining ground, while our tenets are finding a
firmer lodgment in the Masonic heart. Of course, the foregoing observations by ,
no means apply in their full extent to every Lodge or to every Me.son ; but, as ne
cases are presented requiring present discipline, it might seem in vidieus to here
mention the instances to which they do not apply, as that information will generally nppee.r in the proper returns.
I have given considerable time and labor to the investigation of the financial
condition of the several Lodges, and find that very few of them are in debt, a.nd tha.t
these debts are generally unpaid balances incurred in the erection ef ha.II buildings.
N ea.tly all have something on hand, at least enough for curre,nt expenses and the
ordinary calls of charity, while more than one-half of the whole number have

the new administration there is a marked improvement in the business and conduct

It is a source of regret to be compelled to announce that the Inspectors of Districts Nos. two, twenty-seven, and thirty-four have not reported to the Grand
Master, as required by the 15th General Regulation. All the others, being thirty-one
in number, have ferwarded reports within the prescribed time. These reports,
which are now flled for the information of the Grand Lodge, contain a very complete review of the business atfairs and general condition of the several Lodges
within their respective Districts, besides many practical suggestions for improving
upon our present methods of business and infusing additicmal energy and interest
info Masonic work. The reports for the first, third, sixth, seventeenth, twentythird, twenty-fourth, twenty-sixth, and thirty-second Districts are so complete and
s" well prepared as to demand special mention; and it is much to be regretted
that a due relfard for the proper limit oi this address will not admit of a caref.ul
review of thosE> able papers. The excellent and interesting report of the Grand
Lecturer, however, will present in convenient form much of their valuable contents.
A few interesting ceremonial observances have occurred in the jurisdiction during the year :On the twenty-fourth of June last, I convened the Grand Lodge in Special
Communication at Alturas, in the county of Modoc, for the purpose of dedicating
the new and elegant hall of AUuras Lodge, No. 248. It was a grand event for the
fraternity of that distant and somewhat inaccessible county. A large concourse of
Masons were present. From Adin, fifty miles away, came thirty or forty, with a
vocal choir of superior excellence. A large delegation from Fort Bidwell, about an
equal distnnce; quite a number from· Cedarville, in Surprise Valley; a delegation
from Falls City, more than eighty miles away; with a party and band of music
from Susanville, ninety miles distant. These, added to the brethren of Alturas,
made up a large body of enthusiastic Masons, while the citizens vied with the Fraternity in doing honor to the occasion. All had come for a good time, and they
had it. On the afternoon of the twenty-fourth the hall was dedicated with the
formal ceremonies of the Craft, in the presence of a great audience. The building
is a large two-story stone structure, and is not only a lasting monument to Masonic
enterprise and energy, but acredit also to the pleasant town of Altura.a. A Die·
trict meeting had also been called, and for several days the Grand Lecturer
labored with his accustomed zeal and energy in imparting the work and lectures.
After the ceremonies came the usual pleasant entertainments.
On the fourth of.July last, I opened the Grand Lodge at Eureka, for the purpose
of laying the corner-stone of a new courthouse for the county of Humboldt. The
llCcasion is one long to be remembered by those who participated. A large collection of Masons, besides many civic and military societies and the citizenR generally,
joined in the procession. An eloquent oration was delivered, and the corner-Atone
laid with appropriate ceremonieR in accordance with the rules of our ancient Craft.
A District meeting was held at the same time, but in consequence of the absence,
of the Grand Lecturer, who was sick at home, the exemplification of the work was
unsatisfactory to me, and I fear equally •O to the brethren in attendance. There
is probably no place in our jurisdiction where Masonry is in a more flourishing
condition or the brethren more zealous' and devoted than in the county of Humboldt.
On the twentieth of October last, authorizations were issued for constituting the
several Lodges then existing under dispensation, as will be more fully shown in
the Report of the Grand Secretary ; and, on the tenth Gf June last, authority wa•
given to Past Master 'fHOMAB G. LAMBERT to dedicate the new hall of Pajaro

At our last Annua.I Communication, upon the representation that the hall of
Sierra Valley Lodge, No. 184, with all its furniture, had been destroyed by fire,
leaving its members to struggle with a large indebtedness, the Grand Lodge·waa
pleased to remit their dues for the year ending July 31st, 1885. The Inspector of
that District ad vises me that, although the amoant remitted was but a trifle, this
act of fraternal recognition and care upon the part of the Grand Lodge had a very
important influence in stimulating them to renewed efforts, and that tht>ir debt is
now almost paid off. I respectfully submit for your consideration the propriety of
again remitting the dues ef that Lodge.
The committee appointed to investigate the charges against Loa Angeles Lodge,
No. 42, have discharged that duty, ar1d, although none of them have as yet presented any bills for that service, it is clear that they are justly entitled to reason.
able compensation for time and expenses.
This Grand Lodge has repeatedly declared that no Lodge shall expend any part
of its funds in payment for dinners or collations. (See Vol. X, pp.174-5; Vol.
XII, p. 499; Vol. XV, p. 686, Proceedings.) This prohibition has occasioned considerable correspondence with a number of Lodges. Some think it a hardehip
that, after concluding a long and exhausting night's work, a little collation of
coffee, bread, and cold meats cannot be served at the expense of the Lodge, particularly so when many of the members have to travel long distances to reach their
homes; and I have been requested to suggest for your consideration whether this
regulation ought not to be so modified as to permit, within specified limits, such
simple collatiqns at the close of working meetings.
Since preparing the foregoing, the pleasinll' views of our present prosperity and
grand prosp~ctive future, have suddenly been shrouded in the deepest li'loom and
sorrow by the death of our well bel0ved. Grand Treasurer, Bro. MosEs HELLEB,
who departed this lift' at twenty minutes past two o'clock this DJorning. .As a citizen, he was the soul of honor and probity-as a man, the embodiment of those
great moral qualities which atdorn the true man-as a husband and father, the
idol of a family upon whom he lavished a wealth of true lev11 and affection. He
has gone to a higher and better ho~e, an irrepar&ble less to the Craft, and mourned
alike by a loving fraternity and an a.:lmiring public. I recommend the appointment of a cc.mmittee of three to draft an address expressing the sentiments and
feelinis of the Grand Lodie a.nd of the Oraft generally upon this sad occasion.
In closing this brief and imperfect account of my stewardship, I desire earnestly
to.thank the Grand Lodge for the high honor conferred upttn me, the Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer for valuable advice and assistance, and the oftl.cer1 and
brethren generally for their patient forbe,rance, generous aid, and uniform courtesy
and kindness.

At the same Commnnication, as will be seen at page 732 of the Proc~e<lings of
1884, the Committee on Grievauces reported unanimously in favor of the restoration of CHARLES How ARD GORDON; but, the report having been presented on the
last day of that Communication, its consideration was ordered to be postponed
until the second day of the present one. It is probably not improper to call the
attention of the Grand Lodge t9 the facts that this petition for restoration has
been before it at different times since and including the year 1877; that its Co111.
mittee on Grievances during that time, with a single e'xception, has constantly
reported in its favor; that even in that excepted report the opinion was expressed
that the petitioner had been unjustly dealt with ; and that in the next following

Inspector JORN M. MELENDY, of the First District, makes an elaberate and very
interesting report of the condition of the five L@dges composing that district, All
which he had visited save one, and this one he proposed to visit soon. He states
that he found all the Lodges anxious to receive visits from him aij often.a.a he could
find time lo give them, and that the officers were ever ready to receive and profit
by instruction. He considers ~ the Lodges in the district in good working condi·
tion, except the one not yet visited by him, and says that any defects in its work
will be remedied as soon a.a he can find a proper opportunity. 'l'he financial
condition of the Lodges is also good, 11.nd enables them to render that efficient
aid to brethren in distress which so often comes opportunely to relieve want
and suffering. He reports that Crescent, No. 45, has paid, during the greater
part ef the year, twenty dollars per month to one brother to relieve his
necessities. In concluding his excellent report, Bro. MELENDY says :-"I feel
that it may be safely said that Masonry throughout this district has experienced
a rapid and healthy growth during the year last past. The ability of the several
Lodges to assist their needy and deserving members has greatly increased, while
the character of their membership and the energy of their officers has placed the
institution in this section where it always belongs-firllt among civic societies."
This Inspector certainly merits commmendation for the zeal ancj. fidelity with which
he has dischar11"ed his duties.

Inspector \VrLLIAM E. OUGHTON, of the Eighteenth District, reports that he haR
visited fourteen of the sixteen Lodges included therein, and gives a. detailed
and well-prepared account of their condition and workings. Of the five Lodges locat ed in the city of Sacramento, he says: " They are all in good condition, financially and otherwise, although very little work, comparatively,. has been done."
These Lodges all chose new Masters at the last election, an instance which has not
before occurred in many years. These new Masters are all young men, the eldest,
probably, not being more than thirty-five years of age. The financial condition of
the city Lodges is good. Some of them have no money in the treasury, but they
own considerable hall stock, which is a good investment and will ultimately yield
a handsome revenue. It appiiars that there is but one Black Book written up
among the five Lodges. This is wrong, The law prescribes the books which shall
be kept. by the Secretary of each Lodge, and among them is the Black Book. The
fact that all these Lodges meet in the same hall is no reason in favor of, or
excuse for, the neglect of any duty imposed upon nn officer by the Grand Lodge.
I trust that the Masters of those Lodges, whose Secretaries have neglected their

I have noticed but one barrier in the way of progress to a complete umform1ty.

rpetuated. Time will correct this aefect. Most of the Senior ~ ai-dens of the
l:dges have so far perfected themselves in the knowledge of the ritual that they
are even now able to pass a very creditable examin•tion. Many of them can confer the degrees, and several have done so i,n my presence. .All this augurs ~ell for
the future and should my successor contmue the course maugurated durmg my
incumben~y the day will not be distant when we may hope to see the work rendered with ~s !lreat a degree of perfection as it is reasonable to expect. " " *
Harmony has ~enerally prevailed throughout this district, save in one instance,
which, cominl{ to Bro. ANDERSON'S knowledge, he called a meeting of the Lod~,
and, by judicious advice and timely admonition, succeeded in restoring at least the .
umblanoe of itood feelinit, which it is hoped may prove to be permanent anti real.
In this connection Bro. ANDERSON says :It is sad to think that there are in our Lodges many who ~eem.to have no higher
metive in view than their own advancement, and who are willing to pr9~titute our
sacred Institution to obtain for themselves a position and rank among their brethren
which neither their heads nor hearts entitle them to hold. Everywhere the office

Grand Lodge of California.

1hould seek the man; more especially should it in a place so sacred as a Masonic
Lode-e. But we do not always find thiB to be the case. Too oft.in it occurs that the
rttlrmg modesty of the really worthy deters them from assuming the responsibilitlea of a position which they are eminently qualified to fill, while the effrontery of the
tlllrlPRerving as often bears them into place• which their incapacity or unworthiness
oanses them to disgrace. We notice this evil existing in many of our Lodges. In
frequent cases, no sooner is a brother appointP.d Steward than he becomes impressed
with the idea that he is now placed on the high road to the Master's chair. There
111i~ta an impression, too, among the brethren, that the party who is selected a.a
Senior Deacon, must, in turn, be elected Junior Warden, and so on, irrespective of
qualification. "He is a good fellow, and it will not do to supplant him," is the
ory, and thus incompetent and sometimes unworthy brethren are placed in high
J1<11itions t0 the great detriment of the Craft. It is the duty of all good Masons to set
their faces determinedly against this pernicious custom-for custom it has becomeand agree to unite upon the best, the most capable, among them to fill the important
t>OBition• in their Lodges. When this is done, we may hope to see the Oriental
Ohair filled and kept tilled by those who will be an honor to their Lodges and a
benefit to the Craft.
.
In the views expressed by Bro. ANDERSON I most heartily ccmcur, and I trv.st that
the Lodges of this district may long have the benefit of his counsel and instruction.
In1pector FRANCIS A. CUNNING, of the Twenty.fifth District, reports that, becauBe of the urgency of his business engagements, he has been unable personally to
vl~lt any of the Lodges under bis charge. He believes them all to be fairly prosperous and says that most of them have had work to do. He declines a reappointment, justly believing that h_e who accepts a trust so imI>ortant should faithfully
perform the duties which it imposes.
One of the ablest-&nd most interesting reports received by me is that submitted
by Inspector FREDERICK W. LuoAs, of the Twenty-sixth District. There are seven
Lodges therein, all which he has visited, and he gives a most entertaining accGunt
of their condition. All appear to be reasonably prosperous, their officers competent, and the brethr11n zealous, except in one instance. Of this Bro. LUCAS says :My first appt'lintmP.nt was with PeB<Jalkro, No. 239, at their snug little hall in
the village of that name, but, as only feur mambers responded to my call
the work was not exemplifiod ; nor did those present choose to utilize my presenc~
by any rehearsal thereof. The books of the Lodge appear to be we 1 kept, and reveal
nothing- demandin1: criticism-the principal business of the yea appearinit to have
been the openimr and closing ceremonies and reading t e minute~ thereof.
The 1'vler's Register shows that seldom more than the const utional seven were
present, the rPmaining seven, (there being but fourteen me ers,) living at a distance, and evidently deaminir the expense of visitation too ar for the entertainment offered. A i;reneral apa,thy seems to prevail. The Lod~ "sin s-ood financial
condition, but there is a lack of available material within its jur1sdict11>n. Like the
town whose name it bears, the Lodge seems to have passed the period of its mild
prosperity, with scarcely a glimmer of hope in the horizon of its future; and my
recent visit strengthened my oft-repeated helief that it could render the greate•t
mervice to the Fraternity by a surrender of its charter, or by a consolidation with
Ha'lfll!(J,rd, No. 226, at Half Moon Bay.
The details of Bro. LuOAB' visits to the remaining Lodges of his district are
very interesting, but too lengthy to be embodied here. He closes his excellent
report as follows:~ otwit~standing a disastrou~ seas<J>n, I find the Lodges of the twenty-sixth
district uniformly prosperous, with remarkable freedom from those rpetty strifes
and discords which too often invade the sanctity of our Lodges, impairing their
usefulness and even imperilinl!' their existence. Viewing in retrospect my fourteen
years of experience as lnapectnr, I can but rejoice at the vast improvements made
during that period of time, There existed at first a wide difference in the manner
of conferrinit degrees; Lodge-rooms were often small and unsuitable; while 10
ma!ly irregularities were disclosed by the tell-tale books, se many violations of Masomc law occurred, that, on more than one occasion, the Grand Master was oblicred
to interpose his authority, and more than one Lodlfe trembled upon the verge of dis-

solution. An increasing attention is paid to the work, now almost complete in its

The Twenty-sixth District is in good hands and will, I trust, long remain under

Inspector ALVAH R. CONKLIN, of the Twenty-eighth District, reperts that the
condition of the two Lodges composing that district, so far as finances are concerned,
is excellent. Very little work has been done, owing to the depression in mining indu•tries, upon which that district is whully dependent. Of Inyo, No. 221,

also a change in the prospects of the country, will no doubt regulate the matter and
restore it to the prosperous condition which it formerly enjoyed."
Inspector JOSEPH C. \VARD, of the Twenty-ninth District, submits a very satisfactory report of the seven Lodges under his supervision. They haYe plenty
of work, are d0ing it well, and are generally prosperous and progressing. He had
visited five of the seven and found everything to his satisfaction. An unexpected
absence from the State prevented his visiting the remaining two in time for this
report, but he is well assured of their good condition.
Inspector IRVING N. MoGurnE, of the '1.'hirtieth District, reports the six Lodges

tent to do good work when called upon.
Inspector CHARLRS H. KELTON, of the Thirty-first Di•trict, reports the three

doing much work. San Buenaventura, No. 214, he says is a live Lodge, and has
done a large amount of work durin11 the year. Santa Barbara, No. 192, has con.
ferred but four degrees this y~ar, and Magnolia, No. 242, has conferred but f>ne.
The officers of the several Lodges are fairly proficient and the books are well kept.

of the State." Bro. Busa calls attention to the pernicious habit, not by any mean1

Inspector SrnoN L11:vr, of the Thirty-third District, reports that all the Lodges
in his district, four in number, are in good condition and prosperous, with the exception of S an Diego, No. 35. H.e re discord and contention have crept in, impt.ired the usefulness, and even threatened the existence of the Lodge. Bro. LEVI
is making every possible effort to harm1mize the antagonistic elements, and hopes
to achieve success.
Inspector GEORGE E. HowE, of the Thirty-fourth District, reports th11t the one
Lodge under his supervision, Hawaiian, No. 21, at Honolulu, is in a flourishing
c~ndition financially, and will soon be free from debt if no untoward event occurs
to check its prflgress. Good material is being worked up, and, with some few
amendments in the manner of keeping its books and accounts, its conditien may
be pronounced as satisfactory. Bro. HowE calls attention to the fact that no Grand
J.ecturer has visited that district for fifteen years, and strongly urges the importance of a visit from that officer. His request is certainly just, and should I retain
this position another year, I will make an effort either to visit the Lodge myself
or have some qualified hr.o ther commissioned to give them the instruction they
desire.
From the foregoing summary of the reports of the Inspectors I am of the opinion
that the Craft in this jurisdiction has never been in a more satisfactory condition.
It is true that not so much work has been done as in some former years, but this
is no evidence of decadence or lack of interest on the part of the Lodges. In the
history of societies, as in that of states and nations, periods of depression will
occur ; but a reaction is certain to follow, generally bringing increased activity
and renewed prosperity. A large majority of the Lodges are prosperous and flourishing, and an earnest desire is apparent o~ the part of both officers and members
to excel in the work as pre1cribed by the Grand Lodge. Save in one or two
instances, peace and harmony prevail among the Craft, and all seem actuded by
th11t "noble contention, or rather, emulation, of who can best work and best
agree." On the whole, I feel justified in reporting that the Lodges in California
are in an eminently satisfactory condition.
All which is respectfully submitted by
JOHN WERNER SHAEFFER,
Grand Lecturer.

The Board has buried seven brethren, during the year, belongini to other juris·
dictions-three of them at its own expense; and it has been the means of returning
the widow and orphans of onl) brother to their home in England.
The expenditures herein set forth do not include any relief extended to any
member of either of the Lodges in the city of Los Angeles, or to any member of
their families- each Lodge taking care of its own distressed.
More than fifty brethren have found employment through the Board, and it
has collected $5,000 of insurance from other jurisdictions for the widows of deceased brethren.
Many brethren of limited means visit our section of the State in pursuit of
health or employment, and their stay being often prolonged without the reault
hoped for, and their means becoming exhausted, they are compelled to apply to the
Board for advice, recommendations, or pecuniary e.ssistance. The number of ap·
plications is censtantly increasing, and the work and expenses of the Board will be
correspondingly augmented in the future.

The sixty-fourth Annual Communication of the Gr11J1d Lodge of Alabama was

The Address of the Grand Ma8ter, though brief, Is 11 very excellent paper.
rom
the beautiful sentiments expressed we would quote liberally, bnt must content our·
selves with the following:- •

1885.J

Grand Lodge of California.

Freemasonry, viewed from the exterior, presents no marked excellencies which
are not possessed by numerous other orgamzatioos. Those only who have entered
Into the most secret recesses of the Temple, and beheld its beauties, and read its
~ymbols, and studied their hidden meaning, can fully distinguish it from all other
human organizations; and to him who has been thus fortunate, the spirit of iospira·
tion it breathes must always remain without a rival in his affections.
It must be remembered that when 11 brother preseot·s the name of an applicant
ror initiation into the :Masonio fraternity, he presents 11 stone that must go into the
Temple, if not rejected by the V{orkmen when the square, the level, and plumb shall
be applied. No brother should ever so far forget his duty to the Brotherhood as to
present a stone that is not finished in the highest degree. Every one offered should
be hewn from the finest P11ri11n marble, because our Order is in no sense of the
word an institution organized for the purpose of reforming men : and I greatly fear
that some are influenced to seek admission within our portals from selfish purposes,
believing, perhaps, that they themselves will be benefited rather than 11 benefit to
others. Wo man is flt to be made 11 Mason until his desire to do good to others
exceeds his own selfish designs.
The Grand Master pays 11 last tribute of respect to the memory of Bro. JAMES
DAVIDSON, Grand Tyler, whom the Angel of Death had summoned to refreshment
above. Bro. DAVIDSON was the oldest iivlng member of Andrew Jaokson Lodge.
In 1849 he is said to have visited California and assisted in organizing the first Masonic
Lodge ever established in the "Golden State."
During the year the Grand Master had received a large onmber of letters, asking
advice and requesting rulings on questions presented; but not 11 single question had
been submitted that had not been decided by former Grand Masters, or by resolu·
I.Ions of the Grand Lodge. In this connection he says : It now appears that almost every conceivable question involving 11 principle of
Masonic law has been settled, and I must commend 11 closer perusal of the Coosti·
tutiou and Digest and Grand Lodge proceedings to the brethren, and particularly to
MRsters of Lodges. I have no doubt that much confusion, and sometimes angry
debate, would be avoided by prompt and correct rulings' on the part of Masters,
who are at a loss to know how to proceed for the reason that they have not informed
themselves on questions that have been time and again decided.
All this is as trne of the Masters iCl our jurisdiction as in that of Alabama. 'fhe
troth is, too many :Masters think that when they have committed •the manual and the
eeoteric work, they have no need of anything more. Ignorant and unskillful Masters
may reasonably expect to have poorly taught disciples and Lodges that lac.k the
essential elements of interest and strength.
The Grand Master had refused 11 number of 11pplic11tioos for dispensations to
confer two degrees at the same time, and remarks that, while it pained him to do so,
he could not set the example of violating the law. He acted wisely and well. Dis·
peosations had been issued dnriog the year for th6 establishment of five new Lodges,
The Grand Master very feelingly adverted to the death of the M:.
HENRY
WILLIAM MUBBAY, Grand Master of Masons in Virginia, and also to that of Past
Gi·and Master ELBERT H. ENGLISH, of Arkansas, of whom he says: " A chief pillar
In the Temple lies prostrate and broken."
And now comes Alabama with a desire to establish 11 "Masonic Home and Col·
lege." The committee to whom the matter was referred, with Bro. P. J, PILLANB as
chairman, reported that they had not been able to devise any plan, for they believed
that to insure success in so great an undertaking required the united and persistent
efforts of all the Lodges and Masons in Alabama ; and that this could not be accom·
plished by the voluntary contributions of either Lodges or Masons. They thought
that, to accomplish the end in view, 110 association should be chartered by the Legl1lature, that a fixed annual amount should be raised by 11 per capita. tax on each
Lodge, and that each Lodge should be required to send up one-third of all amounts
received for conferring degrees. They add that too many of such undertakings have
failed because of too great haste, and that they cannot expect much to result in their
day; but that with proper car~ and prudenc11 they may lay the foundation for 11

Last year a member of King Solomon's Lodge was suspended for unmasonic con·
duct, and, on appeal to tlie Grand Lodge, the committee, believing the evidence
elicited Insufficient for conviction, and fearing a wrong may have been done for
which the accused might go unpunished, remanded the case for new trial. After
the election of a new commission, and at the instigation of the accuser, it was
agreed to drop the matter. After a thorough examination of the proceedings on the
trial before had, the Grand Master decided that, by unanimous consent of all concerned, the case might be dropped. His suggestions were acted upon. We doubt
the propriety of this action, believing that it.le not within the province or power of
the Grand M"ster to set aside an edict of the Grand Lodge. We think that the new
trial ordered should have proceeded.
·
A petition for the degrees had been favorably acted upon and the Entered Ap·
prentice degree conferred upon one who proved to be almost devoid of hearing. In
due time he passed B creditable examination for advancement, but further proceed·
inge were suspended and a committee appointed to again investigate the physical
qualifications of the candidate. This committee having found him sufficiently pos·
seeeed of that sense, recommended advancement. The second degree was then
conferred as far as the O. B. inclusive. Further procedure was again suspended,
subject to the Grand Master's decision. The Grand Milster decided that he was now
a Fellow Crafi, and, with no other objection, was entitled to the third,degre'0. Thie
is a case for Bro. VAUX and the believers in the "perfect man" doctrine. The "one
eye" believers have nothing to say.
The Grand Master expresses great pleasure in being able to state that the regu·
lation enacted at the preceding Communication, relative to non-affiliated Masone,
had proved to be one of the most beneficial laws adopted by the Grand Lodge; and
recommends that it deliberate upon the enactment of some regulation whereby a
brother of that jurisdiction, wishing to sever hie connection for the purpose of joining
another, should obtllin hie dimit through the Lodge with which be intended to affiliate.
An amendment to tho Constitution of the Grand Lodge, in consonance with the recom·
mendation of the Grand Master, was subsequently adopted by that body,

that the juri~diction can fully sustain itself, there being a balance o~ band, over all
expenses, of $351 40.

1'hat elephant, "ST. JoBN's College," still worries the brethren of Arkansas.
'J'he Committee on Edncation, in their report to the Grand Lodge, say:The most zealous and sanguine friends of BT. Joe:N's College have, long ago,
1ooepted in sadness the conclusion that it cannot be maintained and flourish under
Ke.ionic auspices. The Trustees have, in good faith, as shown by their report, been
1ndeavoring to effect the wishes and intention of the Grand Lodge with regard to the
flroperty, by putting the same 11pon the market with a view to appropriate the pro·
oeeds to the erection of a Masonic Temple for the Grand Lodge, in such manner as
to derive, at the same time, an educational fund from the available rents .
The Trustees bad made strenuous endeavor to sell the property, but had received
110 bid for it, and had no immediate prospect of 11 sale. They suggested to the Grand
l,odge that, as real property was greatly increasing In value in the central part of
the city, a sufficient sum should be appropriated from the surplus fnnds of the Grand
Lodge to be applied to the purchase of a suitable site for a M11Sonic Temple. The
l)ommittee on Education reported resolutions to this ett'ect, but the Grand Lodge
rejected them, and the matter remains in statu quo.
The hearts of our good brethren of Arkansas are fuller, we fear, than are their
money-bags. Not content with one elephant, the Grand Master favors the
11tablishment of a National Charity Hospital at Hot Springs. "One at a time,"
brethren. If Masons are In such great need of the blessings of your great Pool of
Siloam, let their Lodges send them there. The Grand Lodge took no action upon
the suggestion of the Grand Master.
The Grand Secretary presented a detailed report of the transactions of bis office.
rrom it we learn that, like our Grand Secretary, he devotes especial care to the
aocnmulation of a library that may be a source of pride to his Grar.d Lodge. Among
other contributors to this laudable purpose we find the name of Bro. ABELL. , We
trust that the present collection of valuable works may be spared the fate which
befell the library at the burning of the Temple in 1876.
The report of the Grand Treasurer indicates a favorable condition of the Grand
Lodge funds. In conformity with the recommendation of the Grand Master, a com·
111lttee was appointed for the purpose of securing funds to erect a monument to the
memory of Past Grand M11Ster ENGLISH. The committee were clothed with full
power to act.
.
There is no review of the proceedings of other Grand Lodges. It is stated by the
Ohalrman of the Committee that it has become the custom in this jorlsdiction to omit
tho review every other year. He intimatos that this course has many good reasons
for its adoption; we, however, fail to see them.
The committee reported fe.vore.bly upon the application of the Grand Lodge of
Victoria, Australia, bat, the chairman being unexpectedly absent, the report was not
h11nded in until after the close of the session; hence no action was taken. The
brethren of Victoria, and perhaps the brethren of the "Guild," may conclude that
thn "perpetual" Chairman has been Dodge-ing the main issue. We miss his report,
for from it we expected much of interest.
Our review opened with the melancholy announcement of the deatb of Past
Grand Master ENGLISH ; it closes with the sad intelligence of the death of the
B.'. W.'. W. H. Howxs, Senior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge. On the twenty11venth day of February, 1885, he was called from his le.bore on earth to the fruition
of Joy in the Better Sanctne.ry. We deeply sympathize with the brethren of Arkansas
In their loss.

I am much afraid, brethren, tba.t, not only in this Province, but throughout the
world generally, there are too many Lodges unmindful of their duties in yielding to toe
solicitations of' cand idates to be passed and raised. Just a little reflection will teach
us that no one should be permitted to take the second degree until he is thoroughly
grounded In the.first; and that, iu no case, other than one of great emergency, shonld
the third be conferred until the candidate has manifested suitable proficiency In the
principles of the previously mentioned degrees.
It requires no very great fabor to obtain all the degrees of Ancient Masonry, to
possess a fair knowledge of its ritual•, and to he come familiar with its forms and ceremonies; but it is a stupendous work . to learn and understand thoroughly, or even
superficially for our purposes, the deep and profound mysteries of our Institution.
We concur. Fa.r too much zeal is displayed in endeavors to increase the num·
bers In membership, and far too little in the due preparation of the ashlars selected.
Too frequently do we show by our acts, in our Lodges and out of them, that all that
is requisite to make a man a Mason is to confer upon him the degrees. Too much
time is spent in ritualistic work, and not enough In the proper education and instruc·
tion of the members in the teachings of our Order. .As soon as one has taken the
three degrees he is dropped from flirther attention, and is expected to absorb a kn owl·
edge of the more profound mysteries and teachings. Initiation brings the candidate
within the pale of Masonic intlnence, and it should be the constant aim of every Ma·
son to see that the virtnons education is not neglected and tnat the rough ashlars,
under the constant application' or the gavel of good instruction and authority, are
caused, day by day, to approximate more and more unto the standard of the perfect
man and Ma.son.
The Grand Master pays a very fitting tribute of respect to the memory of the V.'.
R. ·. Bro. RoBEBT HALL SMITH, Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge, who, on
the fifteenth dl\y of November last, was called from his labors on e·a rth to the fruition
·
of blessings above.
Among the dispensations granted by the Grand Master were three to allow certain
Lodges to bury deceased m.embers. No dispensations were required to permit the
brethren to die; and one seems to ns quite as necessary as the other.
The Grand Master decided that no dimitted or unaffiliated Mason, residing in the
Province, can take part in any Masonic ceremony, public or private. The decision
is in accord with the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of the Province, bot., never·
theless, seems to be in derogation of the rights of brethren who, by force of circnm•
stances, ma.y he compelled to dimit. Dimission in the Province carries with it the
force of a virtual suspension, the dimitted Mason being allowed the privilege of one
visit to a Lodge daring the period of non-affiliation. Such a regulation may have a
tendency to prevent dim!ssion or non-affiliation, bat the wisdom of it seems prob·
lema.tic.

Referring to the refusal of a Lodge in "°n Eastern jurisdiction to relm burse a

ho BRYS:We think a Lodge that would refuse au.ch an account must have a very weak hold

\hem to die without funds, there would be no help for them except a pauper ftrneral.
Possibly a few members would acoompany the remains to the grave, if It cost them
nothing ; but it is doubtful. It would seem tb,at a Lodge ought to be sufficiently
1rateful to another far away for performing the last rites over one of its me.mbersone who was the personal friend and acquaintance of the brethren, who had been
Initiated, passed and raised with them, whose Masonic home waa with them-suffi·
olently gratefol to pay the expenses incurredj and to do it wltb thanks, and not

So we think. No ceremony in Masonry is more saared than that appertaining to
tile burial of deceased brethren, and .th~ Mason who would refuse or negleot to

The Address of the Grand Master is devoted mainly to matters of local import.
Fitting tribute is paid to the honored dead, among whom is especially mentioned
Bro. ELBERT H. ENGLISH, Past Grand Master of Arkansas, who died at Asheville, in
North Carolina, on the first day of September last:The Grand Secretary reported that the sum of $1 ,472 39 had been received from
the various Lodges of the State for the Ohio Relief Fund, but that, not being needed,
the several amounts had been returned to the respective Lodges donating. A resoln·
tion recognizing the Grand Lodge of Arizona was adopted.
A circular had been issued "cautioning and forbidding holding Masonic inter·
course with any Mason hailing from the so-called Grand Lodge of Ontario, or from
any Lodge acting nnder its authority, as they are not recognized by this Grand
Lodge; and further, that from henceforth no Lodge within this jurisdiction shall
apply for release of jnrisdiction over candidates belonging in another State, excepi
through the Grand Master of this jurisdiction." This action had been taken in conse·
quenoe of a complaint from the Grand Lodge of Canada that a Lodge in Connecticut
had asked consent of tbe Grand Lodge of Ontario to confer tbe second and third
degrees upon a candidate who had received the first degree in a Lodge working
under authority of the so-called Grand Lodge of Ontario.
The Grand Secretary reports that the year had been fairly prosperous, though a
slight falling off from the preceding year had been noticed. A most commendable
zeal had been manifested by Bro. WHEELER in his attempts to secure a complete set
of the original printed proceedings of' the Grand Lodge. Several years ago, when he
was elected as Grand Secretary, there was hardly an original in the office. He now
Jacks only May, 1805, October, 1797, and all prior to October, 1795. It is also
worthy of note thi!I the returns had been received from every Lodge in the jurisdiction, and the dues in all cases except one.
The "Masonic Charity Foundation Fund" has increased in a very gratifying manner, being now $8,146 44. The establishment of a" Masonic Home,'' however, does
not appear to meet with any great degree of favor, and we opine that the brethren
of Connecticut will require the most ardent efforts of the Grand Secretary to prevent
them from abandoning the project before the contemplated sum of $100,000 can be
raised. At the present rate 'Of increase in the fund, several generations will lllt.ve
passed before the design is accomplished. We think it would be wiser and better to
lighten the burdens of the present than to tax the Lodges and members of the
Fraternity in the accumulation of great funds, which too often prove to be sources
of dissension. Besides, we believe in resting the responsibility of the administra·
tions of charity where it properly belongs-upon the Lodges themselves-and where
it can be more jndicionsly and unostentatiously discharged.
The Committee on Jnrisprudence approved the action of the Grand Master relative to application to Grand Lodges for release of jurisdiction over candidates, and,
upon their recommendation, the following resolution was adopted:Resoloed, That no communication whatever from Lodges in this State, to Grand
Lodges or Grand Masters of other Grand Jurisdictions, shall be made, except
through and with the approval of the (jrand Master of' this State •.
This setion we deem eminently proper, being intended to prevent the occurrence
of difficulties between Grand Jurisdictions likely to arise from the ignorance or ill·
advised action of subordinate Lodges.
The Report on Correspondence is again from the pen of the Grand Secretary, Bro.
WHEELEB. It is a very excellent production, just such as we might expect from the
fertile resources and great experience of that brother. We have carefully read it,
and with great interest and benefit. With such " husbandmen" as Bro. WHi<:ELER,

DELAWARE.
The seventy·eighth Annual Communication of the Grand J,odge of Delaware was
held in the oity of Wilmington, commencing on the first day of October, 1884,-tbe
M.'. W.'. JOHN F . SAULSBURY, Grand Master, presiding, and the B.'. W,•, WILLIAK
S. HAYES being Grand Secretary. Twenty-one Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master is brief and of 11 local character. Peace and
harmony prevail, and the Fraternity had enjoyed a year of unusual prosperity.
Relations with other Grand Lodges were agreeable and pleasant. The regulation,
adopted at the le.st Annual Communication, requiring Masters of Lodges to prove their
a.billty to confer the degreesDf Ancient Craft :Masonry and to perform the duties appertaining to the position of Master of a Lodge, had apparently had a wholesome effect
upon the Craft throughout the jurisdiction. The Grand Master recommended the
appointment of 11 committee whose business it should be to exemplify the proper
work to the officers and members of the several Lodges. He favors some plan by
which the different Grand Jurisdictions could be enabled to unite upon and work
under 11 uniform ritual; but, whilst advancing uniformity, he wished it to be under·
stood that he oonsidered 11 thorough knowledge of the great truths taught to be of
greatest importance. A resolution to appoint the committee recommended was
subsequently introduced, but was laid on the table.

The Report of the Committee on Correspondence was prepared by the Grand
Secretary, Bro. WILLIAM R. SINGLETON, It is a well-written review of the proceed·
Inge of fifty.four Grand Lodges. Two questions, "penal jurisdiction," and " the formation of Grand Lodges," in reference to which the action of' the Grand Lodge of
the District of Columbia had been severely criticized, he reserves for the conclusion
of his report, in order that he might answer all the criticisms at once. In his review
Of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Alabama, he says 1-.After many very serious errors were committed in this jurisdiction under the separate ballot rule, we personally undertook to investigate the law and the general
practice, We ascertained officially that all the European LodgeR still continued the
ori!!'inal rule of one ballot only. We then addreRsed circulars to every Grand Lodge
in the United States, and found the three·ballot rule so greatly In the minority (being
less than one·third, and these comparatively yonng Grand Lodii;es,) that upon the
exhibition of thi• fact the old law was returned to and adopted by unanimous vote
In our Grand Lodge. Even·handed justice to every gentleman pre denting himself for
our mysteries required this.
The Grand Lodge of California long since adopted the system of a single ballot
for the three degrees. We regard the three-ballot rule as not only a violation of the
principle of justice to the applicant for the benefits of Masonry, but also en infraction
of the old and well-established custom of the Fraternity, and in contravention of
the interests of Masonry.
We cordially indorse the following, in his review of the proceedings of the Grand
Lodge of Arkansas relative to educational enterprises:Brethren, everywhere, confine your benevolence and beneficenM to the legitimate
works of. Masonry and pore charity; spend your money to relieve the wants and
necessities of our bretbren, and leave education to the States, all of whom are Cally
alive to the great importance of educating the masses, and are doing so faster and
better than yon can do it.
The Masonio Fraternity in the different States can better subserve the Interests of
the rising generation by encouraging education through the Instrumentality of our
public schools, than by the establishment of private enterprises at immense and often
hazardous expenditure of means that would result in much greater good If appro·
priated in supporting those requiring aid during their attendance at schools-good
schools-provided by the State. Enterprises of this nature have been undertaken In
several jurisdictions, bu1. in no case, so far as we are cognizant, have they been
successful,
Bro. SINGLETON expresses the opinion that, when a vote Is taken to dimit a mem·
ber, the act Is final, unless, under parliamentary rules, the vote should be reconsidered. We hold io the view that dimission is the Mt of the member himijelf, and
the term dimlt, or demit, is employed as the synonym of withdraw, Under our Oonstitution a member has the right to withdraw, provided he is In good standing, upon
paying his dues and giving notice to the Lodge, at a stated meeting, of his Intention
so to do. He cannot receive a recommendatory certificate of withdrawal without a
vote of the Lodge, but the act of withdrawal is that of the member. He formally
dimits, that Is, he formally relinquishes his membership In the particular Lodge, It
may be to join another Lodge, or it may be to sever his connection with the Oruer.
The Lodge has not the right nor the power to prevent his withdrawal, nor can it
restore him to membership, except by petition and the same process otherwise as
in the case of any non-affiliate. A motion to comummate the withdrawal Is not
necessary, but a motion is necessary to grant a certificate recommending him to
other Lodges.

Grand Master of Indiana, In which the reverse Is held; also the law of the District
of Columbia to the effect that any one may be admitted who is physically able to

November 8, 1799, WASHINGTON wrote to the Grand Lodge of Maryland that
" the principles and doc trio es of Freemasonry are founded in benevolence aod to be
exercised for the good of mankind."
Gen. W ABBINGTON never forgot Masonry when a soldier. He encouraged ail11
visited camp Lodges Bnd pa~ticipated in their labor, frequently officiatiog as Mastert
It was at the Old .Freemason's Tavern, on the Green of Morristown, N. J., in 17i7,
that Gen. WASHINGTON himself made LA FAYETTE a Freemason. Upon one occasip11
a detachment of the American A.rmy overcoming a British force, captured from them
the working tools, jewels and clothing of a military Lodge. Gen. W ABBINGTOK1
upon learning this, ordered restoration, declaring that "be waged oo war again9'
philanthropy and benevolenoe."
I have dwelt thus somewhat at length to show that Gen. WABBINGTON was devoted
to tho humane principles of Freemasonry from bis minority to his death, io publln
aod private life, and to show that it is especially appropriate for the Masons of this
country to participate in the imposing ceremonies of to-day. This ceremonr, is noo
ecclesiastical. It is the growth of a sentiment along the ages, aod, as such, w11leom4
mand the respect and admiration of mankind long after this monument shall have:
crumbled to the dust. Thus we find that the immortal WABBINGTON, himself a Freemason, devoted his band, his heart, his sacred honor, to the cause of freedom of con'
science, of speech, and of action; and from his successful leading bas arieen this
Nation. To him and the memory of his deeds a grateful people have erected this
memorial in the Capital which he founded, and which will bear his name to remotes~
ages ; a monument towering above other monuments as he towered above other
men.

of welcome pronounced by Grand Master PARKER:BRETHREN: After the lapse of nearly a century, a monoment erected to commemorate aod perpetuate the name and fame of a great man bas ·been dedicated. It
is Dot necessary that I should speak of bis private, his poblic, or his Masonic life.
Fitting eulogies of these virtues have found record through the willing pens !>f Lhe
historians. It is sufficient for me to say tha~ which every school boy knows aod
says: "He was the father of our country."

The Address of the Grand Master is a weU-JJre-pared document, devoted almost
altogether to matters pertaining to his own jurisdiction. He had answered ques·
tions of Masonic law and usage to the number of sever11l hundred. From this we
infer that either tho Mi.sters of the Lodges take little care to inform themselves on
the law and usage, or else that law and usage must be in a somewhat chaotic
state in Georgia. The Grand Master reports nineteen of the decisions rendered.
These are, doubtless, in accord with the fundamental Jaw in his jurisdiction,
inasmnch as the Grand Lodge endorsed the whole of them "as a sound and just
exposition of Masonic law and ueage.'' We, however, are unable to see them all In
that light. We quote one decision that certainly is not in consonance with such
Masonic law as we have been taught:A ballot is had upon an application for initiation. One black ball appears ; held,
first, by unanimous consent, further balloting m11y be postponed until the next reg·
ular Communication; second : that the appHcatlon, by unanimous consent, may be
withdrawn. The first ballot failing to elect or reject was equivalent to no ballot at
all. Now we observe that the ballot must be unanimous ; If so, one black-ball cloeB n·
ject and is a ballot. But, to guard against the possibility of mistake, It is a general ouatom, when but one black-ball is cast, immecHately to take a new ballot. An appll·
cation cannot be withdrawn after it has been once read, or, as in our jurisdiction,
after reference to a committee. This has become one of the fundamental usages of
the Fraternity. It cannot be reconsidered, for this would violate the secrecy of the
ballot; a motion to nconaider must come from one who has voted with the majority,
and to make known that he voted with the majority would make known how be
voted; this be is hot at liberty to do. We think that tlle Grand Master was in
error

A very great Improvement has been made by our Lodges, in the last few years,
ID acquiring the stBndard work, and now, upon visiting the humblest and poorest
furnished Lodges in the jurisdiction, accurate and impressive work will be witnessed,
ID4 you are no longer in doubt whether you are attending a Masonic Lodge or that
or 1ome· ot~er organization. Brethren return home from these schools of instruction
Dot only impressed with the advantages and beauties of correcl work, but with a
blgher appreciation of Freemasonry, and determined to more nearly exemplity, by
tileir lives and conduct, the principles which these ceremonies are intended to make
~~

'

We desire to add the testimony of our own observation and experience. In every
ID1tance where we have seen the Master and other officers imbued with a proper
unse of the importanll'e of the work and the manner of rendering It, we have seen
a llourishiog Lodge ; and equally true is it, that where apathy and indifference exist,
'here langaor and decay mark the affairs of the Lodge.
• The Grand Master reporte.d that, in response to a circular issued by him to the
nrlous Lodges, soliciting aid for the sufferers from the floods of the Ohio River and It.a
tributaries, he had received from the Lodges or the State the sum of $5,52' 40, and
l'rom other sources $656. Of this amount $300 had been returned to the brethren of
Nebraska; all the rest having been devoted to the noble purpose for which it was
provided.
.
It having been reported to the Grand Master that an organization called the
''Egyptian Rite of Memphis," and other organizations of a like character, were
oh~lmiog the right to organize" Blue Lodges," he had referred the matter to the
Oommittee on Foreign Correspondence. This committee, of whioh our able and
tlteemed brother, Past Grand Master THEODORill T. GURNEY, is" the beginning, the
end and the middle,'' after due investigation, made an elaborate report, which was
adopted almost unanimously by the Grand Lodge. As this Involves a question of very
1r11ve importance to the Oraft in this jurisdiction, we give the conclusion of Bro.
GllBNEY's report, which we consider as practically an endorsement of the Massachu·
1etts Departure:It is with pain and mortification that we find members of Lodges, presumably
'lrell advised of the fuo"dameotal principles at the b~ of our organized existence,
auuming to make Masons and organizing them into Lodges without remote oonstltu·
\Iona! authoritv. We most emphatically deny this assumption, and a.s an earnest of
the purpose of this Grand Lodge to maintain and defend rights that we hold to be
11ored and inviolable, It Is hereby proclaimed :Fi1·st. That persons can not be made Masons except by the act of a regular
Lodge, working under the jurisdiction and by the authority of a Grand Lodge doly
oonstituted by the repreresentatives of Lodges of Free and Accepted or Craft
Masons.
Second. That every association of Masons, of whatever name or degree, other
than that of the three degrees of Oraft Masonry heretofore described, that assumes
the right to congregate, initiate, pass and raise persons to the several degrees of said
t)raft or Symbolic Masonry, is clandestine, and is hereby so pronounced and
declared.
AND WHEREAS, The aforesaid 'E~yptlao Masonic Rite of Memphis,' of whloh
D~s1us WILBON is 'Grand Master, together with the 'Ancient and Primitive
Bite of Memphis,' of which ALEXANDER B. MOTT· is Grand Master, declare, by
both positive avowal and implication, that they and their organizations have an In·
berent right, by charters and otherwise, to establish Lodges for conferring the de·
1rees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason; therefore,
Besolvecl, That the said ' Egyptian Masonic Rite of Memphis,' and the said
'Ancient and Primitive Rite of Memphis,' and all other associations of persons ot
'll'hatever degree or name (other than Lodges of Free and Accepted, Symbolio or
tlrRft Masons , and the Grand Lodges duly constituted by the representatives of such
Lodges), that shall arrogate to themselves th·e authority, under any circumstances or
aonditions, to confer the degrees of Symbolic or Craft Masonry, to-wit: Entered Ap·
prentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason, or whose charters, constitutions, laws,
tdlcts or decrees shall assume, or permit the powers organized under them to as·
Jome, the authority to constitute Lodges, or Bodies of any other name, for the oon·
f1rring the said three degrees of Symbolic or Craft Masenry, are clandestine Bodies
within the meaning of the fundamental law of Masonry; and with their constituents,

One of the designs of the framers of our Constitution, in conferring upon the
Master of a Lodge the power to determine, when charges are preferred against a.
brother, whether those charges constitute a Masonic offense or not, was manifestly
to prevent any publicity being given in the Lodge in reference to the charges o~ to
the brother charged. Besides, the Master b.eing presumed to 'lie familiar with the
law, is the proper party to determine whether the charges are of such 11 nature as, if
proven, would constitute a. Masonic offense. It might happen, and, doubtless, often
would happen, that the brethren would be unable to adjudicate 11 matter of that
nature. It is presumed that the Master of a Masonic Lodge is one in whom the
brethren can repose confidence, both so far as Intelligence and integrity are con•
oerned, and it is certainly desirable that a brother should, so far as possible, be
shielded from undue publicity; to this end, commissioners elected to try 11 case are,
under our law, supposed to be Ignorant .of the party accused until the time of the
trial. The plan of procedure Is one calculated, in the most equitable and Impartial
manner, to mete justice to the individual brother, without prejudicing him in the
eyes of his brethren if found guiltless. To avoid useless and vexatious trials, 11 similar method is employed in civil life. Whether or not the matter complailled of con·
stitutes an offense is not left to the judgment of a. jury or of the public, but to
that of a. committing magistrate' or a grand jury.
Bro. GURNEY thinks that a brother may be put upon trial a second time for the
same offense, arguing that 11 trial In Masonic Jurisprudence differs from one in civil
courts. "The civil statute is t'or the protection and maintenance of political government, whlle Masonic Jurisprudence can only exist for the protection of Its good.
name." We think he is right, inasmuch as the object of a Masonic trial is simply
the eliciting of the truth.
Our namesake, Bro. Taos. H.B. ANDlllBSoN, IH complimented upon the character
of his report, from which frequent quotations are made.
Under Kentucky, Bro. Gu&NlllY avers that" there Is no such thing as a' right to
Lodge assistance or Masonio burlal,'-11 right that can be enforced under any construction of law In the premises.'' Very true, If he alludes to rights that could be en·
forced by the laws of the land. All rights originate out of, and have, their corres·
ponding duties. The rights of Masonry, as we understand them, are social rights;
such are the rights to Lodge assistance and Masonic burial, and every Mason can
claim them. Masonry enjoins upon every one the duty to relle'l'e the distressed,
and to render unto him "every kind office which justice or mercy may require "-to
do unto him as, in similar circumstances, we would have him do unto us. Every
Mason, certainly, has 11 right to claim the dlsoharge of every Masonic duty on the part
of his brethren, so long as he deports himself In accordance with the rules and reg·
ulations of the Fraternity. It Is In this sense that we understand the term "rights,"
as used in Masonry, e.nd we are of the opinion that the laws of the Fraternity
possess sanctions, for without sanction law Is not law, The Grand Lodge is the
primal tribunal by means of which these rights are enforced, or by means of which
brethren are compelled to observe the discharge of their duties. Brethren pay into
the.treasuries of our Lodges their fees and dues, with the understanding that in dis·
tress it is the duty of the Lodg~s to relieve them, and to render unto them justice
and mercy ; thus, even the pecuniary prerogative seems to be established.
Under Nebraska, Bro. GUBNlllY quotes the conclusion of Grand Master WA.BREN'S.
Address, and adds:Every man's value to his race will be measured, in time and eternity, by the con·
tributions he makes to the general welfare. There is nothing of sentimentality In
the remarks of the Grand Master. Manhood should be the aim of every Mason.
Every precept and principle of the Fraternity points to such consummation; and
ahould we fall of any achievement In the line of our professions, we have lived
In vain, and to be forgotten the moment mother earth closes over our worthless
remains. Live within the Bhekinah, brethren, and we shall see 11 glory reflected
from the Lodge that w!ll call out benedictions from cottage and palace.

We concur in the opinion expressed by Bro. GURNEY, in his comments upon the
reasons given by Grand Master FARNELL, of Nebraska, why the Grand Lodge of
New South Wales shonld be recognized. We do not believe that a Grand Lodge
formed by less than a majority of all the Lodges in the particular territory should
be recognized. We go farther, and assert, as our opinion, that it is discourteous, at
least, for any Grand Lodge to recognize any new Grand Lodge until the consent of
the parent Grand Lodge has been obtained, unless such Grand Lodge exhibits an
undue opposition to recognition upon the presentation of proper reasons.
We dissent from the opinion expressed by Bro. GURNEY, in his review of New
Jersey, to the effect that the burial of a Mason Is 11 courtesy but not 11 right. Our
jurisdiction holds that "every Master Mason, who is in good standing at the time
of his death, is entitled to be buried with Masonic honors, and that the Master ()fa1
Lodge has no discretion to determine whether he should or;ahould not be so buried. '
We believe with Bro. MACKEY that "the right to be conducted to hiR last home by
· his brethren, and to be committed to his mother earLh with the ceremonies of the
Order, Is one, that, under certain restrictions, belongs to every Master :M.ason."
It la true, "there is not any law that is properly mandatory upon the subject;"
yet, by implication from regulations handed down as a custom in Masonry for a
century and 11 half, the right has been definitely established. Besides, the admission
of Bro. GUBNEY himse!I (under Oregon) is contradictory of the proposition " that
the burial of a Mason is 11 courtesy." He there claims that an unajftliated contributor
"pays his money to acquire, as the law understands it, the right to be cared for in
distress, and the fnrther right to bb cared for in death."
There are very many other interesting matters in this excellent report, but we
have already exceeded our limit. There are in this jurisdiction six hundred and
eighty Lodges, having a membership of thirty-nine thousand five hundred and sixty•
five. The M.·. W.'. JOHN R. THOMAS WllB elected Grand Master, and the B.-.

IOWA.
The forty-second Annual Commnnlcatlon of the Grand Lodge of Iowa was held in
the city of Cedar Rapids, commencing on the second day of June, 1885,-the M. ·· W.·.
CHARLES T. GRANGER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.•. THEODORE S. PAR.VIN being Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from a majority of the
Lodges.
For aymmetry and beauty of design, for system and order, commend us to Bro.
PABVIN, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Iowa; for excellence in execntlon,
to EGBERT, FIDLAR & CHAMBERS, printers, binders 11nd blallk book makers, Davenport, Iowa. The volume before us is simply superb in its ev'9ry feature.
.An address of welcome to the Grand Lodge was delivered t>y the ex-Mayor, C. W•
EATON, Esq., which was happily responded to by the Grand M~ster.
The Address of the Grand Master is 11 paper of great merit, b~ut is confined almos\
exclusively to matters of local import. No question is deeme11~ as h11ving greate~
demand for consideration than has that of discipline. The Gran d Master regard•
the law relative to discipline as defective, and reoommends that ii:'" be so changed
that 11 conviction may be had by means of a majority vote instead ~ f a two-thlrdl
vote. He thinks that there Is" but one defense to the present law-ce1 ·talnty of not
convicting the innocent." We prefer the plan adopted in California-th& t of trial by
commissioners elected for the purpose, no vote of the Lodge being require d for conviction or acquittal, but simply a majority vote of all the commission, with right of
appeal to the Grand Lodge on the part of either the accused or the accuser,
·
The Grand Master very properly condemns hasty legislation, especially re. 'ative
to amendments to the constitution and by-laws, and suggests that the by-laws sh~ 'Uld
be so amended that no action can be had by the Grand Lodge on the report of tL 'le
Committee on Jurisprudence, relative to amending the by-laws, on the same day on
which the report is presented. This we regard as a 'Very timely and proper suggestion. It not unfrequently happens in Grand Lodges, as in legislative bodies, that
Important measures are brought before the body during the closing hours, and are
thus deprived of that scrutiny to which they should be subjected. Important matters.
are apparently often presented towards the close of a session in order to make their
adoption more certain.
"For ways that are peculiar" a Lodge in Iowa must be noted. One J. K. PowERS had applied to Mt. Nebo Lodge to be made 11 Mason. Now, Mr. POWERS ha(} but
one arm. The Lodge pursued the ushal methods to determine his fitness, and he was
accepted as good material for the work. .The first and second degrees were con·
ferred upon him, when tbe Master and Wardens of Bome Iiodge interposed an objeo·
tion to his further advancement for the reason that he had lost his right arm. "The
Grand Master addressed an order to the Master of Mt. Nebo Lodge to desist from.

advancing the brother until further orders. He afterwards revoked this order
"guarding the action by an expression that the order was in no manner to be con'.

Mast~r:s Address reported that there is a eerlous defect In the Grand Lodge By-Laws;
that it 1s a well known fact that the qualifications of oandldates, as set forth In " The
Oharges of a Freemason," are much too obscure and uncertain; and th11t there is

We opine that the Grand Lodge of Califarnia would have shortly concluded that a'
Lodge accepting such a candidate was not possessed of sufficient common sense to
entitle it to hold a charter. The members of Mt. Nebo Lodge do not ha1>:e access
to the able reports of Bro. PABVIN, or having access, fall to avail themselves of such
a valuable means for Informing themselves.
Grand Secretary PARVIN presented his forty-second report. It Is a document
worthy of the knowledge and ability gained by so long a period of successful experience. We quote the opening paragraph:" Dare to do right, dare to be true;
You have a work that none other can do.
Do It so bravelv, so kindly, so well,
That others will hasten the story to tell."
With the words of the poet echoing In oar ears, we have labored the past year as
never ~efor~, to build both wisely and well, and have the house set In order for the
reception ot the guests who come to this annual feast.
. .We write this rep or! beneath the roof erected to shelter the ofllcerR whose labors,
1f rightly conducted, will redound to the honor and the good of the Order for which
the house was builded. In this, as in all the past labors wherein we have served
you for more than two score years," Love has been the source, duty the law of my life "
and the result Is with you, as you enter these wnlls to-day, my bre;hren.
Truly, our good brother has reason to be proud of his efforts In securing for the
Grand Lodge of Iowa so noble a structure as the Grand Lodge Library Building Is
represellted to be, and of being Instrumental In collecting what Is regarded as the
grandest and moat complete Masonic I,lbrary on the continent.
Bro. PABVIN pays a beautiful tribute of respect to the memory of Bro. WILLIA.IC
JAMES REESE, Past Grand Master of Ohio, " the early friend and companion of bis
youth."
Forty-eight years of active", etllcient and honorable service upon the part of Bro.
PARVIN, in the good work of Masonry, bears evidence that whatever defect may have
otherwise existed, there certainly has been none In head or in heart. It will be said
of so faithful a one : "The paseage of time 111 steadfastly making his faults more
superficial and accidental, and his merits more striking and pleasing.''
As Librarian, Bro. PARVIN presents a very full report, showing the condition of
t.his noble enterprise to be most healthful. Iowa Masons have abundant reason to
be proud of the grand structure erected by their mnnificenoe, and doubly so of the
e.xtensive ooll.eotion of valuable works. Bro. PARVIN has had sole charge of the
library In all its details, and, by his zeal and ability In its management, he has not
only erected an enduring monument for himself, but has created an instrumentality
of good whose benefloent lnfiuenoe will be sweet incense to his faithfulness in all the
years.

The followlug case seems to us to be 11 novel, and, to say the least, peculiar way

seemed to do well for a time. 'l'hen all the members but one concluded tbat that one
was, out of spite, determined to blaok·bali every candidate and that no good ooald
come from the longer existence of that J.odge. I would willingly have permitted
the Lodge to p;o down, but for the fact that a strnng body of yrofessed worshiper• of
God were leavirig their own work •;ndone to fight the Lodge.
After mature reflection and with some misgivings, I Informed that Lodge that,
If their entire membership would request the smrender of dispensation and all but
one petition for a new J.odge, selecting the Harne three principal officers, I would
grant a dispensation, They took such action on September 20th. I granted 11 dispensation as Phainlx, U. D., the Lodge first certifying to me the work they had done,
and upon my certificate they have reorganized ( Qu. recognized?) the Entered Appren·
tices nnd Fellow Oraf't~, which have been made therein. I turned over to them all

The rule requiring the proceedings of the Grand Lodge to be read In the aeveral
subordinate Lodges, seems to have met with little favor, and to have been generally
ignored. We agree with the Grand :Master that" If the proceeding• were read and
our laws studied with a tithe of the care bestowlld upon the esoteric work, the Craft
would be benefited and the po1itlon or Grand :Master would become loss of a
drudge; " but we doubt the expediency of requiring the proceedinga to be read In
the Lodgea. To read a volume auoh as Is that of Kansas this year, would require
more time than any Lodge could well devote to such recreatiou.
The Grand Master thinks that the time has come when, wlthput detriment, the Past
Master's degree can be laid aside e.s a useless ornament. Our Grand Lodge requires
the degree to be conferred, (probably only because it Is an old oastom,) but per·
aonally we are Inclined to agree with Grand Master BuoK. We have not been able
to discover any material beneftt accruing either to the Master or to the Lodge from
the conferrlug of the degree.
A number of decisions are reported by the Grand Master. With reference to the
first we remark that it has been held in California:First. "That the Master of a Lodge has no power to authorize a Past Master to
open a Lodge and perform work during the absence of himself and Wardens; and
that the Lodge cannot be opened except by or under the direction and with the
presence of the Master or one of the Wardens."
Second. "That, In the absence of the Master and Wardens, the Lodge cannot be
opened, even for th& burial of a brother, but that any Mason may, on such an
occasion, read the burial 1ervice."
His third decision, that members are not required to give any reason for request·
Ing a dimlt, is in consonance with our practice.
A dimitted member can visit any Lodge in this jurisdiction so long as he is In
1tanding. After the expiration of six months a dimitted Mason is out of standing,
and has no right to visit, until he applies to some Lodge for affiliation.
His fifth, that a Lodge Is duly opeaed, notwithstanding •tlie three lesser lights are
not in position and burning, we see no cause to cavil with.
