Commenting upon Bro. ANDERSON'S opinions of the prerogatives of a Grand
Master, Bro. BROWN says:Well, in Kansas there have been slight Indications In days past of a similar spirit,
bnt no attempt to give it full sway, even in a single Instance. Should a Grand
Master venture on the experiment," roastinf{" would be cool punishment coaipared
with the hot bath to which he would be eubJeote<!. Conet.itntlonR were made for all,
for the Grand Master no lees than for the youngest apprentice In the oorth·eaet corner of the Lodge, and after their adoption, prerogative was relegated to the rubbish
heap, where it should be left to repose and rot.
His opinion on the doctrine of "perpetual jurisdiction" is equally specific, and
meets >tlth our nnqoalified approval :Upon the question of perpetual jurisdiction we stand where we havealwayutood,
it.a uncompromising foe, because it le not and never was a landmark, but principally
because it is unjust, and, when exercised, rank tyrallny. We believe its davs are
numbered, and shall rejoice when the knell of its departure rolls through the land.
Bro. BROWN condemns the resolution which was presented In the last Grand
Lodge of <Jonnecticut and laid over until the next Annual Communication, to the
effe<Jt that no Lodge shall grant a dimit to any member until he has been accepted
by another, and hopes that the Grand Lodge of Connecticut will defeat the regula·
tion. The passage of such a regulation would debar the affiliation of any Connecticut
Mason with a Lodge in California, as, by our laws, the dimlt must be presented with
the application. .A.ny compulsory method of causing a person to continue his membership in a Lodge, or in the Fraternity, is unwise and contrary to the spirit of our
Order. There are many and weight.)' reasons why one mav sever his connection
with the institution even, why not with a particular Lodge? The particular ohar·
acter of the individual or of the Lodge may make It exceedingly desirable and bene·
flcial to both Lodge and member that he should withdraw. Masonry interferes with
no man's opinions. One may at the time of his joining believe all that he Is required
to believe in Masonry; subsequently he may conscientiously be led to the belief that
his former opinions were incorrect. The good of the brother and of M111onry de·
mands that such a one should be permitted to go in peace-voluntarily, as he entered.
His duty, his interests, many of the varied necesaities of life may compel a brother
to change his domicile; why should a Lodge prevent him from adopting a new .Ma·
sonic home, from renouncing his allegiance to a particular Lodge, that he may be
more happily and benetlcially situated, or even from renouncing his allogfance to the
Fraternity, if conscientiously he regards it as his duty to do so?
The regulation of our Grand Lodge on the subject of rejected candidates is In ao·
eordance with the views expressed by Bro. BROWN. After a period of twelve months a
rejected candidate can apply to the same Lodgp, or to any other Lodge withiQ. whose
jnrisdiction he resides1 without petitioning the rejecting Lodge. We heartfly endorse
the following :Nothing is truer, as every Grand Secretary knows, than that an intellfgent and
prompt officer makes a five Lodge ready fnr all good works. Yet by a means little
above the practice of the ring caucus, men get Into offices which they are not competent to fill, and, in order to bide their Inability, defer the work which duty requires
them to perform, or if they attempt It, do It iii such a way as to excite contempt, If
not disgust. We now say, as we have often said, put' none bnt the best men Into
office, and when that is done sustain them with the good will and energy becoming
Masons.

The reports of the Grand Treasnrer, Bro. li&LLBR, the Grand Lecturer, Bro,
BBAEFFER, and the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence are all favorably
noticed. Bro. STATON, however, takes issue with Bro. ANDERSON relative to the
action of the Grand Lodge of Massacbusettl! in regard to higher degrees. He says:Our judgment is that the less such things are stirred, the better for Symbolic.
:Masonry. We do not believe that Grand Lodges of Symbolic Masonry should be
made the battle-ground for contending rights of so called higher degrees. As Master Masons, we know nothing about their legitimacy or illegitimacy. If Symbolic
Masonry is to be uprooted by the contentions of these rival rites, It would be better
to overturn everything beyond the three first degrees in Masonry, and let us g.e t
back to first principles. All tJJ.at is practical is embraced in Symbolic Masonry, and
the balance Is tinsel and show.
We are of the opinion that the Grand Lodge of Massachusett8-bellev1ng that
boldly advertising In the public prints for candidates for these degrees, and that the
hawking of such degrees by irresponsible and unscrupulous persons for their own
emolument was calculsted to bring discredit upon the Oraft,-dld right In prohibitini
Masons from the illicit traffic. If a Grand Lodge has no power or right to enforce
Its own edicts, to protect its Freemasonry among the brethren, to exclude
what it may deem wrong, to enforce its recognitions and exclusions, and to prevent
Individuals from prostituting it to disgraceful and profane purposes, then what ia
the object or benefit of having a Grand Lodge! If a handful of " schismatios and
disturbers" can defy a Grand Lodge in one particular, what is there to prevent them
from doing so in others? If the principles of the Symbollo Lodges are to he made
the standard of admission to unrecognized higher deirees, what is there to prevant
their being employed as the basis of any organization, however objectionable? We
believe it to be a duty that a Grand Lodge owes to the membership of snbordlnate
Lodges to protect them from the Imposition, the pecuniary loo, and the mortifl·
cation which would ultimately result in distrust of one .another instead of that conll·
dence, respect, and harmony whlcb conRtitutes the strength of our Fraternity.
Divers papers and pamphlets had been received from the Grand Orient of Spain;
the Independent Grand Lodge of Symbolic Masonry, Sevllle, Spain ; the Grand Lodge
of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Portngal, etc., eto. No action, however,
was taken relative to the matters therein contained. The Chairman of the Com·
mitt.ee on Correspondence presented resolutions relative to and recommending the
recognition of the Grand Lodge of South Australia and the Grand Lodge of Pern;
also recommending that the recognition heretofore accorded to the Grand Lodi& of
the Island of Ouba be transferred to the United Grand Lodge of Colon and the
Island of 011ba, the unhappy strife between them having been amicably adjusted.
The resolutions were, however, at the request of the chairman, laid over until the
Annual Communication of 1886.
There is much of Interest In Bro. STATON'B valuable review which we would like to
notice, but time and space will not permit, and hence, regretfully, we must part com·
pany. The general soundness of sentiment expressed by our good brother has been
pleasing to us. We wish that our brethren of this jurisdiction could enjoy the
same opportunity for profit and pleasure that we have whilst engaged on this beautiful volume,-a volume, by the way, still more Interesting to us from a knowledge
of the faot, indicated on its title page, that it was entirely printed .at the Wido.wa
and Orphans' Home. God bless and prosper the Institution that is engaged in auch
noble work, and with it the good brethren who are In the true spirit endeavorlni to
support it.

LOUISIANA.
The seventy-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana was
commenced in the city of New Orleans on the ninth day of February, 1885,-the
M.·. w.·. JAMES L. LOBDELL, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. w.·. JAMES c.
BATCHELOR, M. D., being Grand Secretary. Fifty-two chartered Lodges were represented. The proceedings are prefaced with a portrait and sketch of the life of the
Grand Master.
The Address of the Grand Master is a well-prepared paper of very considerable
length, in which he adverts to many topics, mainly of a local nature. He pays re·
spectful tribute to the memory of several distinguished Masons of his own and other
jurisdictions, whom death had carried to his silent mansions. Many letters had
been received asking for information upon various points of Masonic law and usage.
As in other jurisdictions, very many of the questions asked were such as were fully
answered in the by-laws of the Grand Lodge. It seems to us a reflection upon the
intelligence, or the attention and industry, of Masters of Lodges, to find that so
many questions are propounded to our Grand Masters, Grand Secretaries, and Grand
Lecturers upon trivial points, or upon such matters as are fully answered in the laws
and proceedings of the Grand Lodges.
It appears, from a decision of the Grand Master, that a law obtains In the juris·
diction of Louisiana. which forbids any Lodge to remit any pa.rt of the dnes of a
member who had been suspended for the non-payment of dues. It occurs to us that
such a provision is calculated to work hardship to worthy brethren, perpetually de·.
barring them from the benefits of the Fraternity.
The Grand Mastel' represents the financial condition of the Grand Lodge as encouraging, the balance of assets being $112,160. The "Overflow Relief Pund" has
unfortunately become a bone of contention, and there seems to be a disposition to
appropriate it to any purpose, even .to the payment of per capita tax and dues of
impoverished Lodges.
For very proper reasons the Grand Master had, in every case, declined to answer letters from members of Lodges asking questions up.on almost every subject.
We think he acted wisely. Members of Lodges should recognize the fact that
Grand Masters, !'rand Secretaries and Grand Lecturers have not been elected for
the purpose of answering the thousand and one questions that curious, querulous, or
ignorant partijjB think proper to ask. If a Master rules contrary to their opinions,
many hie themselves to the Grand Officers. hoping for comfort, and feel themselves
aggrieved if they fail to receive a reply.
The Grand Mastet recommended that a member, suspended for non-payment of
dues, be reinstated on the payment of his arrearages without. a vote of the Lodge,
and the Committee on Masonic Law and Jurisprudence recommended the adoption
of a regulation to that effect; but the Granrl Lodge refused, by a large majority, to
make any change. As the Jaw now stands a brothel' suspended must pay his arrear·
ages, and can only be reinstated by a two-third vote. Should the brother fail to
obtain such a vote, he would be deprived of his rights and privileges as a Ma.son,
a.rid thus be subjected to a penalty more severe than expulsion would be. We
deem this action of the Grand Lodge unwise and wrong.
The Grand Master also recommended the repeal of tbe edict authorizing Grand
Masters to exercise their discretion in the matter of allowing Ma.sonic Lodges jointly
to occupy halls with other societies; but no action thereupon seems to have been
ta.ken by the Grand Lodge.
"ro a communication trom Feliciana Lodge, No. 31, of that Jurisdiction, relative
to the request of Mount Moriah Lodge, No. 44, of San Francisco, for payment of
the funeral expenses of H. H. KKEBING, a member of Feliciana Lodge, who
was on his way to New Zea.land, and died in San Francisso, the Grand Masin re-

1885.J

Grand Lodge of California.

101

piled that it was a matter in which he could do no more than give his opinion, which
was that such a claim was not actually legal: "a Lodge cannot and should not be
oompelled, by any Masonic Law, to pay a debt they had no part in contracting."
Tbe facts, in this case, seem not to have been presented to the Grand Master.
Mount Moriah Lodge simply performed the service for the Masonic Boa.rd of Relief
of San Francisco, and hence had no claim against Feliciana Lodge. 'l'ho Secretary
of that Board telegraphed to the proper officer of Feliciana Lodge, wishing to know
if the brother was in good standing, and if the Board should bury hiifi. The reply was
1nmewhat curt-" You may bury him, if you wish." The Board construed this as
equivalent to a request to bury him, and did so, Mount Moriah Lodge taking charge
of the body in behalf of the Board. The Board then sent the bill of expenses to
Feliciana Lodge, by which the payment was declined on the ground that they were
not in the practice of asking the return of any sums expended in Masonic charity, and
that they had not auLhorized the contracting of any expense. They further stated
that they had been subjected to such outlay in behalf of strangers in their own midst,
brothers of the Order, that they were unable to pay the claim, and laid the matter
before the Grand Master of their jurisdiction. It is true that there is no law upon
the statute·hooks of Masonry that would compel the payment of this claim; but there
Is a higher law in the moral code. We do not think it right or just that the Ma·
sonic Board of Relief of San Francisco should provide for all distressed Masons in
their midst without any remuneration, nor is the Board able to do so. A Lodge is
morally responsible for the aid and support of its own membership when in distress,
and so the Lodges of this jurisdiction bold and practice. The Board of Relief of
San F'rancisco is mainly supported by a voluntary tax on the Lodges of the city.
These Lodges are responsible for the care of their own members, and not a <lollar
of the Board's funds is expended in their behalf. If the Board must, without return,
In a city like San Francisco, relieve the distressed and bury the dead, the time must
soon come when this noble source of benefaction must itself be buried. It should
he a cause of thankfulness, as well as for return, on the part of ll'elioiana Lodge,
that her membership are cared for when found here in distress-for a return that the
means of heneflceut charity may be continued. We do not think that the Lodge
haR, in this matter, acted up to the letter or the spirit of that law, "Do unto others as
ye would that they should do unto you."
The Report of the Grand Secretary is a production very full in detail, and evincing great care in its preparation. Several Lodges are reported as having forfeited
their charters, and a number had surrendered theirs. The report shows the finances
of the Grand Lodge to he in a flourishing condition.
Bro. RICHARD LAM;BERT, Secretary of Louisiana Relief Lodge, No. 1,. reported that
the sum of $1,273.45 had been distributed in re\ief to applicants from a number' of
Jurisdicti'ons, among the others, $!6 to applicants from California. We trust that
the same has been returned, and feel confident that it has been, if asked for and the
recipients were in good standing.
The Special Committee of the Grand Lodge on Louisiana Relief Lodge, No. 1,
reported that they had communicated with all the Grand Jurisdictions in the United
States in reference to their systems of relief, and had received replies from about
one-half. The "Masonic Lodge of Relief," of the city of Baltimore, is represented
as the model body amongst those heard from. No report of the system of relief
adopted by the several Boards in this State was received, but from an examiQation
of those plans reported, we feel confident that the methods of relief employed here
will compare favorably with the best. Many of the .)'urlsdictions have no organized
system of relief, each Lodge attending to its own applicants. For the information of
our brethren in other jurisdictions we will say that, in California, Boards have been

TheRe are all formed by mutual compact of tbe Lodges in those places, and their
funds are derived from 11 per capita tax on the. membership, 11 specified sum for each
degree conferred, liberal contributions from the Grand Lodge, amounts returned by
beneficiaries, and from miscellaneous sources. The Boards are composed of the
Masters (with sometimes other officers) of the Lodges in the respective cities, who
select from their own body 11 President and Treasurer, and 11 Secretary from their
own body or otherwise as they may determine. The Boards hold weekly meetings,
at which the cases requiring relief are presented, and such cases as require continued attention are referred to 11 p'artloular member, whose dnty it is carefully to
look to their wants, and to render such assistance as may be required. During the
thil'ty years of its existence, (to and including 1885,) the San Francisco Board of
Relief has expended, in the relief of distressed Masons, their widows and orphans,
the sum of $217,234 97, and this is but 11 part of the noble work which these Boards
are doing. The Grand Lodge shows its appreciation of the beneficent work of these
organizations by the liberal manner in which It has always contributed of Its
fonds to the support thereof. As an illustration of the esthnation in which the Grand
Lodge holds the work which the Boards are doing, at the last Communication it
cheerfully voted the sum of $4,000 to the Board or Relief of San Francisco, $400 to
that of Oakland, and $300 to that of Los Angeles; and it is probable that this year
the appropriations will be very much larger. It is hut jnst to add that as the work
of these Boards becomes better known, It is more fully appreciated by the Grand
Lodge and the brethren of the jurisdiction.
Monday, the ninth day of February, having been chosen by the Grand Master of
Masons of the State of Louisiana as Freemasons' Day at the Exposition, was duly
celebrated. The ceremonies were public, and were conc\ncted in the presence·of 11
large assemblage of Masons and others convened in the body of the Music Hall.
Addresses of welcome were delivered by Grand Master LOBDELL and Grand Senior
Warden BuoK, and were responded to by the M.·. W.·. Bro. FURNAS, ex-Governor of
Nebraska, and the M.·. W.·. Bro. YouNG, ex-Governor or Ohio. The addresses were
brief, but replete with beautiful, brotherly, instructive and happily expressed sent!·
ments. Among other good thing~, the Grand Master said:Fell.ow-citizens and Brother Masons: It is not usual for Masons, in extending
fraternal greeting. to emplc,y this dual form of address; but there is 11 special sig·
niflcance in this occasion which separates it from ordinary meetings of f'elluwship
and hospitl!.lity. Yon have come from the four quarters of the edrth to participate
in the civic celebration, which not only marks 11 new· era in the development and
progress of our individual commonwealth, but also furnishes 11 glorious epoch in the
progress and evolution of the race. Yon have not come merely as Masons, but, as
the Queen of Sheba and the dwellers from all parts of the land, far and near, came
to behold that mystic temple raised in unparalleled magnificence, without the sound
of hammer or implement of iron, so yon h11.ve come from continent and island, trom
marts of trade and agrarian districts, to join in thi\!,graud festival of peace.
Masonic brethren are here assembled between whom, 11 few years ago, rolled II
gulf of fire, kindled by civil strife; but to-day their hands and hearts are united, the
memories of the past have paled away, and wretched anger and hate have given
place to graceful competition in the kindly offices of peace. Loyalty to country and
11 willing submission to the mandates of its lawful rulers are of the cardinal doctrines
of Masonry; but there was a time when, battling from 11 just conviction of right, our
brothers met in deadly conflict upon the field of war, Victor and vanquished forgot
their strife in acts of mutual benefaction inspired by Masonic teaching, In these
times of peace the divine lesson of love to God and our fellow men, inculcating the
principles of friendship and morality, prevail, to the encouragement of stability in
civil alfairs, tLe arts and sciences, and the promotion of our nob le mission as apos·
ties of the Mystic Order. Whether peace prevail or war rage, the benign influence
of our institution will always be effective.
Fellow-citizens from the world, I welcome you. Brethren of the mystic tie from
every clime and nation, I welcome you. I know that you speak in tongues unknown
to one another, but you all comprehend the universal lan!!uage of Freemasonry.
Some of you have come from the kingdom where FREDERICK THE GREAT, as Grand
Master of the Masons of Prussia, encouraged the Fraternity ; some from the sunny

If space permitted we would reproduce the general refiections of the Grand
Master. We must quote the following as containing sentiments that should be vividly
impressed on the mind of every Mason :-.
It is a self·evident truth that the character of every institution is moulded by the
moral and social standard of the individuals composing the membership. Assuming
such to be the fact, it is obvious then to every intelligent Mason that Freemasonry
has derived her greatest popularity from the moral and social worth of her members.
As proof of this, it is only necessary to examine her lists, where we shall find the
names of men illustrious in the affairs of government, in educational institutions, aod
in all the benevolent enterprises and business relations of the world. I assert, then,
that the Institution has drawn to it such men as have given it dignity and character,
and being entitled to their confideuce and support, it has won their love and !)evotion.
To you, Masters and Wardens, I would say that, if .vou desire your Lodges to
flourish and command the respect of the best ritizens ot your town or city, you must
insist on a degree of moral worth and exalted manhood that can admit of no doubt.
Suffer no man to be admitted, and to enjoy your presence, whose life cannot be tested
and found reasonably perfect by the square, level and plumb. If you desire a true
manhood in your Lodges, you must insist on such a manhood when admitting mem·
hers; and if we want to command the respect of the pure and good, we must, as
individuals, conduct ourselves so as to win it. Me.sons should not forget that the
daily life of a man is the ind.ex of his character.

And this from the response by the Rev. Bro. WILLIAM R. ALGER:Ooe of the most profound thinkers and writers of our age has given currency
to a question which has been often asked: Is life worth living? It has been very
easily replied to, in a double sense : That depends upon the liver. If yon have
a healthy liver, and ·good, sound digestion, and all things go along without discord,
life is worth living; and if not, we are tempted to cast it off, even unbidden. Then,
in tbe other sense, whether life is worth living depends upon him who lives it.
Some men find life not worth living; others have found it tolerably easy to endure ;
and some, I am happy to believe, find it an Inestimable privilege and delight to be
alive. They are ready to exclaim, " How goodly a thing it is to behold the light of
the sun; how pleasant it is to look upon the fiowers, and inhale their perfume; to
meet our brethren and take their hands, and listen to their voices and let them hear
ours, and to think of God and the illimitable eternity, and the glories which are con·
tained in those two words, God and Eternity, which furnish gtonnd for unwearying
thanksgiving and exultation I" There is no fallacy profounder, and I am afraid there
is none more common, than that which we are tempted to yield to, that everybody
is like everybody else ; that there is very little difference in human beings, and that
they are all about the same thing. There is an infinite difference in human beings.
There never were two alike in the world ; never will be, till the end of time, two
who were just alike. It is one of the standing miracles of the human face that,
though not larger than your hand, no two faces and features are alike. There is the
human voice, and all human beings in the world sing or speak; but there are no two
alike. There is also vastly more difference in the experience of human beings.
Brethren, let me commend to you to cherish this idea, that there is an illimitable
and indescribable difference in the experience In life of every human being from
that of all other human beings; and, however narrow, however unsatisfactory, how·
ever mean and trying our experience may be, we may find a spring of consolation
and joy in the fa.ct, that though our experience may be a pretty small and poor thing
now, yet there are millions of others to whom it maybe perfectly glorious, and we
may outgrow ours and come into theirs in an indefinite degree. There are to us
these grounds for hope, and encouragement, and joy ; but if we think that all are
alike, we shall be tempted to cry out that life is not worth living.
And thia, from the response of the Grand Secretary, Bro. NroKERSON, illustrating
so well the truism, "many mickles make a mockle."

the provinces, two shillings to the Grand Lodge and two to the Provincial Grand

How can you better distinguish wisdom and folly than bv this sign-that the
wise man knows all he tells, while the fool tells all he knows? The landmark of
Masonic secrecy which has come down through the ages is a Mentor of prudence
and circumspection in character. To decide what should be revealed, and what
concealed; to weigh possibilities and consider conseq_uences:; to regard relations and
obligations; all this is culture of the judgment, and imparts firmness and decision to the mind. Were this the solitary benefit of our secret tradition, I would
cherish it as an invaluable instrumentality for education. The mysteries I admit;
but that mischief lurks behind them I deny. Time enough for those who misunderstand them to decry them when they can trace disorders to the door of the
Lodge. Their trail does nQt lie that way; for which reason we, who have the
matter under our own control, may be expected to speak when the inclination takes
us, and to be silent when when we are in the silent moed.
We regret that our space does not permit more copious extracts from this
beautiful oration.

is as follows:Can 11 brother, under charges, who is notoriously obnoxious to the members of his
Lodge, be refused admission by the W.·. Master?
Answer. The w.·. Master is justified in refusing such brother admission if he
was so notoriously bad and obnoxious that members would not sit with him. : I
would say that the W. ·• Master may act in his discretion, but will be answerable for
any arbitrary abuse of his power. Of course, no written law can be found justifying
such a course, but a complete justification is found in the necessities of the case. It
jg a question of the life of the Lodge, and that is of more consequenoe than the assertion of any individual brother's rights.

While we think the Grand Master to be correct in the foregoing, in his eleventh
decision we do not oonour; it is as follows:Qnestion. Is a brother Master Mason, In good standing and clear on the books,
entitled to 11 dimit, and is a Lodge obliged to grant him a dimit?
Answer. A Lodge is not bound to grant 11 dimit under any clroumstanoes. An
application for dimit shall be submitted to the Lodge. If the Lodge votes in favor
of granting It, that is the end of the matter. If the Lodge declines to grant it, there
Is no power to compel its issue.
Our law is that "a member of 11 Lodge, In good standing and whose dues are
paid, ml\y withdraw therefrom at any time by giving notice of his Intention so to do
at a stated meeting, and he may receive a certificate of the fact of such withdrawal
In the form prescribed ; but no recommendatory certificate shall be given him except
by a vote of 11 majority of the 111embers of the Lodge then present." Freemasonry
Is a voluntary association. The applicant must come of his own free will and aooord,
and with such free will and accord he should be permitted to go. Nor do we sub·
soribe to the doctrine that, If the Lodge declines to grant a dimit, there is no power
to compel its Issue. We apprehend that It will not be gainsaid that the Grand Mas·
ter or the Grand Lodire has power to compel the issuance of 11 dlmlt, unless the fundamental law thereof forbids its issuance. We can see many reasons why suoh 11
fundamental law should not exist. Oommon custom in all associations, and the
polity of nations, acknowledges the right of withdrawal of allegiance, in tow, from
any organization; we can see no good reason why the opposite course should pre·
vail among Masons. Our Jurisdiction, as does a majority of the Jurisdictions, reoog·
nizes no right existing for a Lodge to even inquire as to the reasons for 11 member's
withdrawal.

Lodges with power to incorporate and enable them to hold property. The Grand
Lodge is an incorporated body under the laws of the State, and as such is em·
powered to hold real and personal property of subordinate Lodges in trust for the
use and benefit ofsuoh Lodges, and, likewise, to conny the same under the dlreo·
tion of such Lodges, and to pay to such Lodges all moneys received in consideration
for said property. The Grand Lodge can exercise no right of management or con·
trol, but Is simply the legal cnstodian of the property, and must re-convoy at the
option of the beneficiary. The property does not belong to the Grand Lodge, but is
simply held in trust. The committee maintains that all Lodge property is Masonic
property, and that once Masonio property it ie always Mssonic property, and indi·
dividnal ownership has ceased. Should the Lodge cease to exist, the property does
not cease to be Masonic property, nor does it revert to the individuals composing
the Lodge, bnt continues sacred to Masonic uses. The committee farther contend
that permitting Lodges to incorporate would be an abandonment ot the foregoing principles, and an acknowledgment of individual ownership of Lodge property, and the.t to invest the Lodges with the power of suing and being sued wo,uld
ca.use conflicts to arise which would be detrimental to the interests of Masonry. The
Grand Lodge of California te.kes simillu ground, e.nd prohibits Its subordinate Lodges
from incorporating. This is as it should be, for in a corporate capacity members of
onr Lodges would have property rights which they could invoke the aid of courts to
protect or enforce, and the manifest result would be danger even to the esoterio
work of the Fraternity, as well as a possible diversion of the property of onr Lodge1
from the purposes designed.

The proceedings are embellished with a fine engraving of the first Grand Master
of New Hampshire, Major General JOHN SULLIVAN. General SULLIVAN had the

Judge. A Jover of liberty, a paritot, a phllantbroplst-he was worthy to be the first
·
Grand Master of the Granite State.
The Address of the Gr~nd Master is an interesting statement of his official acts
during tho year. It contains nothing, however, of general Interest. Masonry In the
jurisdiction is represented as fiourishlng. The reports from the District Deputy Grand
Masters exhibit the Lodges in the several districts as being in a prosperous condition.
The greater portion of the proceedings is appropriated to the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, and to a historical sketch of the Ancient and Accepted
Scottish Rite, prepared by that committee. Both papers are elaborate and exhaust·
ive statements of the views of the committee on the important question comprehended in what is known as the "Massachusetts Departure." In order to arrive
at a correct conclusion, the committee have made a very thorough examination Into
the history of Grand Lodges, and of the purposes for which they were established.
We regard the arguments of the committee as simply unanswerable, and commend
these able papers to the study of all Me.sons who wish to be Informed upon this Important question. The committee arrive at the following oonolusions, recommend·
ing, at the same time, that no action be now had by the Grand Lodge, The Grand
Lodge unanimously concurred:Resolved, That this Grand Lodge declares its understanding of the law in relation
to its powers and authority over the Craft within its jurisdiction to beFirst. That it is the supreme authority in Masonry.
Second. That it has the power to determine what Masonry Is.
Third. That it has the power to decide what Masonic bodies a:e regular, wliereln
Symbolic Masonry is used, shown, or made a part of the ceremonies.
Fourth. That it has power and authority to prohibit the Masons of its obedlenoe
from practicing, as Masonic, any other rites than those which it declares to be Masonic · and from using any of its esoteric ceremonies as Masonic ceremonies In any
other 'bodies than those it shall hold to be Masonic.
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge 111!1rms the well-established doctrine that it is a
violation of the jurisdictional rights of any Grand Lodge or other Grand Body, for a
foreign organization of the same grad~ ?r rite to establish subo~dinate~ within the
jurisdiction of such Grand Body, and it Is due, as well to Masonic comity as to the
watchful care of our own rights, that all attempts of such II nature should meet with
the stern disapproval of this Grand Lodge.
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge, trusting to the fidelity and intelligence of the
Fraternity, deems it unnecessary to legislate at this time in the manner of the pro·
posed amendment.
As usual the Report of the Committee on Correspondence was prepared by Bro.
ALBERT S. WAIT. The work is executed in a masterly style. Commenting upon
the decision of Grand Master HrNEs, to the effect that it would not be proper for a
Lodge in California to receive and act upon an application for affiliation from a Mas•
ter Mason who at the time resides in another State, he says:-

1885.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

137

Had the Grand Master contented himself with advising the Lodge, in its discretion,
to decline to affiliate the applicant, of course the propriety of the advice would not
be open to question. But when he 11Bsumed to lny It down 11s Jaw, that for a Lodge
In one State to affiliate a Master Mason In another would be an invasion of the rights
of the latter, we cannot withhold an expression of surprise. In our civil courts we
have heard of judge-made law, which never, we believe, found much favor with
really sound or learned jurists. There may be Masonry In such a thing as Grand
Master-made law; if so, we do not think it of a much higher type. If this decision
of our Most Worshipful brother of California shall be received as Jaw by the Fraternity at large, It will not be because it is to-day the law of Masonry, for it certainly
Is not, but because the brethren shall be found to have accepted a new departure,
having no better origin than a very bold assumption by a most fortunate Grand
Master.
Whilst to a!Hllate a Master Mason In one Jurisdiction who is a resident of another
may not be an Invasion of the rights of that other, we deem that such action would
be detrimental to the best Interests of the Fraternity, Many and forcible reasons
will suggest themselves to any thoughtful and prudent Mason why such action would
be unwise and wrong; but we can see none favoring such 11 course, unless it be that
"a prophet is not without honor except In his own country." It occurs to us that
the great principle of Masonic equity In Masonic jurisprudence, as in courts of 111w,
would justify the decision of Grand Master Hrn11s. We have elsewhere expressed
our views upon this subject.

In the Jurisdiction of New Mexico the three-ballot rule obtains. The Grand Master
enunciates, in hie third decision, that the first ballot on the petition.of the applicant
elects for the three degrees; and, in hie fourth decision, he represents that, after the
candidate has taken one or two degrees, the ballot le taken to determine the proftcienoy of the candidate ! The Grand f,odge declined to sustain him in either decision,
as we think, rightly.
The fifth decision, that a petition received and referred to a committee can be
disposed of in no other way than by ballot, is not in accord with the rule In Cali·
fornill. With us, if the committee report adversely, or If any one of the committee
reports unfavorably, the action is held as being equivalent to a rejeotion, and no
ballot is deemed necessary. If the applicant le found to be disqualified in consequence of insufficient residence or physical disability, the Master may direct the
withdrawal of the petition, so that the candidate may not suffer the possible and un·
just opprobium of a rejection.

In hie review of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Connecticut, Bro "H."
asks the question, when speaking of the prerogatives of the Grand Master, "Should

and is under expressed, as well ae Implied, obligation to recognize its fundamental
laws, edicts and regulations. Blnue the days of written constitutions Grand Masters

We dissent from the views expressed by Bro." H." In hie review of the proceed·
ings of Kentucky, relative to non-affiliates. He seems to think that oo distinction
should be made between these and thpee who remain in the Lodges, A Mason, oo

which entitles him to the beoell.ta and privileges of the Order. The tranaformatlon
from profane to lultiate conaleta In the assumption of duties, and when by dimlssion
he absolves himself from the obligatlona1 he relinquishes hie right to the privilege&
and benetl.te. The mere fact that he remains hone.s t and troe la not enough. He
must aeelet lo bearing the burdens incident to Lodge organization, otherwise he vol·

dimieelon from the Lodge does not unmake him a Mason, but merely debars him,
during such dimiHloo, from right.a which he would otherwise enjoy. Hie assumption
of duties was voluntary, and the rights of Masonry are accorded to him, not ln con·
eideratlon of "hie thirty, or II.tty, or hundred dollara,'' under a contract, but In oonsideratlon of his performing the duties Incumbent upon him as a member of the
particular Lodge and of the Fraternity. When he voluntarily renounces his duties,
he equally renounces all claim to any of the rights or benefits appertaining thereto.
Were any otilier doctrine to obtain, It would be impossible to sustain Lodge organi·
zatlona.

sonic burial?" His answer was :I know of no reason wh.v a Mason who had committed suicide should be denied
Masonic burial. Dethroned reason calls for our sympathy, not for our censure,
How better can we heal the wounds of the affiicted than by depositing the ever·
green as an emblem of our faith in the immortality of the soul?
In 1870 the Grand Lodge of California adopted a resolution leaving to the Master
and Wardens of the particular Lodge the determination of the sanity of a brother
in case of suicide, and whether It was proper to inter him with Masonic honors.
This resolntion was rescinded in 1879, and there now exists no positive enactment or
d.ecision upon the matter. Individually we are of the opinion that the resolution of
1870 was a most equitable solution of the question, and should have been permitted
to remain. That many who commit snioide are sane there is no doubt, and such
should not be accorded the honor of a Masonic burial : but that there are caeee
caused by dethroned reason le equally true, and the et~rn arbiter, duty, demands that
such should be viewed with Muonic charity. We would err, If at all, upon the side
of charity, and deposit the sprig of acacia in sympathy for the affilcted.

We dissent from the views expressed by Bro. CHADWICK regarding the right of a
brother to know the party objecting to his advancement, or the reasons for such
objection. One who has received the Entered Apprentice or tbe Fellow Craft de·
gree occupies a status very different from tbat of one whose original petition has
been rejected, and has rights which the uninitiated cannot claim. After initiation he
is received as a brother, and, as such, Is entitled to more consideration than the
mere profane, and any allegation reflecting upon his character or qualiflcations
should be carefully examined. Our Grand Lodge has wisely provided that objec·
tions to advancement shall be made known to the Master, and referred to a committee, that their validity may be inquired Into and determined by the Lodge. Io
order to arrive at a proper conclusion as to the fa~ta, the committee should hear the
testimony, not of the objector alone, but of the applicant also. As a Mason the candi·
date should be heard in his own defense, and in order that he may make his defense,
it is but just that he should be informed of the nature of the allegations made against
him and of the party urging the objections. Any peace or harmony purchased at the
cost of justice is worthless. Masons, however good, are possessed of the weaknesses
incident to frail humanity. Bro. CHADWICK says," all will know the cause of the
objection in due time." Troe, but why hold a brother in suspense, or deprive him
of a right, until the cause of the objection leaks out. Such a course, it seems to us,
would be a most fruitful source of discord and wrong in our Lodges. The law upon
this matter adopted by the Grand Lodge In the District of Columbia Is identically
the sam& as that adopted in California. Bro. CaADWIOK predicts that it will not meet
the occasion. It has met every occasion in California, for over a quarter of a century, without any infringement of the peace and harmony of our Lodges, and is not
with us an experiment; it Is a regulation founded in equity and justified by experl·
ence.
Bro. CJIA.DWIOK is not friendly to perpetual jurisdiction; he believes that Lodges
are moraJJy bound to refund aid furnished by other Lodges, and that Lodges, as
such, are not under any obligation to aid the distressed outside of their own mem·
bership ; he does not believe in suspension for non·payment of dues, buffavors drop·
ping from the roll. On this latter point we think bis argument subject to crftiofsm.
We have not been incl!ned to the belief that suspeusion for non-payment of dues dis·
graces a brother, or bas any particular tendency to refiect upon his character. We
do believe, however, that one who neglects or refuses to pay his dues, rightly snbjectR himself to a deprivation of Masonic privileges. We cannot comprehend how "a
very good man and Mason" can be " dropped from the roll" without impairing his
Masonic rights; nor can we understand that a brother, who permits himself to become
in arrears for dues to such an extent as to require his being " dropped from the
roll," he complied with the regnlations of the Grand Lodge or of his own Lodge.
Punishment means, in this case, a loss infiicted in consequence of failure to comply.
It is suspension from the enjoyment of privileges which membership entitles one to.
Dropping from the roll, having no sanction accompanymg it, is no punishment, if it
is to be understood tbat this dropping can be done without impairing one's Masonic
privileges. It is true his Masonic rights, as rights, are not impaired; they are simply
held In abeyance. One cannot take advantage of his own !aches. Our civil courts
have adjudicated this question, and a brother who fails to comply with the letter of
the law of the organization to which he belonged, would have no standing whereon
to take legal steps. Besides, suspension for non•payment of dues has nothing to do
with the nharacter of the brother.
But we are admonished that our space is all occupied, and we must dismiss this
excellent report from further present notice. We shall give it a convenient place on

The Grand Master delivered an able and eloquent address, giving a summary
of his actions through the year. He very forcibly deprecates any departure from
the ancient usages, customs, and landmarks of the Fraternity. Harmony and
prospenty had prevailed throughout the jurisdiction; and the fraternal relations
with other Grand Lodges had remained unchanged. Convinced of the sufficiency
of the number of Lodges already in existence in that jurisdiction, he had discour·
aged all applications for warrants for new ones, and had therefore granted none.
This action we deem eminently proper, as there is too much of the same ~pirit
growing up in the Masonic Fraternity which characterizes many modem institutions,-th&t of constituting n1iw bodies, as it were, to give opportunity for office•

Peace and harmony prevail among fhe Lodges. More than the ordinary amount

interdicting all Masonic intercourse "between the Grand Lodge of Quebec, its sub·
ordinate Lodges, and all brethren in obedience thereto, and such other Lodges and
all members io obedience thereto, holding allegiance to any foreign Grand Lodge."
The Grand Master adds:T~is decree has gone forth. Unfortunately it has been made public. An eager,
ambitious press has scattered the news abroad that there is a Masonic quarrel in
Quebe~ • .The unsy~pathizing and our opponents will rejoice. My brethren, while

Ahl~, dlstmgu!sbed ~n~ esteemed brethren are to be found in the J,odges declared

are contending only for a principle and for our right.
The Grand Lodge of England, through her Grund Master, avers that she cannot
submit to the doctrine that Lodges lawfully existing at the time when a Grand
Lodge was formed in a territory, become unlawful if they do not join in adhering to
the newly formed body. The question, "What will those Grand Lodges that have

one. They cannot well stand aloof.
The Grand Master concludes his interesting Address in the following language,
and we donbt not that brethren everywhere will join in his prayer for peace and
harmony:·
During these years associations have been formed which I hope and trust will
strengthen with advancing years, and in the decline of life will be looked back upon
with great pleasure. This Grand Lodge, which we all love so much, and of whose
record we are so proud, may again be thrown on a turbulent and tempestuous sea.

With reference to the npplications for recognition from France, Spain, Peru,

have always felt great interest in their prospedty, and most heartilv wish them Godapeed in all Masonic progress, it has been eontrary to the settled po)icy of our Grand

From the papers before us it appears that the Grand Lodge in Mexico has baen

time been in Mexico. When that is assured we slrnll gladly recommend recognition.

I

Bro. FosTER is not an advocate of the" perfect youth" doctrine; nor does he "at
all" believe in dispensations for the purpose of re-balloting upon the application of
rejected candidates. Notwithstanding the opinions held by our Grand Lodge, we
concur with Bro. FOSTER in the view that one should be eligible to receive the degrees who can conform to the ritual; bufwe dissent from his latter opinion. We can
see no reason why a body of individuals should be exempt, any more than a single
individual, from observing the dicta of justice. To right a wrong is a duty imposed
upon us by the most sacred teachings. Of all men, Masons, who are enjoined in the
most solemn manner "never to deviate from the minutest principles" of justice,
should be the most eager to see the mandates thereof most carefully obeyed. Nor
can we see why the re-rejection of an applicant "ought to be a very signiflcalit hint''
that dispensations to re-ballot are wrong.
.Bro. FosTER considers that non-affiliation is not a crime for which a Mason can
be tried and punished. Very true. But when a Mason voluntarily absolves himself
from the just burdens of membership, he excludes himself from its rights and privileges, and, in our opinion, is no more entitled to Masonio consideration than a pro·
fane. "If ye will not work, neither shall ye eat." We deem unaffiliated Masons a
reproach, a shame, a dead weight upon the body of :Masonry, and, as such, they
should be cut off from all participation in its rights, benefits, or privileges. The
mere withdrawal of a Mason from his Lodge, or the remaining out of membership,
is not a crime. Of their own free will and accord bee1tme they Masons, and assumed
the duties and responsibilities of Masons, thus entitling them to the benefits and
privileges; voluntarily let them go, but with the understanding that, in relinquishing
and voluntarily ignoring their duties, they relinquish all right to Masonic considera·
tion. Our Grand Lodge views non-affiliation in this light, and has enacted, we think
very rightly, that if a Mason resides in this Jurisdiction non-affiliated for a period of
over six months, he shall be considered out of :Masonic standing, and entitled to no
privilege except that of putting himself in standing by applying to a Lodge for affiliation, accompanying his application with the proper affiliation fee (if any there be,)
and six months' dues. Common justice demands that Masonic delinquency should
be followed by deprivation of Masonic rights.
Commenting on a decision of the Grand Master of Arkansas, to the effect that a
vote authorizing the granting of a dimit does not constitute a dimittal, he gives an
apt illustration, as follows:In Tennessee, in common with a large majority of jurisdictions. it is held the.\
the vote ot' a Lodge is the actual dimit, the Secretary's certificate being simply the
proof of the fact to the outside world, and in no sense the dimit proper. Marriage
certificates are common; and in many cities where board of health raws require it,
physicians' certificates of the death of a patient are required. In one case we suppose, by the Arkansas rule, a man is not married, and in the other case not dead,
until the official certificate is properly made out and signed.
California for 1883 receives very favorable notice. Bro. FoSTER quotes with ap·
proval the first and fourteenth decisions of Grand Master TAYLOR,; but does not
indorse his ninth, relative to one who is ruptured being ineligible as an applicant
for the degrees of Masonry. He considers this the" quintessence of physical perfectionism," and believes the same rule would reject a petitioner subject to headache or chills and fever.
The reports of Bros. ABELL, HELLER and SHAEFFER are spoken of with favor, as
is also that of Bro. ANDERsoN on Correspondence. Most of the opinions expressed
by the latter he indorses ; but does not think the one-ballot rule the best, or that the
officers of a Lodge can resign, or that suspending the charter of a Lodge suspends
the members thereof.

The Grand Master belongs to the "Perfect Youth" school of believers. The
loss ot the middle finger on the left hand to the first joint, the )(las of an eye, or 11

will bar the reception of a candidate. That such is his opinion doth plainly appear

ell on eur ancient landmarks, and the only safety is a rigid adherence to them.

The financial affairs of the Grand Lodge are aatisfactory, notwithstanding poor

The Grand Master believes that "corporations have no souls," that Masons
should act in their individual cap"city, and that "corporate charity neither promotes liberality in the souls of the givers nor gratitude in recipients." Perhaps we do
not comprehend his meaning; if it be that the Lodge should not attend to the dispensation of charity, we dis11ent. This is onA of the cardinal duties of a Lodge,

Suspension for non-payment of dues we believe to be more a result of indiffer·

Bro. DRINKARD believes in the "prerojl'ativee," and that Grand Mastera are

protection of the Fraternity against the undue aasumption or exercise of power.
llro. DRINKARD represents the right to grant di1pensations as havin1r been obtained by the founders of our Order from the Catholic Church, and allflles that as
"no orthodox Pope -no Pope worthy of the name-will ever admit that his pre1·ogative to grant dispensations can be taken away from him by any man or body of
men," so "no Grand Master worthy of the name-no orthodox Grand Master-will
ever admit that his prerogatives can be taken away from him." We don't believe
in the infallibility of Grand Masters any more than we do in that of Popes, imd
hence we do believe that there should be some authority which will hold a Grand
Master to a proper exercise of prop1>r powers, and to a responsibility for their abuse.
We don't believe in the feudal idea that the "Kin1r can do no wrong." The
safety of our Fraternity and the safety of our law demands constitutional limitations, and that these should never be set aside· by Grand Masters.

candidate should suffer the inconvenience of waitina- the regular time before a new
petition ceuld be presented, th9n that any encouragement should be given the
brethren to disclose how they liad balloted. We are at a loss to understand how
the issuing of a dispensation to re-ballot should encourage or require any parties to
disclose how they had balloted ; nor can we comprehend what harm would result
from a manful acknowledgment of mistake. Even-handed justice should be done,
even though the heavens fall, and a Lodge has no right to protect itl! ballot by an
act .of positive injustice to an individual. We think the Grand Master was wrong
in refusing to grant the dispensation asked for. We consider this a clear case of
doing evil that good may come, and that, too, a very doubtful lj'ood.
The Grand Master had also declined to grant a dispensation to M11stic Lodge, No.
75, to ballot upon the petition of a candidate resir!ing within the jurisdiction of
another Lodge, the latter having refused its consent. This was proper. A Lodge
has no right even to receive the petition of a party residing within the jurismction
of another.

pile fro171 the data before us a brief history of the Fraternity in that Republic, so
far as the symbolic degrees are concerned, from the year 1882 down to the present
time. The earlier history of Symbolic Maeonry therein m11y be diAposed of by
saying that, prevlou1 l.o 1882, it wa1 exclueively under the jurisdiction of a Supreme
Council of the Ancient and Accepted 8oottieh Rite, and practl~d the ritual prescribed by that Body.
Early in 1882, three.Symbolio Lodgee obtained charters from the United Grand
Lodge of Colon and the Island of Cuba, and were established in the city of Vera
Cruz. The Supreme Council of Mexico protested agaln1t that which it d~med to b8

an invasion of its jurisdiction, but the Grand Lodge of Colon and Cuba claimed
that, as no Symbolic Grand Lodge then existed in the Republic of Mexigo_
the territory was practically unoccupied, and that, by the general u~age of the
Craft, it had the right to establish Lodges under its jurisdiction therein. It is true
that at this time certain so-called Grand Lodges existed in sevr.ral States of the
Republic, but these received their authority from the Supreme Council and were
~irectly responsible to that Body for their acts. In order to establish this fact It
is only necessary to refer to the Constitution of the Supreme Council which in
Artie!~ 612, says; "_The Grand Lodges are bodies delegated from th~ Supr;mt
Council to the subordinate Lodges of each State, and are directly dependent upon
it;" in Article 616, "Grand Lodges will receive their charters from the Supreme
Oo~ncil irratis;" •_nd in Article 62.'l, "Grand Lodges which do not comply with their
tluties, etc., or whrnh do not pay the respect and obedience due by them to the Supreme Council, will be suspended and their charters forfeited."
It will thus be seen that, at that time, there were ne Free Symbolic Grand
Lodges in Mexico, but that all the so-called Grand Lodges held their tenure at
the will and pleas~re ?f the Supreme Council. In the month of January, 1883,
the three Lodges m~t1tuted by the United Grand Lod1i1e of Colon and the Island
of Cub~ met in convention for the purpose of orll"anizing an Independent IJraud
~y~b?h~ Lodge, (La Gran Logia Simbolica Independiente Mezicana,) whose
Jurisdiction should extend over all jru Symbolic Lodges in the territory of
the Mexican Republic. By this movement we do not understand that the new
Grand Lodge proposed to interfere with those Lodges holding allegiance to the Supreme Council, but only to regulate and govern such Lodges as miJlht be chartered
by itself, and t~ prevent foreign jurisdictions from occupying its territory. The
Supreme Council appe:i.rs also to have taken this view of the case, for in its Official
Journal of 1883 appears a manifesto to the effect that if those three "free" Lodge•
solem~ly promis~ not ~ practice the system of the Scottish Rite, the Supreme
Coun01l would withdraw its protest and charge of invasion, and allow those Ledges
to pursue the even tenor of their way as bodies with which it had nothing to do.
Accordingly the United Grand Lodge of Colon and Cuba, on behalf of its subordiuates, made a solemn declaration that those bodies did not practice the Rcl)ttish
~ite, whe~eupon the protest of the Supreme Council was withdrawn, as appears
m the serm-annual report of that body in January, 1883.
INDEPENDENT SYMBOLIO MEXIOAN GRAND LODGE.-On the twenty-eighth day
of January, 1883, a Body thus entitl"d was organized at Vera Cruz. It then
claimed jurisdiction over all the "free" Symbolic Lodges existing, or that might
thereafter be established, in Mexican territory. That it had the right to do this
ma! perhaps be que~tionable; but it appears to have been the first and only Symbohc Grand Lodge m the country, and it is said, in its publications, to have been

It was not until June, 1883, that the so-called "Grand Lodge of the State of
Vera Cruz" was formed, being some six months after the organization of the "Inde·
pendent Symbolic Mexican Grand Lodge," and despite its declaration of sovereignty.
This "Grand Lodi;re of the State of Vera Cruz" claims to have been organized in
1869, under the auspice1 of the Supreme Council, and to have lost none of its powerH or authority by reason of the action of the Supreme Council in surrenderinir
juriediction over the symbolic degreea. There might be some force jn this argument if this Grand Lodge had been organized as an independent Grand Body,
having full juriediction over the symbolic Lodges within its territory. But that w&11
not the fa.ct . . It then owed allegiance to the Supreme Council, and, without its conaent, could take no action independently. Such so-called Grand Lodges were aim·
ply committees of the Supreme Council, appointed to attend to the affairs of the
1ymbolic Lodges; and they were directly responsible to that Body for all their acts.
'l'he Independent Symbolic Mexican Grand Lodge is an entirely different Body.
Organized under the American system of Masonry-practicing the York Rit&oonferring only the degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Ma1on-formed by Lodges deriving their authority from a Gre.µd Lodge which we
recognize as legitimate-and recognized by several Grand Lodges with which we
hold fraternal communication-it has much reason for commending itself to us as
11 proper Body for recognition, if either of the two Vera Cruz Grand Lodges were
to be recognized.
By volunteering this opinion we do not desire to create any prejudice, our
object being only to iPve a fair and impartial exhibit of the situation, for the con1ide1"11tion of those whose province it is to decide upon the legality or legitimacy of
either Body. The Independent Symbolic Mexican Grand Lodge solemnly declares the.tThis Grand Lodge, by preserving, since its organization, the general jurisdiction over all the Republic, ha• not done so in order to constitute itself the sole
ll'overning Masonic power in Mexico, but, on the contrary, to be better able to
defend the American doctrine of a Sovereign Gro.nd Lodge for each State-not con•enting that any irregnlar Grand Symbolic Lodge should he organized in any State,
nor permitting either that any should falsify it• sovereignty by means of centrallr.ing its power. Accordingly this Grand Lodge of Mexicl) has been, sinco January
28th, 1883, the one which has preserved under its jurisdiction all the States of the
:Mexican Republic, thus providing, in due time, fnr the establishment in every
tltate of a Sovereign and Independent Grand Lodge ; in which ~ase it cedes the
necessary territorr 1 as has been done succe•sively in The Federal District, Tlaxoe.la, and Guanaiuato. '.1.'hus, if any symbolic I,odge or Grand LodgP. were to
ln~tall itself to-day in any of the States of the Republic, without obtaining from
this Grand Lodge the cession of the necessary territory, etc., it would be declared
Irregular and would appear as an invader of recognized jurisdiction.
This declarntign is published by the authority of the above entitled Grand
Lodge, "by virtue of its being the most ancient in Free Symbolism in the country,
and the one that has planted here the American Me.sonic Organism, which is the
most perfectly ordered, since it permits the creation of a Sovereign Grand Lodge
for each State as an Independent Power." The declaration ends as follows:Thus this Grand Lodge enjoys the honor of making known to you the real state
of Symbolic Masonry in Mexico, hoping-from your recognized justice, as well as
from the regular conditions of its organization since the 28th day of January, 1883,
when a Sovereign Grand Lodge did not exist in Mexico, and as being the Masonic

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the trial-record from
Mountain Shade Lodge, No.18, in the case of HENRY CLAY KELSEY, (of Olay Lodge,

No. 101,) who was expelled from all the riirhts and privileges of Masonry on the
second day of December, 1884, have considered the same and find as follows:That said Lodge was not convened in a special meeting to elect trial·commi1sioners of which the brethren had notice; that the charge and specifications were
presented, read, and placed on file at the special meeting which was held to elect
Commissioners; that no time or place was designated by the Master for the meeting
of the Commission; that the Commissioners did meet, apparently by agreement, on
the twenty-first day of November, 1884, at a place not appointed by the Master and
at a time two days after their assumed election; ti.at no notification af their elec·
tion appears to have been given to the Commissioners i.n any manner; that neither
the accused nor the accuser were notified of. the time and place of tbe meeting of
the Commission; and that no copy of the charge was directed to be served, or was
served uprom the accused, so far as the record shows.
It may be said that the accused, by appearing through an attorney, waived all
these essentials and informalities. In order to give a Lodge jurisdiction of a
Me.some offense, it is required, as primary steps, that the charge should be pre-

1885.J

Grand Lodge of California.

199

ferred, that the Ml\Bter should pass upon its sufficiency, and that he then should
call a special meeting to elect Commissioners, of which the brethren should have due
notice. Upon the Lodire convening in special meeting, it designates the number of
the Commissioners, tellers are appointed, the Lodge elects by ballot, the Master
delivers the charge to the Secretary, and directs him to prepare a copy for service
on the accused, with a summons for him to attend, and also noti'fications to the Commissioners of their election, and to them and the accuser of the time and place of the
tirst meeting of the Commission. When this is done, and not until it is done, does
the Lodge acquire jurisdiction of the offence. These matters are not waived bv an
appearance, neither will consent or appearance confer jurisdiction. They are con·
stitutional requirements and roust be compliet with.
Aside from other and great irregularities in this record, or whatever there is of
it purporting to be a record, it ia not endorsed as approved by the Master, 8.11 re·
quired by the 24th of the General Regulations; and from our inspection of thia paper
we are the more firmly oonvinced of the wisdom and necessity of strictly adhering
to the demands of that Regulation. For the foregoing ree.sonM your committee
offer t.he following reaolution and recommend ite adoption:Reaolved, That the proceedin!l'B of the trial-oommiasion convened by Mountain
Shade Lodge, No.18, in the cas~ of HENRY CLAY KELSEY, (of Olay Lodge, No.101;)

the forms and rules of our Masonic law.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of tbe trial-record from
Brotherhood Lo8KB 1 No. 2151, in the· case of SYLVESTER REDIOK HOUSER, expelled

1885, have had the same ~Qder ooQsi4err.tlon, Bnd report as follows:-

The record, as shown by the transcript, does not disclose the fact that the Com·
missioners were elected by ballot; nor that the accused was notified by summons,
or otherwise, of the time and place of the meeting of the Commission; nor that
ther~ was ar.y evidence of a copy of the charge and specifications having been
served upon him. These are essential pre-requisiteM to the acquisition by the Lodge
of jurisdiction over an accused brother, and that fact must appear by the record.
A portion of the evidence received by the Commission consisted of ex pwrte
affidavits, and was, therefore, incompetent testimony. As those affid~vits bore
directly upon a vital point alleged in the specifications, we are necessarily forced
to the conclusion that they had their weight in influencing the minds of the Com·
missioners in arriving at the results foreshadowed in their attempted findings,
were prejudicial to the rights of the accused, and were subversive of that equity
and fair dealing which the Constitution provides shall be observed when a brother is
tried for an offense and his Masonic standing an.d character are placed in jeopardy.
The record in this case ~hows that the Commissioners, in their finding, passed
upon the three specifications and the charge iri a body, that is, collel'tively. The
Commissioners must find the accused "guilty" or "not guilty," upon ·each specifi.
cation and also upon the charge. A finding upon the charge, separate and distinct
from ~he specifications, is as necessary as a finding upon the specifications; for,
while the accused might be l<'Uilty of the facts set forth in the latter, it does not
follow that they constitute a Masonic offense and that he would be guilty of unmasonic conduct. Without these findings your committee are unable to determine of
what the Commission found the brother guilty, and, for all these reBsons, they offer
the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the proceedings of the trial-commission convened by Brotherhood
Lodge, No. 251, in the case of SYLVESTER REDIOK HOUSER, expelled fr<Jm all the
rights and privileges of Masonry on the twenty.second day o~ August, 1885,, be and
are hereby disapproved ; and that the case be remanded to said Lodge with mstruo·
tions to try the brother for the offense therein charged, accordini' to Masonic law
and in conformity with our prescribed mode of procedure.

your committee, to whom was ri>ferred the transcript of the trial-record from
Crescent Lodge, No. 45, in the case of RoBEKT WILLIS MILLER, expelled from all
the right~ and privileges of Masonry on the thirtieth day of March, 1885, have duly
examined the same.
'Ve find that the record abounds in errors ; in fact, that they are the rule instead
of the exceptions. The testimony consists of hearsay evidence contained in various
letters, and of a deposition irregularly taken ; at least these are a portion of the
testimony. We believe that these letters, inadmissible as they were, operated to
a great extent upon the minds of the Commissioners in arriving at their conclusion,
for, without them, supplying as they did the important links in the chain of evidence necessary to convict, the Commissioners never could have reached the result
they did. The admission of this evidence was error and prejudicial to the rights
of the accueed.
While the Commission found the accused guilty of the •pacifications, they failed
to find upon the charge, thus making the omission to determine whether the facts
averred in the specifications constituted a Masonic offense, and rendered the ac·
cused amenable to Masonic law and subject to the penalty imposed. From the
so-called appeal in this c~se, your committee are unable to determine whether it
was or was not taken within the time required by the Constitution, there being no
date thereto. But, whether it was taken in time or not is immaterial in the dis·
position of the case, as the penalty imposed by the Comml~sion is of such a character as renders it the duty of your committee to pass upon the validity of its
proceeding•, irrespective of the appeal.
We feel in this case, as in some others, that we would be derelict in our duty
did we fail to again impress upon Masters who preside at trials, as well as upon
Secretaries and Commissioners, the duty of urgently adhering to the positive requirements of the mode of procedure in. Masonic trials as prescribed by the Constitution and General Re1<"11lations, and which are so fully and plainly exemplified
in the 11 Form of Records of Trials a.nd Transcripts thereof," heretofore adopted by
this Grand Lodge. We earnestly hope that future committees of this Grand Body
will exact a strict compliance therewith from all whose duty it becemes to adminis.
ter our laws. There is safety only in the observance of the law. If Masters are permitted, and the same is true of Trial-Commlssio11ers, simply to approx1mate to an
observance thereof, our system of jurisprudence will soon become so slack and
loose that it will be made to bend to suit the whims, caprices or ignorance of any
and all, until there will be no safeguard thrown around an accused by which hie
rights will be protected; and justice, so called, will be determined as equity was
administered in other times, without rules or precedents, varying as much as did
the length of the feet of the Chancellors who happened to preside upon the bench.
Let us live by the law, which is the result of the wisdom and experience of ages.
Your committee offer the followin!I' resolution and recommend its adoption 1 Resolved, That the action of the Commission convened by Crescent Lodge, No. 45,
in expelling ROBERT WILLIS MILLER from all the rights and privileges of Masonry
on the thirtieth day of March, 1885, be and is hereby disapproved and reversed;
and that the case be remanded to that Lodge with instructions to try the brother
for the offense with which he is charged, according to our Masonic law.

guilty of any offense to which a penalty would attach. When such palpable and
inexcusable errors occur in the transaction of business by Calif<Yrnia Lodge, No. 1,
as are shown to exist in this record, it certainly becomes the duty of the Grand
Lodge to demand a strict adherence to our forms end precedents, and a full compliance with our laws and regulations from each and every one.
The accused is charged with the grave offense of diRturbing the peace and harmony of the Lodge and disobedience to the Master's gavel. Of these acts the
Commission found him guilty and affixed therefor the penalty of suspension.
The evidence fully justifies the findings and warrants the punishment imposed.
Your committee, from the evidence adduced, are force:l to the conclusion that there
was a studied, persistent, and willful disobedience of the Master's gavel on the part
of the accused. The gavel is the emblem of authority. It is the lever which
moves the Masonic worlcl. When wielded by the Master in his Lodge it is more
potent than a Monarch's sceptre. The Master there is sovereign, and his will
alone becomes the law by which the Craft are governed and to which they must bow
with graceful submission and strict obedience. .For the Mester to permit the

204

. Procf3edings of the

[Oct. 14,

slightest deviation frol!\ this rule, would sap the foundati1m of his prerogative and
plant the seed that would produce turmoil, discord, dissension and, ultimately,
anarchy.
It is the province of the chosen few to command, while it is the duty of others
to obey. Upon the very threshold of Masonry the novice is instructed that the
peace ~nd harmony of the Lodge must not be disturbed. Whenever a Mason so
far forgets himself as to bring anything offensive into the Lodge whereby disturb·
ance may be caused, or fails or refuses to render obedience to the powers that be,
he becnmes guilty of one of the greatest offenses known to our Masonic calendar,
and amenable to the severest penalty which our Masonic Code can impose. In
many instances of this character the refractory brother is not alone at fault. The
Master. by his indulgence or his desire to court the favor and good will of the
brethren, may so far slacken the discipline of his Lodge that members will feel
warranted in encroaching upon his known prerogative. When such is the case the
Master should be held responsible. He who loses sight of the dignity of his high
office, or fol'ICets or forbears to exact the strictest respect therefor, is unworthy to fill
the Master's chair. Our discipline, to all, is exacting; it must be observed,
respected, and obeyed; and the r~ins must be held by the Master's hand.
The object of all punishment and the efficacy of ite administrati.on being not
only to reform the offender, but to deter others from committing similar offenses
and from the errors exhibited in this transcript, your committee offer the following
resolution and recommend its adoption :Ruolved, That the record of the proceedings of the Trial-Commission convened
by California Lodge, No. 1, by which HARRY PEROY WILLIAM HUTTON was SUB·
pended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry on the sixth day of AuiWlt,
1885, be and is hereby disapproved ; and that, by the action of this Grand Lodge,
the said HARRY PERCY WILLIAM HUTTON be, and he hereby is, expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the record of a so-called
Trial-Commission convened by Friendship Lodge, No. 210, in the case of JAMES
GRIERSON KENNEDY, suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry on
the first day of January, 1885, have had ·t he same under consideration, and report as
follows:With reference to the appeal in this case, your committee are unable t o deter·
mine from the record whether or not it was taken within the time prescribed by
the Constitution, viz :-thirty days after the judgment was announced to the Lodge

1885.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia• .

205

by the Master. The recerd shows that the result of the trial was declared by the
Master, in open Lodge, on the date above given. The only record of the giving of
the notice of appeal to the Master is that contained in a certificate by the Secretary, "that the notice of the appeal set forth in the record is a true copy of an original notice of appeal as presented by the Master and filed at the stated meeting of
our Lodge held on Febl'Uary 5th, 1885." If this date is the time when the notice of
appeal was given to the Master, the appeal was not taken in time. There is none
other gh•en. We do not, however, now attach as much importance to this omission
as we might under other circumstances. But, for the guidance of future commit·
tees, and for the information of future appellants, we would say that the matter of
when a notice of appeal is given is a very necessary item in getting the appeal before the Grand Lodge for ite consideration.
The record in this c..se shows that the Lodge was convened in special meeting
to elect Commissioners on the nineteenth day of June, 1884, and that, after they were
olected, the Master designated the tenth day of July, 1884, as the time for their first
meeting. At the time appointed by the Master the Commission failed to meet, but
It did meet on the eighteenth day of September, 1884. There is no showill!f in the
record 0f any reaAon wliy the.CommiHioners did not meet at the time appointed,
and then adjourn for a time exceeding ten daye, for good reason shown and by the
1anction of the Master. Neither is there any reason shown why the Commission
met on the particular day it did. It having failed to meet on the day de<1ia-nated
by the Master, it was, ipso facto, dissolved-fallen to pieces from its own negll'Ot
and inaction. This is the rule when a Oommi11Sion fails to meet pursuant to adjournment and no further time is granted by the Master, (See G. L. Prooeedings,
Vol. X, page 570.) For a more cogent reason would this be the ;rule when the
Commission did not meet at all. Under this rule the Commission lapsed, became
functus officio, and Rny action which it did take was extra-judicial, a usurpation of
power and authority, and void. It will not avail to claim that the accused, by be·
ing present, waived this. The accused by his presence, or by his consent, cannot
~reate this body. It can ouly be brought into existence by the mode prescribed by
tlie Constitution, through the aotion of the L odge. It having ceased to exist, no
consent of the accused, or act of the Master or Commission, could revivify and restore
it, any more than they oould create it in the first instance. The power was not
given to them, or either of them, to breathe the breath of life into this dead body.
It would be no excuse for the failure of a Commiasion to meet at the time designated by the Master, that the accused could not be served with summons, he being
absent from the State. Our Constitution provides the method for acquiring Juri~­
diction of the person of the accused when he is without the State, or without the
jurisdiction of the local Lodge, but within the State, and this method should have
been pursued. In any event, and under any circumstances, the Commission should
have met at the time designated, and, if not ready to proceed, should have ad·
journed in tile manner provided by the law, and thus have perpetuated itself. Having failed to do so, it ceased to exist, and any act which it performe<l was void.
Again, the Commission adjourned on the thirteenth day of November until the
eighth day of December, 1884, being a periQd of more than ten days, without good
reasons being shown, or any reaRon in fact, and without the sanction of the MRster.
This is prohibited in Sec. 7, .Art. IV, Part VI, of the Constitution. Besides, the
charge is supported by three specifications, and the Commission find upon them,
but omit to find that the accused has been guilty of o. Masonic offence by failing to
find him guilty of the charge; and there was therefore no basis upon which this socalled Commission could attach a penalty.
The Constitution provides that the record a.n d finding shall be signed by the

the following resolution and recomme.nd its adoption :RflllOlved, That the proceedings of the Commission convened under the action of

The hour for the special order, made yesterday, having arrived, the
