Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the trial-record on
appeal from the action of San Benito Lodge, No. 211, in the case vf "\VAL~'RiltD C.
DAVIS, an Entered Apprentice, expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry on the twenty-fifth day of April, 1885, have duly considered the same and
submit the following report thereon:The record in this case shows that the Commission met pursuant to the appoint.
ment made by the Master, that all the members were present except Bro. HEYLllf
B. HARRIS, and that the Commission then proceeded to take testimony in the trial
until the close of the day, when it adjourned until the twenty-eighth day of March.
Upon re-assembling, Bro. HARRIS apIM'.ared and took his seat in the Commission.
and continued to act thereafter. There is no evidence in the record to induce your
committee to believe that the testimony produced in the absence of Bro. HARRIS
was ever read over to him or by him, or communicated to him in any manner. We
therefore take it, so far as he is concerned, that Bro. HARRIS must have sat in
judgment upon the rights of the accused without any knowledge of tho evidence
upon which he was to or did base his judgment.
During the proceedings, the regular Secretary being necessarily absent, the
Master appointed a Secretary pro tem. who proceeded to act for some time, and,
upon the return of the Secretary, the recording was surrendered to him and he pro·
ceeded to co111plete the record, and thereupon certifies to it as being a full and cem·
plate record of the proceedings. To sustain this record would be to submit t~e
accused to the judgment of a Commission (for though it is composed of several 1t
is nevertheless a whole body,) which has condemned him without having heard the
evidence in the case as it was adduced, and he is therefore depnved of a hearing
before them. The record is not properly authenticated, it coming to us under the
certificate of a Secretary who was present for vnly a portion of the time, and was
consequently incapacitated and unable to certify to its correctness.
The chargt! of unmasonic conduct against the accu~ed was predicated upon three
specifications. Upon the first, the Commission found him "not guilty;" but
upon the second and third he was found "guilty," and the Commission then proceeded to fix the penalty. This was done without determining whether the facts
constituted a Masonic offense of such a nature as rendered the accused amenable to
Masonic law. In the absence of a findi~g upon the charge there is nothing upon
which a Commission can attach a penalty. Without a finding upon the charge the
Commissi"n which assesses a punishment does so without having found the accused
guilty of any off~nse; for the offense is the accusatien that the accused has been
guilty of "unmasonic conduct." Before a person can be punished for an act it
must first be determined by the Commission whether he is guilty of a crime.
The changing of the Secretary during these proceedings goes to show the necessity of a strict adherence to the requirement of the 24th of the General Regulations making it obligatory upon the Master to authenticate the record by endorsing
his a~pi·oval theron. ·This requirement was adopted by this Grand Body at its
session in 1882, and incorporated in the General Regulations, upon a report made
by your committee at the Annual Communication of that year. It is a salutary
and beneficial one, and, as long- as it remains a law among us, it should be observed
and obeyed. Without the Master's endcrsed approval thereon, no record should
be received or countenanced by this Grand Body, whether it be on appeal or other,

and the great Hall was at once filled to overflowing by his thousand

The Grand Master announced in fitting terms the sorrowful cause
of the convocation; at the request of that officer the Rev. Dr. ELXAN
CoHN, Rabbi of the Congregation Emanu-El, offered prayer; the
Grand Organist and his choir furnished beautiful and suitable music

the Lodge-room ; and Past Grand Master LEONIDAS E PBA'l'r addressed
the assemblage as follows :BRETHREN AND FRIENDS :In ~n ?lell'ant mansi~n on yonder eminence ()Yerlooking a goodly p<1rtlon of
your fair city, so near this Temple that the heart-throbs of its stricken mmates
almost reach our ears, a widowed mother and her fatherless children have been
groping through blinding tears to gather up the torn and severed tendrils of their
own heart-strings, There the patriarchal chair is vacant-here the accustomed
seat is unoccupied save by the habiliments of woe. There the dead idol of a sorrowing househitld-here the living memory of a good man and Mason, There a
shattered fireside-here a fallen and broken column. There a deep and measureless sorrow, a sorrow so sacred that even our sympathy seems almost an intrusionhere the double burden of our own Rrief and the mingling echoes of their lament·
ations.
MosES HELLER is dead ! Deall., as the world phrases it, but, in fact, not deadnot even sleepmg. True, the drapery of mortal flesh, in which for almost three
score years and ten he had been imprisoned, has b<.len laid aside. But that mortal
drapery wa1 not Mons HELLER. The personality which, for more than twenty
yean, has lent us its counsels in this hall, still survives. Our own measured and
nmfHed steps, tM subdued and half whispered utterances which we hear are our
own unconscious reoornltion of the fact that a living but invisible presen~e iR still
m•ving in our midst. Not dead I He still lives in the example which he haa left
~ his. children, and i~ the noble influence which he has exerted among us. He
hves m the irood which he has done, and in the kindness and charity which he
has so unostentatiously administered. He lives in the lives of a score of young
men who owe thE'ir ~very hoP_e to him, He lives in the sweet and tender memory
of all who knew him, and m the respect, the veneration, and the love of his
Masonic household. Not dead, not Bleeping, but still here I
At the very hour almost when you were gathering for your annual Grand
Communication ; at the very moment almost when you expected to meet and
greet him as in years agone; without fear or dread, but calmly and serenely, like a

tired child lying d1>wn to refreshing slumber, he laid his cares and toils aside and
wafted a"ay over the silent river to that unknown land which is the near destination of all of us who linger still behind him, And I am glad that the final mes·
senger came as he did come-not through pain and citnscious suffering, but with a
touch as gentle as that of an angel; for we too would have suffered in kn1>wing
that MOSES HELLER was a sufferer.
I had the fortune, as I believe, to enjoy his confidence and respect. I was one
of the few who reached the most secret chambers of his heart and read his inmost
character better even th.an he kne" it himself. I know, therefore, whereof I am
about to speak, I shall ~peak the truth only, and in this case truth needs no em·
beIiish ment.
Few men could bear as triumphantly as he did the crucial test. of long and
intimate acquaintanoeahlp. The counterfeit, if neither challenged nor analyzed,
may pass for the genuine. But the closest analysis left no tinge or discoloration
on the reputation of our absent brother; and the unanswerable evidenCfl as to the
genuineness of his quality is in the fact that those of us who knew him best
honored and loved him most.
Public life, in the popular acceptat ion of that term, had no charm for him. By
his instincts he was a merchant-not a mere trader, or speculator, or: maker of
corners in the market-but a merchant in the highest and best s!'nse of that honorable title. At no time could a public office have been forced upon him, and we
therefore know not what qualities he might have developed in such capacity. But
in his own choaen ephere of action, as merchant and master of commerce; as
neighbor, friend and hoat; as citizen abroad and as husband and father in his home;
as director and adviser in a score of monetary associations; and as the depository
of a thousand penon"1 trusta : in all these capaeities his character was above
reproach. His penonal tidelity was a co111piouous element in his organization,
F ew men held so many sacred confidences; few men h.ave ever been charged with
sv many private and penonal trusts; but not one was ever neirlected, compromised,
or betrayed. To him a trust, whether great or small, was a thing as sacred as
the tombs of :hi1 fathers.
In buslneH he was methodic.J, precise, and exacting, and In this he was right.
Once or twice I have heard it vaguE'ly intnnated that he sometimes seemed hareh
and oppre&1iv1 to an unfortunate debtor. If he ever seemed so it was because the
facts of the particular case amply justitied him. The founrlations of his own fortune had been laid in persistent toil, hardship, and self-denial; and to him,
naturally enough, toil, ener11y, and frugality were the avenues to success. He had
no sympathy for the younll' man who leaned forever upon some one else, and who,
without effort or sacrifice of his own, was waiting to be driven into fortune and success over some royal road. And still he was right. But I deny that he was ever
unjust, and I assert that he was alway1 generous when there was an occasion or a
circumstance which called for ll'eneroaity. The young man who was correct and pru.
dent in his habitR, firm in his integrity, willini' to toil and eager to help himself, if
unfortunate, was al.,.aya met with a kind word and a helping hand. Ia all such
cases Mos Es HELLER was the first to say to his brother merchants-" This man has
learned something now. He will make a success if we help him a little. It won't
hurt us. Let us give him another chance." And so the young man was ti dad over
hie troubles an~ probably saved from despair and ruin. But of shams and frauds
Bro. HELLER was intolerant to the la11t degree.
Of the extent of his daily benefactions, great and small, few men have any
adequate conception. Trivial things, of frequent occurrence, indicate the true
charaqter of the individual IJ!Ore um:11ista~ably thall does one grand effort. The

former are the quick fruits of a natural impulse, the latter is too often the result of
vanity or ambition, or of a studied and ;;elfish purpose to secure notoriety or renown.
Let me illustrate. A hundred times on the streets of this city I have seen him
hand a. coin to some robust and stalwart beggar, and when I s'miled as if in derisi_on
of his credulity, he answered-" I know what you think. But that man says he is
hlmgry; how can I know? Probably he is an impostor; how can I tell? But I
would rather be imp<tsed upon a thousand times than to think that one deserving
man l{Oes hungry because I refuse to give him a quarter of a dollar."
Suffering, in any creature, was a torture to him. I haYe seen his eyes moisten
when a dog limped by him cm a broken leg, moaning piteously as it tried to touch
the earth with its wounded limb. And I have seen his indignation kindled to a
fever heat at hearing of the ill-usage of a def•mseless ehild. These things may seem
to you like trifle•, but they are none the less the keys which unlock one side of our
lost brother's character, and reveal to us the humanity which warmed his heart.
Born a Jew, of the Jews, and proud of his lineage, as he deemed that he had a
right to be, in his religion as in all things else he was loyal to the last. He died in
the house of Israel and an ardent supporter of the Synagogue. But the humanity
in hirn was too broad and catholic te be cramped or circumscribed by the precise
letter of any articles of faith. Of wide and liberal Yiews himself, while be was
firm in his own faith he was tolerant of all others. In the pra.ctical affairs of life
he did not stop to inquire too critically whether a fellow-beinlj' drew his inspiration
from Sinai or Oalvary, from Christ or from the Prophets whf> preceded him.
Every man, whether Jew or Christian, he measured by the same unvarTinl{ standard--his own personal character and worth. In brief, the dominant factors in his
Hligien, the factors which toned and tempered and guided his life, were faith in
immortality, humanity towards all, and a confidence, sublime and never shaken,
that in all things truth and justice would ultimately prevail. Men guided. by such
impulses cannot materially err.
Hypocrisy, fraud, or deceit, never found a lodgment in his breast. I doubt if he
ever get so far as to seriously ask his own conscience whether a given proposition
would be right or wrong; for the mere fact that there was in it enough of doubt
to evolve such a question would, by his ethics, be sufficient to command its prompt
and emphatic rejection. His social and domestic relations were unsullied. He
kept his own fireside pure an61. spotless, and neither wife nor child could ask a
question which he could not answer truthfully without a blush.
But the g..and secret of all this manly and well rounded character-not so much
the secret, perhaps, as the reason of it-is the fact that MosEs HELLER was a man
of pure instincts and unblemished thoughts. There was no earthy residuum in his
composition, no mean or groveling vein in his nature, but eTery aspiration was up·
ward toward the higher and the better. On that broad basis he builded his charac·
ter, and he builded better the.n he knew-better than we comprehended until we
stood face to face with our irreparable loss.
And these elemel'lts of character, sustaiMd and supplemented by a cal!f and
patient devotion to whatever task or duty he had in hand, great or small, important
or trivial, crowned his career with an enviable success. Let the young men who
aspire to like fortune and success-the young men who are soon to become the
merchant princes and commercial magnates of the land-let them study his character, imitate his virtues, and copy his example.
No, not dead, not even sleeping ! There is a something in such men-call it
soul, spirit, mentality, what you will-over which this thing which we call death
has no p!lwer. Not dead! Such men pass away, but they do not perish.
What more, my brethren, shall I se.y? What more should be said? The estllem

Past Grand Master LEONIDAS E PRATT, on behalf of sundry other
Past Grand Masters and himself, presented the following memorial
and resolution:2'o the M. •• W. ·.Grand Lodge of C<dif(YT'flia:-

In the infancy of Freemasonry on the Pacific Coast one character was perhapR
more conspicuous than all others. His devotion and fidelity were never challenged,
his zeal and activity were tireless and unflagging, and, in the days of his prosperity,
his charities were unstinted and unmeasured. Thirty.five years ago, then in the
full vigor of his mature but unimpaired manhood, he presided over the deliberations and guided the counsels of this Grand Body. There is much in his careflr
and character to command our affectionate pride. Few men have led more active,
tryin1r, or adventurous lives, and few have acquitted themselves with more uniform
credit. As ci•ilian and as soldier, as public officer and as private citizen, as lawyer
and as layman, as husband, father, friend and Freemason-in all these capacities
he has faithfully redeemed every trust that has been reposed in him.
He is with us still, but the merciless hand of Time has wrought its inevitable
changes. His zeal, devotion, and fidelity are una.b ated, but health, strength, and
resources are materially depleted. At a little less than fourscore and six years
of age (and threescore and five of these years have been spimt in our Masonic
family,) misfortunes, which no prudence or sagacity could avert, sit heavily upon
him and his invalid household; while the infirmities of age cruelly aJmonish us
that the great destroyer is too rapidly wasting and consuming his vitality.
We need not say that 'we refer to our first Grand Master, JONATHAN DRAKE
STEVENSON-justly entitled to be hailed as the founder and father of Freemasonry
in California. He deserves some testimonial from us. Let us take the patriarch
still nearer to our hearts and make him the life-guest of this Grand L odge. Let
us mellow and soften his pathway to the tomb by tran•ferring from his to our own
le88 weary shoulders some of the cares and burdens of hie declining years, and
teach him to realize that bread cast upon the waters will sooner or later return
to bless the lfiver.
In furtherance of these suggestions, in earnest of our sincerity in making

1885.]

Grand Lodge of Oal,ifornia.

235

them, and to give them practical effect, we propose the fallowing resolution and
commend it to your kind thoughts and considerate attention:Reselve.d, That in token of our appreciation of the early services of our venerable
Past Grand Master, JONATHAN DBAKR STRVENSON, and in evidence of our continued esteem and affection for him as a man and a Mason, the sum of twelve hun·
dred d1>llars be set apart and appropriated to his use from the general fund of
this Grand Lodge, to be remitted to him, under the direction of the Grand Master,
in monthly installments of one hundred dollars each.

Bro. JosEPH C. WARD, from the special committee upon the Report of the Grand Lecturer, presented the following report:To the M. '. W. '. Grand L'Xige of Oalif<l/"llia :-

Your committee, to whom wae referred the Annual Report of the Grand Lecturer, consisting principally of a well-prepared and highly interesting summary of
the reports of the several Inspectors, together with valuable comments and sujlgestions by himself, have had the same under consideration.
We take pleasure in noting that the Inspectors are beginnini to realize their
duties toward this Grand Lodge in the matter of reports, and that, at this writing,
there remains but one of them delinquent. A little more promptness, however, on
the part of some of them in getting their reports before the Grand Lecturer, is
desirable.
Former committees have commended the reports of the Grand Lecturer to the
consideration of the Fraternity-especia.lly to the Masters of Lodges and the Inspectors of the several Masonic districts. Your present committee regard the re·
port under consideration as one of more than usual interest, and our commendation of it to a careful reading by the officers oi Lodges and the Fraternity generally, we desire to emphasize. Especially to the Inspectors would we recommend
a thoughtful consideration of the Grand Lecturer's criticisms and suggestions.
We call attention to his comments on the manner of inspection adopted by Bro.
BusH, of the Fourth District, and we concur with him in the opinion that this
method of inspection would prove fatal to the system. The Grand Lecturer does
not cen~ure Bro. BUSH, and your committee will not; as, under the circumstances,
it would be an injustice to do so. But we do say, emphatically, that no brother
should ·accept the position of Inspector, whose other duties will not permit him te
perform faithfully those of that office.
We call the attention of Lodges to the Grand Lecturer's remarks on the practice of appointing meetings for the installation of officers before the Master has
received his certificate of qualification, or before it is known whether he is quali·
fled or not; to Secretaries we call attention to the charge of neglect, in some instance•, to write up the Black Book, as required by the Constitution; and to Masters the charge, made many times heretofore as well as now, of neglect to sign
their records.
We would kindly remind Anaheim Lodge, No. 207, that, as the Reiulations require the Inspector to visit the several Lodges of his District, it follows that, when
notified bv that officer of a proposed visit at a certain specified date, it is the duty
of the Master receiving such notice to convene his Lodge for the purpose of inspec·
tion; and we would remind all the Lodges of the Jurisdiction that it is obligatory
upon the Inspector to make these visits; but that to do so involves an expense
which it is not intended should be borne by him alone, and that it is the duty of
the Lodges to defray the necessary traveling expenses of that officer.
We cannot close this report without reference to the valuable auggeetion1 con·
ta.ined in the report of Bro. JAMES W. ANDERSON, Inspector of the Twenty-fourth
District; and we call particular attention to his pointed ami truthful rimarke rela-

llonora. We commend the reading of Bro. ANDERBON'li remarks in this connecllnn, not only to the subordinate Lodgee, but to the Grand Lodge as well.

months, and within the jurisdiction of the Lodge during sia: months, next preceding the
date of his application, except in tlie case of a person belonging to the army or
navy 'of the United States.
This inhibition is explicit, and we know of no provision of the Constitution
which in any way modifies or relaxes it; and we finrl nothing in that instrument
which authorizes a Lodie to take any action in respect to a person, not a Mason,
resident within its territory, until he has made application to it for the degrees.
Upon the presentation of such an application, its jurisdiction over the person ia
called into exeroise. It can then elect or reject him; and, having elected and con·
ferred the first degree upon him, it can aurrender its jurisdiction over him to another Lodge at his request.
In the case before the Grand Master, it would seem that one Lodge had in'
form surrendered and another had asaumed Jurisdiction to receive and act upon
an application for degree1, and, as the applicant was rejected, thA queation was
whether the Lodge, within whose territory h11 was a resident, could receive an ap·
plication from him within twelve months from the date of such rejection.
'l'hat queetion is answered by the second clause of thA section of the Conatitu.
tion that we have quoted, which add1-" Nor ahall any Lodge Nceive auoh application from any person who, within twelve months ne~t preceding, Rhall have been
rejected by any Lodge, unlees by di~pensation from the Grand Master."
If the queetlcm wAre new we should certainly hold that the action of the tWG
Lor!ges in respect to such an application was wholly void, and that the olauae of the
Constitution last cited applied only to caaes where an applicant had been rejeoted
by a Lodge havWig jurisdictitm to receive and act upon his application, and not to a
case where he had been rAjeoted by a Lodge which had no authority Aither to receive
or to aot upon auoh application, We find, however, that in 1870 the Grand Lodge
approved a report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, to the effect that when a
Lodge had, withont right, received the application for de1rree1 from a person re•
siding within the territory of another Lodge, and had rejected him, the latter
Lodge could not receive hia application until the expiration of the twelve montha:
and we think it well to adhere to the rule then adopted. The decision of the Grand
Master appears to have been in acoordanoe with that rule.
The remailling decisiona are bdieved to be consonant with our laws, and it is
recommended that they be approved.
The Gr nd Master refers to the Regulatifln forbidding the expenditure by
Lodge11 of any part of their funds for purposes of refreshment, iiinnera, or ool·
lationa, and sU1:11ests that that Regulation might be so modified as to permit of a
moderate expenditure for auoh refreshment~ in oert11in caRes. The Regulation
referred to waa adopted by the Grand Lodge for the protection of Lodge funds
which are sacred te purposes of charity, and expres~ed the protest of the Fraternity
against their misuse or appropriation for light or trivial causes. Your oolllmittee
regard the Regulation as a most proper and Masonic one, and would regret to see
its prohibitory features in any way modified.

aurrtmder juriadiction over a person not a Mason, who resides within the territory
over which its jurisdiction iR exclusive? 2d. Can any Lodge in this State law.

[Oct. 12,

Twenty-nine years ago I commenced to attend and observe the proceedings of
this Grand Lodge, and, when I compare the small number who then met in convocation with the numerous body now before me, I am forcibly reminded of the
grand success, prosperity and influence of our Order in the Golden State.
These are matters for our earnest and serious consideration, and should admonish us to continue in the well-beaten path.
Through the united wisdom of the Craft our acts and legislation have been kept
within the bounds of reason and common sense, and the vast army of cranks and
irreconcilables, who now so largely punish mankind by the introduction of their
departures from the laws of civilization, have been unable to sow the seeds of their
discord here. Let us, then, rejoice for the wisdom of the past, and let it be a
bright example for the future.
Owing to other duties which I could not control, I have not been able to visit
as many Lodges within the jurisdiction as I desired. But from such observation
as I have had, and the reports from the lnspectors of the several Masonic Districts,
I am pleased to be enabled to inform you that the past year has been one of general
prosperity and advancement for our Order within this Jurisdiction. The efforts at
discord and confusion have been generally rejected, and the few unsettled cases are
in a fair way for adjustment and adjudication.
The Supreme Ruler of the Universe, in his inflictions of death, has been unusually lenient towards our brethren during the past year, but among the few who
have been taken it is my sad duty tt> announce the name of JOHN PAUL JONES
DAVISON, a Past Master of GrorgekrWn Lodge, No. 25. This venerable Mason,
perhaps the oldest and longest in the service of any on the Pacific Coast, died at
G1lorgetown, in El .Dorado County, and was buried with due honor and ceremony
by his Lodge, assisted by many of the members of the neighboring Lodges, whG all
united in doing every honor to this venerable relic and devotee to Masonry.
Having learned that Santa CT.an-a Lodge, No. 34, was becoming disorganized in
consequence of the trial therein of Bro. PARKER Bu•rTERFIELD HOLMES, a member
and Past Master thereof, for unmasonic conduct, I visited the Lod&'& and personally investigated the matter. I became convinced that the good of Masonry
demanded that the charter of Santa Ckura Lodge, No. 34, should be arrested 1 and
on the seventeenth day of February last I demanded and received the charter, seal,
and other documents belonging to the Lodge.
While the majority of the members of Santa OT.an-a Lodge are withGut Masonic
blame in this matter, there are a few who seem to be the originators of all the
tr<1mble, and who persist in their evil ways. I therefore exempted from the penalty of suspension, in consequence of the arrest of the charter, such of the members
as I believed to be blameless. It appears that the Lodge has funds yet in the
hands of its Treasurer, and the same was drawn upon to pay such debts as the
Lodge owed at the time of the arrest of its charter. That instrument is in the
hands of the Grand Secretary, and I ask that you give the matter your earnest
attention.
On the tenth day of April last I learned that Bro. ISAIAH L. HOPKINS, one of
the members of Santa Clara Lodge, No. 34, who had been exempted from the penalty of svspension in consequence of the arrest of the charter, had died at Gilroy
and requested a Masonic burial. I telegraphed to the Master of Keith Lodge, No'.

duty was duly performed and that a bill for $143, the expense of the burialj sick•
ness, etc., has been rendered by Keith Lodge, This bill should be duly considered
in the affairs of Santa OT.an-a Lodge, as it should be an account against the fund•
and property of that Lodge.

Quuti<m. Can a Master Mason's daughter, after her marriage, re-instate her
claims on the Order, by virtue of being the daughter of a Master Mason?
AnBWe'l'. No. When she married she severed her rights in the Order by and
through her father, and thence can only retain her rights therein by and through
her husband.
Question. When does a Master Mason's son cease to have any claim on the
Order?
An8Wer. When he arrives at the age of twenty-one years, unless he becomes
himself a member of the Order.
Question. A brother was a non-affiliate and paid to the Lodge the sum of six dollars, and thereupon petitioned to the Lodge for affiliation and was rejected.
Within a short time the brother petitioned to another Lodge for affiliation and was
accepted. He now wants the first Lodge to return him the six dollars.
Answer. The sum paid the first Lodge was to place the brother in standing so
that he could petition, and it belongs to the funds of that Lodge. If that Lodge
so desires, it can return him the money, but is under no obligation to do so.
When a member of the Lodge objects to the initiation of a candidate who bas
been elected to rec•i ve the degrees of Masonry in the Lodge, that objection stay•
all further proceedings in the matter for sixty days or until withdrawn, and if the
objection is not withdrawn within the sixty days, the Secretary of the Lodge must
report to the Grand Secretary that the candidate was r~jectee.
'
It is not necessary for the brother who makes the objection to the initiation of
the candidate in his Lodge to state to the Master, or to any other person, what hie
objections are.

Excelsior LortJte, No. 166, proposed the following' amendment to itA by-laws, and
submitted it to me for my approval:Any member of this Lodge, who has been such in good standing for twenty-fi're

membership, under the seal of this Lodge, signed by the Worshipful Master an'.i

.Thi~ would Sfero to be an effort on the part of this Lodge to establish a system

violation of our Uniform Code of By-Laws, which Uniform Code has been adopted
and rigidly adhered to on all occasions by this Grand Lodge. I therefore refused

A communication was received a few days since from the Grand Mlll!ter of
Masons in South Carolina l'elative to the distress pre,·ailing at Charleston in con1equence of the great earthquake which lately occurred ;;t that city and vicinity.
B•lieving from the newspaper reports and other information that the immediate
wants of the sufferers were being supplied, I thought it proper, as the meeting of
this Grand Lodge was so near at hand, to refer the whole matter to you, that you
mii;cht take such action as you deemed right and proper in the premises.
A careful invest;gation of the matter oi trials, and other proceedings connected
therewith, has convinced me that we are rapidly departing from the ancient usages
and customs of the Craft, and that we are drifting into the customs of the criminal
oourts, where paid attorneys, stays of proceedings, and legal quibbl•s and demurrers are the rules of practice. We want justice plainly adminiatered, not legal
technicalities and delays.
The mechanical mind and Master Workman who is by the vote of hie Lodge
elected a Commissioner to try one of his brethren for an offense against our laws,
1its there in a different position from a juror summoned in one of our criminal
courts to try a criminal for an offense against the State laws. The Commissioner
la not inclined to '.lea! harshly and unjustly with the defendant, for there are sympathies and obligations between him and his defendant that do not exist with the
juror and hie defendant. Then why should the Commissioner, his judgment and
hie verdict, Le subject to the same procedure as the juror and his verdict in our
State courts?
It is plain to the practical mind that the procedures in our criminal courts under
the State can only be conducted by learned judges and attorneys who are exP6its
in those procedures, and who among themselves invariably differ as to the interpretation of the law. Tben why should those who are known not to be legal experts
be held to strict accountability in matters which they do not understand? As our
laws impose up"n the Master Workman the duty of sitting and determining in hie
judgment the kind and extent of the offense of his Brother Workman, let us not
surround him with strict forms and ceremonies, such that his honest and just decision may be set aside and the criminal go unpunished for the want of technical
knowledQ'e on the part of the Oommissioner.
During the time in which you have honored and placed me in the highest position within your gift, owing to the many other duties which I was compelled to
perform, I have not been able to give that attention to the duties of this office
which it wus my desire to give. In many of the labors whi<-h I have performed I
have been greatly assisted by our Grand f:lecretary and his aasietant, whose kindneas and to me valuable assistance have greatly lightened the burdens on me, for
which I desire to express to each of them my sincere thanks.
I have now, my brethren, presented to you a synopsis of what I deem the more
Important issues presented to me for my action, and I trust that you will deal with
them in the manner which you think w.m be for the greatest good of the Order.
In conclusion, I thank you for the high honor you have bestowed, and the confidence you have reposed in me. At this convocation, with your permission, it is
my desire to sever my official, but not my personal, labors with you.
WILEY JAMES TINNIN,

Grand Maater.

during several years past, there having been no alteration of the order of the Grand

More than the usual number of books received during a year have been added
to our library, and the increase has been so great since the publication of the
latest catalogue of its contents, in 1883, that the undersigned proposes, if bis health
permits, to prepare a new one as soon as may oo after the close of the present Communication. It will probably be his last, and, aij be desires that it may be as full
as po~sible, renewed efforts are being made to procure such missing numbers of the
earlier Proceedings of the many Grand Bodies with which our Grand Lodge is in
correspondence as will enable him to bind, in consecutive and complete order, as
much of the vast mass of pamphlets still on hanll, unbound, as may be practicable.

KINS, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Florida, giving information of the
destruction by fire of the library of that Body, and modestly intimating that it
would be very gratifying if the Proceedings of California:, thus lost, could be replaced. Years ago Bro. DAWKINS, at various times, very kindly rendered such
eood service to the undersigned and to our Grand Lodge, by procuring for and
tran~mitting to us many missing Proceedings of the Grand Bodies of Florida, as
well as others, -that we now have those of all the Bodies of that Rtate complete
from the dates of their several organizations; and, remembering this, as well as
sympathizing with the misfortune of our brethren of Florida., a full set of our
bound Proceedings, comprising sixteen large octavo volumes, was at once forwarded to that Grand Secretary as a gift from our Grand Lodge, with the conviction that the act was but an anticipation of its wishes. An acknowledgment of
the receipt of the books is herewith presented.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To the M. '. W, '. Grand Lodge of California:! herewith sabmit my annual report of the condition of the Lodges in this
jurisdiction, as compiled from the reports which have been forwarded to me from the·
Inspectors of the following Masonic Districts, viz.: Nos. 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, II, 11, 14, '111,
16, 11, 18, 19, 20, 21, 28, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, :w, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36. I have, aa
usual, given instruction to such Inspectors, Masters and Wardens as have personally applied to me for that purpose, and, in one instance, have qualified in our
work a brother of a n eighboring jurisdiction.
On the seventh day of June last, I received a letter from theM.'. W.·. Bro. George
H. DAVIS, Grand Master of Idaho, stating that, in visiting the subordinate Lodgea
of his jurisdiction, he had found a painful lack of uniformity in the ritual. N<>
two worked alike, and the result was confusion among the Craft. He also stated
that the Grand Lodge of Idaho had never adopted or promulgated an authorized
work, although recommending tbat of California; and that a few years ago some
instruction in the California work was given in Idaho, but, as there was no standard or authority within reach, to which appeal could be made, changes and inn~.
vations had crept in, and finally each Lodge worked upon the "go as yon please•~

Grand Lodge of California.

plan. He further stated th11.t it was his desire to perfect a number of bis brethren
In the California work, to exemplify it before the Grand Lodge, and to rEocommend
Its adoption ; and to that end he wished to' know how h~ could obtain the authorized work of this jurisdiction.
I replied that, if he would send an authorized brother to San Francisco, I would
with great pleasure qualify him to teach the work, which measure seemed to be
the easiest way out of the dilemma. On the twenty-seventh day of July following,
Bro. C. B. HUMPHBBY, Master of lJoiBe Lodge, No. 2, of Idaho, presented himself
to me, bearing tbe authorization of the Grand Master of Masons in that Territory,
with the request that I would give him the desired instruction. In compliance
therewith I fully instructed Bro. HUMPHREY in the work and lectures of the several degrees, and sent him on his way rejoicing. As the Grand Lodge of Idaho
holds its Annual Communications in September, I have not yet learned what
action, if any, it took in the premises.
The reports of the Inspectors which ha1·e come to hand show the Lodges in this
jurisdiction, in most instanoes, to be in good condition, financially and otherwise,
and their officers proficient in the work and zealous in the discharge of their duties.
I regret that several of the Inspectors have failed to report, and that among the
number are some of our oldest and most reliable officers.
·
Inspector JOHN M. MELBNDY, of the First District, reports that the ti ve Lodges
under his supervision are in good working con~tion and constantly increasing in
membership-the officers universally manifesting an earnest desire to promote the
welfare of their respective Lodges and to conform strictly to the work as laid down
by the Grand Lodge.
Inspector GEORG& H. KNIGHT, of the Third District, reports that the Lodges
therein, four in number, are in a flourishing condition, and that, with one exception,
Surprise Valley, No. 235, all have had work during the year. Adin, No, 250, of
which he is a member, has a membership of forty-six, is out of debt, owns its hall,
and bas a small balance in its treasury. Bro, KNIGHT saysThe good effect upon the LodffeS of the visit by the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer, in June of last year, 1s evidenced by the increased attendance at the
meetings and desire of the members to perfect themselves in the work.
Bro. KNIGHT further states that the urgency of business engagements renders
It very inconvenient for him to attend to the duties of Inspector as faithfully as he
would desire, and suggests that perhaps the best interests of the Craft would be
1ubserved by the appointment of some brother who has more time at hie disposal.
As Bro. KNIGHT has made an excellent Inspector, and has ever been faithful in
the discharge of his duties, it is hoped that he may be induced to remain in the
1ervice.

~d intelligent report of the condition of the nine Lodges composing hie district,

the third degree upon the only candidate who has been admitted into that Lodge

Although the town ha• lost much of its former prosperity, the members of the
Lodge have lost none of their zeal. They have a comfortable hall ;· the Secretary's
books are well kept ; and the treasury is well supplied with funds. He witnessed
the conferring of the third degree in Northern Lighe, No. 190, and compliments
the officers and members highly upon their proficiear.y. He sayA-

'

Inspector WILLIAM E. OUGHTON, of the Eighteenth District, makes an elaborate report of the condition of the sixteen Lodges under his supervision. The
paper does him much credit and shows that he has faithfully performed the duties
assigned him by the Grand Lodge. He reports the five Lodges meeting in the
city of Sacramento to be in good condition, all having done some work during the
year. In his last report he called my attention to the fact that these five Lodges
kept but one common Black Book, a matter which I deemed of sufficient import·
ance to bring before the Grand Lodge at its last Annual Communication, descanting at some length upon the impropriety of such a practice. Bro. OimHTON reports
that there has been no amendment in this particular, the Secretaries of the various
Lodges asserting that they obey the apirit if not the letter of the law, as the book
is open to all the Lodges; and that, to obey the letter of the law, all that would b6
necessary for them to do would be to change the covers from night to night--oalling
it one night Black Book of Sacrament<>, No. 40, and another night Black Book ef
Tehama, No. 3 ! So silly a proposition is unworthy oJ a moment's consideration..
Suppose that, by accident or design, this partnership book should be lost or destroyed,
or that one or more of these Lodges should see fit to change its or their place of meeting? As well might the Lodges in San Francisco, which meet in the Masonic
Temple, claim to fulfill the Bpirit of the law by having one common Black Book !
Yet they are strictly required to keep each a separate one. It is plainly to be seen
that the course pursued by the brethren of Sacramento com plies neither with the
spirit nor the letter of the law; the disposition to evade it should be rebuked, and
the Secretaries should be compelled to conform strictly to its requirements.
Bro. OUGHTON reports that, in one or two of the Lodges, it is asserted that applicants are rejected without good Masonic reasons, and that prejudice, passion and
Helt-interest are allowed to influence the action of some of the brethren. With
these unfortunate exceptions, there appears to be great harmony throughout the
district. Natoma, No. 64, he says, has done no work during the year, having
rejected six applicants. N eb't'aaka, No. n, has had no work for several years, and
it is reported that the Lodge is about to surrender its charter. With these two
exceptions, the Lodges are reported to be in good condition, their officers fairly
proficient, their books well kept, (except in the instances of the Black Book,) and
their finances in sound condition.
Inspector FRANOIS NroHOLLS, of the Nineteenth District, reports that he hail
visited all the seven Lodges therein, except Georgdown, No. 25, and that harmony
prevails, although little work has been done. He says that some of the Ilod1res
have very little prospect thereof for the future, and should consolidate. All except Georgetown, No. 25, have money in their treasuries. Their officers are proficient in the work and always willing to be instructed where they may be wrong,
and their books arfl well kept, without exception.
Inspector RoBERT .ArrKll:N, of the Twentieth District, reports that he has
visited each of the eight Lodges therein, and found them all competent to do,
good work if they had the opportunity; but that opportunity had seldom presented '
itself durin'!' the past yea~, and that to three of the Lodges it had not come at
all. He reports them all in good condition except St. Mark'a, No. 85, and Volcano,
No. 56. The former, he says, is considerably embarrassed by a debt due to the
Sacra.mento Board of Relief for expenses incurred during the long illneBB of one of
its members in that city. The latter is in a languishing condition, 11id to sick
members, funeral expense5 and other charities having caused a depletion of its
treasury. Its membership has been steadily decreasing, and the decadence of the
town in which it is located gives little hope of a reaction, Although it is still out.
of debt, the brethren are despondent, and many of them think that consolidation
with a. neighboring Lodge will soen be advisable.

Inspector WILLIAM G. LONG, of the Twenty-first District, reports that the
five Lodges entrusted to his care enjoy an average degree of prosperity, that the
officers are proficient in the work, that the books are well kept, and that harmony
prevails throughout the district. Not much work has been done, but that which

Inspector JAMES RANKIN, of the Twenty-third District, gives a very favorable
report of the four Lodges placed under his supervision. Not so much work has
been done as in some former years, yet the officers are zealous in the discharge of
their duties and are proficient, the books of the Secretaries are well kept, and the
average attendance is fair.
Inspector JA111:e:s B. MERRITT, of the Twenty.fourth District, makes a very
clear, interesting and exceptionally well-prepared report of the condition of the ten
Lodges confided to his superintendence,-giving the results of his inspection in detail. He is a faithful officer, and his duties are performed with aHBiduity and zeal.
Such of the Lodges as he found deficient in the work he took pains to instruct, and
·by perseverance and patience induced their officers to study and practice until
they became proficient. Oakland, No. 188, he complimentd very highly for the
manner in which its work was done. He visited this Lodge on July 17th, in company with the Grand Master, and reports that : "The work was more than well
done." Of one Lodge he says: "The Master conferred the third degree as nearly
correctly as I have seen it done for a long time. He has a good memory but a poor
delivery, and the lecture acted somewhat as a narcotic upon a number of the brethren present." In Alameda, No.167, he intimates that some element of discord has
disturbed the good-fellowship of the brethren, and, notwithstanding his efforts to
restore peace and concord, he fears that it will be some time before good feeling
and tranquillity can be restored. Of his own Lodge, Oak Grove, No. 2115, he saysThe black-ball reignE supreme in this Lodge. It is to be hoped that more wia-.
dam will bd shown in recommending candidates, or in their treatment after recommendation. Several have been deservedly rejected, as has been plainly shown•
others appear to have the necessary internal qualifications; while still others wh~
have conceived a favorable opinion of our Ancient Institution, fear to present their
petitions lest they, too, be deemed unworthy.
He reports that the books of the various Lodges are well and accurately kept,
and pays a special compliment to the Secretary of Oak Grove, No. 215, who "writes
like copper-plate a.nd never makes a mistake." The report is a model one, and
from it I infer that the Craft in the Twenty.fourth District, as a whole, is in a
flourishing condition. .

In April last, Bro. WALTER S. ABELL, of Occidflntal Lodge, No. 22, was
appointed by the Grand Master a Special Deputy Grand Lecturer, and waA authorized to proceed to Honolulu, Hawaiian Islands, for the purpose of giving the
officers and members of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, such instruction as he might
deem necessary in the work and lectures of the several degrees. The report of
Bro. ABELL contain11 so much of interest that, notwithstanding its considerable
length, I deem it proper to give it in full, as follows:To THE W,". JOHN W, SHAEFFER,
Gmnd Lecturer of the Grand Lodge of California:DEAR Sm AND BBO. : I have the honor to report that on the 15th day of April
1886, I received from yo!-lr ~ands a certificate of qualification as Deputr Grand
Lecturer, and an authorization from the M. '. W. '. Grand Master empowermg m~ to
exemplify the Work of Masonry to Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, at Honolulu, Hawaiian
Islands, and give the brethren thereof such instruction in the ritual, usages and law
as I might find necessary. On the 17th day of that month, in company with the
Master of that Lodge, Bro. JAMES M. MONBARRAT, I sailed for Honolulu. Many
pleasant hours during the seven days' voyage were passed in explaining and
teaching the work to that officer, whose zealous attention and interest I co.n not too
highly commend. We arrived safely on the 24th day of April, and on the 26th a
special meeting was called for the purpose of presenting my cred entials to the Lodge.
I briefly explained the object of my visit, defined the general duties of a Lodge
and its officers, and called special attention to the necessity of earnest co-operation
among the members, and particularly among the officers, if they wished to do good
work. After which an informal Lodge of Instruction was held.
A series of such Lodges was thus inaugurated, and they were continued with
more or less success during my sojourn of five weeks with the Lodge. I also met
the C)fficers privately for the purpose of instruction whenever their time would
permit. I was a little disappointed in the attendance at the L orlges of Instruction,
and in the lack of zeal displayed by Mme of the officers in endea vorinir to obtain
the work. The condition of the Lodge was certainly deplorable. and nothinlf but
the most strenuous efforts on the part of its officers could straighten out the work. ·
Such efforts I was unable to arouse, except among the tew, and consequently I can

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

not truthfully say that I feel entirely satisfied with the results of my mission. . I
endeavored to impress upon their minds the necessity of eleotinl!' and apJXJinting
oflic~rs who would attend regularly and learn the work correctly ; and, in this connect10n, I can not do better than quote the words of Bro. ANDERSON, Inspector of
the 'l'wenty-fifth District, ·in his report to you at the last Annual Communication, in the hope that it may meet the eyes of our Hawaiian brethren and that they
may profit thereby. Bro. ANDERSON said·
"'He is a good fellow and it will not do to supplant him,' is the cry, and thus
incompetent and sometimes unworthy brethren are placed in high positions, to the
great detriment of the Craft. It is the duty of all good MA.sons to set their faces
determinedly against this pernicious custom-for custom it has become-and agree
to unite upon the best and most capable among them to fill the important positions
in their Lodges."
A general feeling of apathy ssemed to prevail, attributed by many to the enervating effects of the warm olimate in which they dwell, but perhaps more correctly,
to a lack of energy on their own parts. I learned that for a number of years no
Master had given the lectures in the different d0j!'rees, and, in fact, that no M••ter
now living there had ever learned that o{ the third. I directed their attention to
the resolution adopted at the first Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge,
making it obligatory upon Masters t<> deliver the lectures; and intima·ed that any
future remissness in that respect might meet with the extreme disapproval of the
Grand Master. That the captious mar not declaim against the Inspector of that
District (whom I found to be a verr estimable and zealous brother,) for giving certificates of qualification to successive Masters when they were not qualified, I will
say that the fault lay in the fact that for some fir teen years the Lodge had not been
visited by any one for the purpose of inspection or instruction; and that to this,
consequently1 was due the deterioration in the work and the ignorance on many
im~>rtant \)otnts of ritual and law.
That this will not be so in the future I feel very confident, for, previous to my
departure, at the request of tt.e Inspector himself, anrl of the officers anil membera
as well. I instrncted Past Master THEODORE C. PORTER in the work and lectures,
with the hope that our M . '. W. '. Grand Master may, in his discretion, sM fit to appoint him Inspector of that District. I make this suggestion, not only as the evident
desire of Hawxiian Lod~e, hut with the knowledge, acquired by an intimate association with Bro. PORTER that he is the moAt competent and efficient brother
within the jurisdiction to fih that position. I am indebted to him for assistance
and encouragement during my stay, and am much pleased to have this opportunity
of further thanking him therefor.
At the stated meeting of the first of May, at my reQuest, the Master appointed a committee, consisting of Inspector HOWE and Past Master PORTER, to
Bllsist me in inspecting the books and condition of the Lodge. I found the Lodge
in a very satisfactory condition financially, the owner of the very hanrl.some
building in which the hall is situated, and with a re1•enue from rentals and dues
that is fast diminishinir the debt now existing on the building, so that its early
extinction may be safely prophesied. I disagree with Bro. H owE in his report
of last year, where he HYB that, " with some few amendmPnts in the manner of
keeping its books and account•, its conrlition may be pronounoed satisfactor7." On
the contrary, I think that there ought to be a most decided reformation m thoM
particulars before such a satisfactory condition could be assured. fn many respects
the Lodge has failed to meet the requirements of the Grand Lodge. In the collection of dues many members are allowed to be in arrears for years without action
thereupon. This is P.artly accounted for by the fact that some of them reside
on other islands, whilst others are sea-faring men engaged in long voyages. The
latter may be a t enable reason, but the former, with the efficient postal service
inaugurated under the present reign, will hardly hold good. • No reason can be
olf~r~d1 h_owever, f.or ,the failure t'? comply wi~h the law requiring complete records
of 1mt1at10ns, affihat1ons, suspens10ns, expuls10ns, etc., tn he kept in o. Roll Book
and Black Book, as required by Sec. 2, Art. V, Part IV, of the Constitut10n.
These books were absolutl'ly unknown there, but have since been sent to the Lodge,
and the Master has promised to see them written up in proper form. All the books
evinced a lack of neatness and carerulness which is greatly to be reprehended. Yat
I have much hope that this will be avoided in the future, and tho.t, having now
been set in the right track, there will be no need of further animadversion.
In closing, I desire to thank the officer~ and members of Hawaiian Lodge for
their Bl!Bistance and co-operation in my labors, and for their manifold kindnesses
to myself. That I am proud to have been the instrument of our Grand Lodge
in the work done need not be said. I foresee a prosperous and successful
career for the Lodge. There is an amplitude of available ma~erial in the juris-

It is to be observed, as always heretofore, that these expenditures do not include,
nor have they ever included, any outlay for any member of a Lodge in this city, or
for his wife, widow, or children, as each Lodge here takes care of its own destitute
and distressed. And it is to be noted also, that the word "case," as used in this
report, means either an ind£11idual or a family and includes all the relief afforded,
whether at one time or more, and in one instance has for some time represented a
widow and seven children.

the two Lodges above mentioned, still refuse to join in the compact under which
this Board was established, or to share in its responsibilities; although the last named
Lodge has contributed to its funds, since May 10th, 1886, an amount equal to the
per capUa assessment under the compact,

The Grand Master decided that when a member, objecting to the initiation of a
candidate, states bis objections in open Lu<lge, the matter is placed by him in the
hands of the Lodge, and may be considered and determined by an onaoimoos vote
thereof, the objector excepted; and if the Lodgo shall decide by such vote that
the reasons given are not sufficient, the Master may confer the degree. Such Is not
the law in California. In Alabama the three·ballot rule obtains, and we presume
this decision applies to each degree.
The Grand Master also decides that one who had taken the first two degrees,
had proceeded with the third degree as far as the conclnsion of the obligation, and
had then decliued or refused to proceed further, occnpied the status of a Fellow
Ure.ft, and could not be hel,d or treated as a Master Mason, in any sense of the word.
Also, that one who holds a 32° patent, " Scottish Rite," cannot be admitted into a
Lodge on the presentation of his patent and taking the test oath, but must be examined by a committee of the Lodge. We give these two decisions as they involve
questions that have not heretofore met our notice. We think that both are good
law.

Quite a long and carefully prepared report was presented by the Com_m ittee on
Jurisprudence relative to the powers of the Grand Master. The committee arrive at
the conclusion that the Grand Master possesses and may e.~ercise powers and pre·
rogatives not expressly given by the Constitution. We respectfully dissent from
such a conclusion. The Grand Lodge of <Jalifornia has put. itself upon the record
upon this Important matter, and believ~s that the Grand Master, like 11.ll other
Masons, is to be governed by its Organic Law.

Whatever may be the IR w in Arizona relative thereto, we are clearly of the
opinion that the decision of the Grand Master "that a Past Master, as deft·aed in the
Constitution, was one who bad gained that title by service •within the jurisdiction of
this Grand Lodge;' and that by this latter expression Is meant service in a Lodge
chartered by this Grand L<ldge and acting under its Constitution," is wrong. The
Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom the decision was referred, eay "that this last
implies that this service shall have been since the organization of this Grand Lodge
and the adoption of tl1e present Constitution." This excludes, it seems to us, all those
who became Past Masters during the time that Arizona was subject to the Grand
Lodge of California. This to our mind appears manifestly unjust. It furthermore
seems to us that the decision, as well as the . opinion of the Committee on Jurisprudence, excludes the very parties who framed the Constitution, unless such parties have
since the adoption served a term as Master of a chartered Lodge. An amendment
to the Constitution was subsequently introdnced, to the effect that all those who were
borne on the rolls . of the several Lodges within the Territory of Arizona as Past
Masters, at the time of the organization of the Grand Lodge, should be entitled to sit
and vote in the Grand Lodge. We would not favor even the amendment; we think
ft should limit Past Masters to those borne on the rolls of the Lodges who bad ob·
tained the title by service within the limits of the Territory of Arizona.

We do not speak disparagingly of the re views that have heretofore been made; they
are creditable alike to the writers and to the Grand Lodge, and have been so considered
by the numerous able writers to whose scrutinizing judgment they have been submitted. But we are led, by oar brief experience, to the conclusion that this work: ie
BO important, so great, and so arduous, as to require more time and space than le
usually appropriated to it. We acknowledge, candidly, that we entered upon the
dlscl)arge ol' our duties, in our last review, impressed with the opinion that these
reports were comparatively useless. It wae an opinion formed, as opinions often

ARKANSAS.

The forty-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas was held
in the city of Little Rock, commencing on the twenty-fourth day of November, 1885,-the M.·. W.'. W. H. H. CLAYTON, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.·. FAY
HEMPSTEAD being Grand Secretary. Two hundred and ninety Lodges were represented, being the largest attendance that there has been at any time since the organ·
ization of the Grand Lodge.
The Address of the Grand Ma•ter opens with greeting and congrntulation upon
the fact that peace with its manifold blessings had prevailed, and prosperity bad
abounded. Becoming respect is paid to the memory of those who bad passed the
silent river during the year. Among these the Grand Master mentions the names of
the R.·. W.·. Senior Grand Warden, Bro. W. H. HOWES ; Bro. R. P. PULLIAM, a
veteran Past Grand Maoter; and Bro. E. R. DUVAL, also a Pa•t Grand Master.
Dispensations had been issued for the formation of seven new Lodges, and the
charters of two Lodges had been arrested. Twenty-two decisions are reported.
We quote the following:2. A brother having received the degrees of Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
in a Lodge of another Grand Jurisdiction, was there tried on charges and regularly
suspended. He afterward move<l. into this Grand Jurisdiction and was raised by
one of our Lodges while under this sentence of suspension,
Held, lat. That the act of the Lodge in conferring on him the Master Mason's
degree was void, whether the Lodge was aware of the fact of his suspension or not.
That the brother w~s not made a Master Mason by the ceremony, but remained a.
suspended Fellow Craft.
2d. That if the suspended Fellow Craft knew, atthe time he made his application
for the Master Mason's degree, that he was suspended or thnt charges were pending
against. him, and did not disolose that fac1 to the Lodge, charges shon1d be preferred
against him as a suspended Fellow Craft, and be be expelled.
Sd. That if the Lodge had information of the fact that he stood suspended, when
it conferred the degree, it was guilty of a grave Masonic offense for whioh its charter
should be arrested.
6. A brother living within the jurisdiction of a Lodge of which he is not a member, cannot be tried by that Lodge for a Masonic offense committed by him out of,
and previons to, his moviug withiil, its jurisdiction.
6. A Lodge may try its own menibers for any .Masonic offense, no matter where
comll\itted, whether within if.a territorial jurisdiction or elsewhere.
7. A Lodge, while working nnder a dispensation, is subject to the same Grand
Lodge dues as those working under chartars.
·
19. A Mason who resides in this Grand Jurisdiction, but is a member of a Lodge
of another Grand Jurisdiction, cannot join in a petition for a dispensation for a new
Lodge until he has procured a dimit and affiliated with some Lodge in this State.
20. A candidate, having applied for initiation, was rejected, and the Secretary
neglected t~ return the fee. At the end of t.wo months the rejected c1mdidate gave
H., a member of the Lodge, an order on the Secretary for it. H. owed the Secretary
$15, but refused to allow the $10 fee to he considered as part payment. The Lodge
then appropriated to H. the amount oqhe fee and cha.rged it to the Secretary.

1886.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifor-rtia.

525

The Lodge did right. As soon as the candidate's application for initiation was
rejected, it was the duty of the Secretary to at once return the fee, and bis failure to
do 10 was a grave fault. The fee ought to be paid in all cases, if possible, upon the
rejection of a candid..te's application , directly to him, and at the earliest practicable
moment. And when orders or directions to pay to third parties are received, the
whole amount of the fee, regardless of the state of the account between the third
party and the Secretary, mu•t be paid to him who bolds the order. These fees must
not be used by the Secretaries of our Lodges as a means of collecting debts due
them from either the rejected candidates or other parties, With reference to No. 5 we remark that, under Section 1, Article II, Part III, of
our Grand Lodge Oonstitution, a Lodge bas power to discipline all Masons within Its
Jarisdiction. No limitation is specified.

The Address of our Grand Master, Bro. HINl!S, receives favorable notioe. His
decisions are represented as sound, "with, perhaps, the exception of No. 7." Commenting upon that, Bro. Dooos· says :-

Proceedings of the

[Oot. 12,

We cannot see the harm in permitting a Master Mason to belong to as many
Lodges as he is willing to pa.y dues in, and in as many different jnrisdictioDB as he
desires, if there is no positive law prohibiting it. lf he is fit to belong to one Lodge,
we cannot but believe that both the Lodge and the member would be benefited by
multiplying and strengthening the ties of Lodge fellowship.
We recently had the pleasure of helping to "vote in" as a member of the Lodge
to which we belong, no less a Mason than the venerable and distinguished ALBERT
Pu:s. He has not "resided" in this State at any time during the past twenty years.
We do not nnderstand that the decision rendered by Bro. HINES had any relevancy
to dual membership, but that it referred to the case uf one who bad dimitted from
his Lodge in the Grand Jurisdiction in which be resided, and who, while still residing
there, desired to connect himself with a Lodge in California. We do not think well
of an application to one of our Lodges for affiliation from a person who lives "ten
thousand miles away." Our Grand Lodge Constitution prohibits the reception of
an application for membership in a Lodge, unless it is "accompanied by a proper
dimit from the Lodge of wbich the applicant was last a member, or a satlsfacto1·y
explanation, in writing, of his inability to furnish such dimit." We do not believe
that a Mason should be a member of more than one Lodge at one and the same time,
and our constitution expressly forbids it. Distinguished as Bro. ALB&BT PIKE is, in
onr jul'isdlction he wonld be compelled to submit to the above rule before he could
join one ol' our Lodges.
Bro. DODGE makes pleasant reply to the criticism of Bro. HILI. upon the Address
of Grand Master RoOTS, and thinks a few extra "triplets of adjectives" should not
be stingily withheld when, by heaping the measnre, a benighted brother can be
enabled to arrive at proper conclusions. We fear, however, after a perusal of these
proceedings, that the following requires a slight modification:The liberality which Bro. HILL discerns only I~ the prodigal scattering of " trip·
lets of names and adjectives,'' he will. find, upon closer acquaintance, characterizes,
not only the speech, but the sentiments and actions of the brethren which Inhabit
tbis luxurious clime of ours.
The conclusion of our brother's excellent review contains the following ; no
apology is needed for its quotation :As we read with admiration the noble and exalted sentiments expreRsed in the
Grand Masters' Addresses; note the fairness and fidelity displayed by them in the
administration of their official duties; observe the calm, judicial temperament ex·
hibited In the consideration of important que8tions by the Committees on Juri•pru·
deuce; and the usually clean out and equitable disposition made by the Committee
on Appeals and Grievances of the cases which came before them: as we reflect on
all this, we not only find the secret of the stability and grandeur of our ancient and
honorable Institution, but are placed under the conviction th11.t if the same ability,
toned and tempered by the same spirit, were exerted in the administration of our
State and National Governments, then would we be indeed that nation and that
peoole "whose God is the Lord."
One more reflection before we close. 1f the brother who has Jost the freshness
of bis first love for Masonry, who has neglected the Lodge·room and gone off after
the "strange gods" of glitter and novelty-if such a brother were placed In a situ·
ation where he had nothing to read for awhile except the proceedings of the various
Grand Lodges, he would experience 11 st,range and salutary aw&kenlng. He would
come to the conclusion that himself, and not Masonry, had been standing st!ll and
doing nothing. He would be compelled to admit that time had not diminished nor
age weakened that powerful conservative influence which Masonry has !'or ages past
exerted upon all the affairs of civil, religious and political life,

The Address of the Grand Master is a good, practical, well-written paper, containing a recital of the official acts of his term. Dispensations had been granted for
the formation of six new Lodges. Twelve Special Communications had been held
for the purpose of layinir corner-stones, constituting new Lodges, and consecrating

seated as being $68,394 49, an increase over the preceding year, notwithstanding the

The Grand Master expresses strong svmpathy with the Grand Lodge of Quebec
in its eft'orts to secure unconditional recognition from the Grand Lodge of England;
and, whilst he believes that the Grand Lodge of Que bee is not bound by the con·
ditions that applied to the recognition of the Grand I,odge of Canada, he considers
that his Grand Lodge is bound to carry out honorably the agreement entered into
with the Grand Lodge of England. The substance of this agreement is, that the
Lodges which declined to join the Grand Lodge of Canada should be permitted to
continue their allegiance to the Grand Lodge of England, and the latter Grand Lodge
agreed in the future to establish no more Lodges in any part of Canada. In 1867,
the Parliament of Great Britain, by the passage of the British North American Act,
provided for the voluntary union of the several British Provinces of America under
one confederation. This Aot designated Canada West as tho Province of Ontario,
and Canada East as the Province of Quebec. In. 1869, the brethren of Quebec, claiming that the polftioal changes entitled them to form a Grand Lodge, met at Montreal
and established the Grand Lodge of Quebec .. The Grand Lodge of Canada refused,
until 1874, to recognize this new Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodge of England at the
same time expressed a willingness to recognize it on the same terms as had been
agreed to by Canada in 1860. This conditional recognition was refused by Quebec,
which declared it would accept nothing short of recognition of supreme authority.

We know of no provision in Masonry which precludes voting by ballot upon any
proposition. The mere fact that the Constitution prescribes a ballot In certain cases
is not a prohibition against using this mode of voting in other cases, if the Lodge so
determines; and we think it not only allowable, but. in many cases, even desirable,
that the vote of a Lodge should bll taken in this way. There are questions con·
stantly arising in our Lodges upon which a fair expression could not be had in any
other way, without materially endangering the peace . and harmony that should
prevail.

The Address of the Grand Master is confined to a statement of bis official acts,

year had been one of sure and steady progress. Peace and harmony bad prevailed,
and relations with other Grand Lodges were most cordial and fraternal. The Grand
Master reported three decisions, as follows :1st. A person blind in one eye, the other being good, may be ma.de a Mason.
2d. Examination as to proll.ciency of applicants for advancement can be made
at stated communications only.
3d. An application for a waiver of jurisdiction over the rejected material of a
Lodge must lie over until the 11.rst stated meeting in the succeeding month, and the
application can be granted only after a ballot unllnimously in favpr thereof.
None of these are regarded as law in our Jurisdiction. As to the first, though
it differs from our regulation, we are inclined to think that if a candidate can see dis·
tinctly, albeit with one eye only, it is all that should be required of him. We are
not very II.rm believers in the " perfeot·man " doctrine. The Grand Lodge did not
approve the decision.
As regards the second, we remark that we can see no good re a~on why the examtnRtion should be bad at a stated meeting. We would exa.ct proficiency, but bell~ve
that such proll.ciency can be determined as well at a special meeting. Such is our
practice in California. We agree with Grand Master BLATT that the ballot, or right
of objection, is the" Magna Cbarta" of Masonry; bnt we are unable to see what
connection that has with his decision. Dakota adopts the one-ballot system. If
the candidate bas been elected and initiated he is entitled to advance, unless some
valid objection is made thereto. If not proficient, objection may, and should, be
mane; if proficient, what harm can result if such fact is determined at a called
meeting ? If n ew facts have been learned relative to moral character, or fitness
otherwise, the right of objection pbtaios as well at a called ae at a stated meeting.
And as to the third, with us, if material h as been rejected, a Lodge can do noth·
Ing with it (except by dispensation properly obtained from the Grand Maeter, ) until
the expiration of the time specified in the fundamental law of the jurisdiction. After
the expiration of that time the rejected part.y can again apply, and the Lodge can
take action. Our law recognizes the right, after snch time, to apply to any Lodge ·
within whose jurisdiction the applicant may at that time reside. Our Gra.nd Lodge,
rightly, we think, rej ects the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction.

The Deputy Grand Master referred the case of San Benito Lodge, No. 211, of
California, to the Committee on Jurisprudence. It appears that Bro. W. C. 11£.t.xWELL, a member of Spring.field. Lodge, No. 4, of Illinois, had met with an accident,
while in the vicinity of San Benito Lodge, by which he sustained a fracture of the
leg, in addition to other severe injuries. The brethren of San Benik> Lodge took
charge of the brother, and incurred in doing so an expense of $563 55, Thie snm
they claimed should be refunded to them by Springfield. Lodge. The latter refused to
reimburse San Benito Lodge, on the ground that the expenditure for this purpose was
unauthorized. San Benito Lodge thereupon laid the matter before our Grand MBilter
HINES. At the time the accident befell the brother, the Master of San Benito Lodge
wrote to the Master of Springfield. Lodge relative thereto, among other things say·
ing:-" We would be ple&iled to bear from you anything regarding him or hie affairs,
whereby we can be aided in assletiug him." The Master of Springfield Lodge im·
mediately telegraphed to the ,\ faster of San Benito Lodge to aid the brother all he
could, and at the same time wrote, closing with the expression: "N. B.-lf he Is
In need of financial ast.istance, at once telegraph at my expense amoan t wanted."
Thie San Benl.to Lodge failed or neglected to do. The Deputy Grand Master of llli·
noie decided that, in consequence of this fa!lnre, Spring.field. Lodge could be he!<\ re·
sponsible only for the amount of aid rendered between the reception of the tele·
gram and that of the letter. Grand Master HINES concurred in that opinion. Evidently San Benito Lodge was In fault in not telegraphing to Springfield. Lodge the
amount of financial aid required. The telegram t o San Benito Lodge was an author·
ization to contract indebtedness on behalf of Springfield. l,odge; but, taken with
the letter mailed at the same time, it could not be so construed. We think, however, that in the decision of this matter there are other things to be considered.
Individual Masone have obligated themselves to administer to the wants of dietreBBed
brethren to the extent of their ability. When, however, a poor brother, or a weak
Lodge, rather than permit a worthy distressed brother to suffer for lack of aid, ex·
ceeds the purview of their obligation, a sense of nommon equity should prompt the
Mason either in his individual or Lodge capacity to refund. San Benito Lodge was
not able to bear the great ex pense incident to the care of this brother, bnt In !ts
noble charity saw that he was well cared for. Put on the ground of moral obligation, the Lodge was not responsible for hie case, not being able. The members of
the Lodge as individuals were not able to render the aid required without eerlone
Injury to themselves and those dependent upon them. We think that a Lodge is
morally and legally responsible for .the distressed of its own membership whereever they may be. The practical working of an opposite doctrine would perhaps
be extremely painful.

:Master of a Lodge as responsible for the government of his Lodge, and, as such,
possessed of the right to remove from it one who should 'so far forget the propriety
of a gentleman, to say nothing of the do ties of a Mason, as to enter it in an intoxicated
condition. We go farther; we believe that the Master woohl be but discharging his
duty to his Lodge by having the intoxicated member removed and afterwards having
charges of unmasonic conduct preferred against him. Upon the peace and harmony
of a Lodge depends its strength, and a Mason who so far forgets or neglects this
cardinal virtue as to render himself obnoxious, should be summarily dealt with.
Privilege of attendance is "a very sacred right," but others have sacred rlirhts•
also, which a drunken member should not he permitted to infringe. The trial by his
peers, and upon the spot, would simply be impraoticable without great injury to a
Lodge and its members. Bro. GURNEY cert11inly would not attempt to maintain so
unreasonable a proposition as that the work of a Lodge, say in conferring a degree,
shonld cease in order to conserve the rights of a member who, by improper conduct,
had forfeited all right. In civil polity must one who disturbs a meeting of any kind
not be removed, lest some of his sacred rights should be endangered! Suoh doctrine
seems to· us as savoring of nonsense. The Judge upon the benrh exercises the right
to maintain the dignity and decorum of his court by the summary removal and pnn·
ishment of one who would disturb it. We think the Master of a Lodge should exer·
cise the right vested in him to govern his Louge, and see that Its peace and harmony
be not disturbed by the presence of such as pel'111lt themselves to trample upon one
of its most important teachings.
Bro. Gu&N&Y also dissents from.the decision of Grand Master HINES that a" Lodge

of reason than a government could admit to citizenship a non-resident petitioner for

criticism has to the decision rendered by Bro. HINES.

California, for 1884 and 1885, Is reviewed io condensed style. The dechiions of

•commissioners appointed.'" He thinks the Lodge ought to have an opportunity to
try the offender, not a selected few, and adds that he would be very slow to vote to
discipline a brother on the" say so·" of a "committee" of Masons. We incline to
the opinion that our good brother has " jumped " al this conclusion. California has
tried both methods, and tlods that "even-handed justice " is more surely meted out
by her present plan than is possible In any other way. As we:! might be argue
against the trial by jury. It is practically impossible, even in our smallest Lodges,
