546

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 12,

innocence of the party charged without hearing the evidence for or against him.
We find dilllcnlty even in getting a proper majority of a commission to be present at
all meetings. We imagine that jnstice. would have little chance, in a Lodge such as
Oalifornia, No. 1, with over four hundred members, bad the Lodge, as a Lodge, to
meet and try such cases as we have known to arise. If Bro. JOHNSON would not vote
to discipline a brother on the "say so" of a Mason on the commission, how will he
reconoile his vote upon the "say so" of a witness? He must cast his vote upon the
say so of&omebody. Thie "say so" carries with it a very great degree of solemnity!
Besides, in our method of trial, the members of the Lodge are not called upon to
vote upon any matter connected with the trial or discipline of a brother, except the
election of the commission. The commissioners, who hear the evidence pro and con,
determine the guilt or innocence of a party charged, and the penalty; both which
acts, as is everything connected with a trial, are subject to review in the Grand
Lodge. Our method throws around a brother every safeguard which justice or
equity requires, and has always worked well.
We have exceeded the limits, and must stop. We join nearly six hundred thou·
eaod Masons on this continent in the expression of mutual admfration and rejoicing
over the happy condition of our Indiana. brethren, and wouldn't consider him a good
Mason who wonld not. May the joy of their jubilee prompt them to continued noble
effort.

of the Oommittee on Lodges U. D., and the entire year just closed, has been to me

U. D. have been and to-day are organized in this jurisdiction: A town springs up by

Oustodian or Lecturer is called for; the ritual is memorized ; the nearest Lodge sees
them exemplify the work, recommend• their petition, and a dispensation issues:
the character of the material in this organization we do not know, they do not them·
selves know until it is tested, and if the test is applied and the material is unfit for
the Masonic edifice, disintegration, dissolution, and ruin are inevitable results.
The fault is not in want of care in your Grand Masters; they do the best they can
with the means and information at their disposal ; the fault is in the system itself;
there is too much harry-too little deliberation-too little knowledge on the JlBrt ?f
the one organizing, of the material organized; the stones are laid np in the Masonic
edifice before they have been tried by the square of a Master Overseer.

when Masonry, in aid of that church, carried the banners of the cross to victory
against the infidel hosts of the false Prophet.

and spesrs into pruning-hooks. ·

The proceedings form a handsome volume of over six hundred pages, printed at
the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home. The execution of the work reflects great
credit upon the Inmates of the " Home" who have devoted themselves to this kind
of work, and indicates that that institution is a charity sustained largely by the
inmates, and at the same time made doubly useful by affording employment and the
opportunity to learn useful means of support.
The Address of the Grand Master is a long, able, and interesting paper. The Craft
throughout the jurisdiction are represented as having been singularly fav ored with
the blessings of health and happiness; peace and tranquillity bad prevailed, bountiful
harvests had crowned the labors of the husbandman, and all industries had prospered.
Nine dispensations had been issued for the formation of new Lodges, and each
dispensation contained the provision that the Lodge established should In no event
draw more from the Grand Lodge iu the way of mileage and per diem, than it had
paid in the way of dues. 'l'be tendency of such a provision is In the right direction
-discouraging the formation of weak Lodges that are a burden not only to the
Grand Lodge but also to their own membership, Io many of the Grand Jurisdictions
there are too many J.,odges composed of so few members that all Interest lag1, and
the purposes of the institution fail.
The Grand M.aster holds the right views r elative to delinquency on the part of
Lodges in making returns and paying does. He bad summoned sixty delioquen.t
Lodges to show cause, by duly accredited representatives, why their charters should
not be arrested. Such action will clear the docket , and bring the membership to a
proper conception of their duty in seeing tb ..t the officers are more faithful.
The decisions reported by the Grand Master are for the greater part of a local
character. His plainly expressed views in reference to the right of any officer to
resign bis position, are, In our opinion, eminently proper. The " iron rule" that
exists in some of our Grand Jurisdictions, to the effect that no officer can r esign
during the time for which he has been elected, is calcull\ted to work great inconvenience and hardship in iLodges; and has nothing to recommend it. Such a rule
does not obtain in Californ\ia.

The Grand Secretary, a• well as the Grand Master, recommends a change in the
time of electing the officers of subordinate Lodges, from ST. JOHN'S Day, in December, to the last month of the Grand Lodge fiscal year; and thinks that such a
change would lessen the failures In making proper ret urns to his office. The elections in our jurisdiction occur at this season, and we have never lieard of any complaint from our Grand Secretary originating out of election at such time. It seems
to us that the election of officers in the last month or the Grand Lodge fiscal year
would result in sending to the Grand Lodge, as representatives, a body of IDen but
lnditrerently acquainted with the wants of their Lodges, and but poorly qualified 88
members of the Grand Lodge. The evil of failure to make returns cannot be remedied in this way. We opine that there is bot one way of compelling promptness in
this matter, and that is for the Grand Lodge to a~sert its authority and hold the Lodge
falling to a strict accountability. If Lodges are made to know that they cannot vlo ·
late the edicts and r egulations of t he Grand Lodge with impunity, they will be ob1
servant. No temporizing should be permitted in the case of recalcitrant or neglect·
fol Lodges. Make them come to time or take away their warrants. We don't believe
in the giving of " prize jewels" to Lodges for best returns, or for prompt returns;
we would execute the law, and enforce its penalty . When Lodges feel that this
will be done there will be but little can•e for complaint. Such a course will bring out
the membership of the Lodges with forc e enough to compel the officers !o do their
duty. Arrest the charter of the Lodge until such time 88 it signifies its intention to
elect a Secretary who knows his duty and will perform it, and failures will cease.

The Grand Master delivered an Address replete with information relative to the

Past Grand Masters, were permitted to be in attendance.
No name on the roll of Grand Lodge officers had been erased by death, and only
one of the permanent members had passed "into the silent land." Nothing had occurred to disturb the peace and friendship existing between this and other Grand
Jurisdictions. The Craft at home had enjoyed a year of harmony and prosperity.
A number of' dispensations had been granted for various ceremonial purposes.
Dispensations to enable Lodges to receive and act upon petitions in Jess time than
that required by the fundamental Jaw, had been refused. A dispensation to permit a

the Grand Lodge of his own State.
Believing that Maine has already too many weak Lodges, the Grand Master had
discouraged the formation of others; hence no dispensations for this purpose had
·been granted. He had been called upon to answer a great number of questions,
He reports ten dec.isions, from which we quote the following:3. It is not proper for Lodges to meddle with domestic troubles.
4. A candidate presents himself for initia.tion the same evening that he has been
accepted. Can a member prevent his initiation after he has been taken in charge by
the J. D.?
Answer-An objection by a member of the Lodge to the initiation of a candidate
is equivalent to rejection by ballot, if made at any time before the candidate has
been "received into" the Lodge by the H. D.
5. A candidate who received his second degree eighteen months a.go, evades all
questions in regard to receiving his third. Shall we Jet him take his own time?
Answer-There being no Jaw compelling a candidate to receive his second or third
degree, there can be no penalty for neglecting to do so. He infiicts his own punishment, by depriving himself of the rights and benefits of Masonry.
6. A dimit should not be granted to a member who has disgrnced himself and
the fraternity by acts of intoxication, but charges should be preferred and a trial
had. In teaching the cardinal virtues we commence with temperance.
7. A man becomes an actual candidate when his petition has been received by
the Lodge and referred to a committee.

Bro. DRUMMOND discusses at considerable length the law relative to the Issuing of

Lodges and Masons that snob party has dimitted. It Is true that a deed is the instl'Ument by which title passes, so far as the parties thereto and the rest of mankind are
concerned; but, as between the parties themselves, title passes by the act of agreement, and the deed Is only a formal way of indicating to all others that such agreement
has been made between the parties. After a dlmit has been isRued, If a member applies to another Lodge for affiliation, he must produce hie dimit as evidence of the
fact that his former membership has ceased, or else show why be cannot produce It.
This appears to us to be tbe primary object of a dimit.

We also quote the following as beiug fully in accord with the views held by oar

The Address of Grand Master SJIRYOCK is a condensed statement of the business

Grand Master SHRYOCK has made his position anything but a sinecure. He had
made fifty-seven official visits during the past six months, and had examined every
Lodge in the city of Baltimore except two. He had also visited several Lodges in
the country, and asserts, as the result of his observation, that I.here is now more interest felt throughout the State than has been shown for many years past. He had, in
making his visita, adopted a method which would enable him to discover the actual

drop in upon you "-was the substance of a notice which he had issued to nll the Lodges
of the State. At the same time he reminded the brethren that these official visitations
were not to be considered occasions for festivity, "but for the inspection of the manner in which they conducted their meetings and did their work." Jn some Lodges
he found the work done in a creditable ma nner ; in others he discovered a great
many deficiencies on the part of the officers, which had since been corrected; in
others he "found the work and general ensemble simply atrocious." He had threatened to arrest the charters of this latter cle.es, unless within thirty days there was a
marked Improvement. Tqls had the desired effect. We have thus commented as a
prelude to the remark that we believe that strict accountability is the basis of all
good work, and, we may add, of all lively interest in Lodges, as well as in everything
else. Our own observation convinces us that we need a modicum of snch inspection
in many Lodges in our own Jurisdiction.

Under Dakota, Bro. ·WROTH says that Maryland does not require payment of dues
during suspension for non·payment thereof. California does, and we deem it just to
do so. We even go farther in our belie!: we deem it justice to the Craft that a

566

Procetdings of the

[Oct. 12,

brother who permits himself to be sqspended for this cause should be excluded dnr·
ing such suspension from all the rights and privileges of Masonry. We consider non·
payment of dues a Masonic offense and as such deserving of punishment. .A law that
has no penalty is virtually no law. There is no excuse that a brother can allege for
permitting himself to be thus suspended. If he is not able to pay, it is his right, it
is his duty to himself and his Lodge, to make known the fact. It he neglects to pay
his dues, or if, being unable, he neglects or refuses to make known his inability, he
does a wrong to the -Lodge and to himself. The requirement to pay dues daring
suspension is a penalty that a brother can absolve himself from at his pleasure.
Every Mason is bound by the ties of honor to help sustain the burdens of his Lodge.
It is to our mind manifestly unjust that a member should be permitted to enjoy any
of the privileges of membership when he is unwilling to contribute his share to defray
the expenses incident to membership.
Bro. WROTH considers the degree of Past Master a neceBBary part of the installation ceremony. :Maryland, he says, has an excellent Assoc.iation of Past Masters.
He thinks that each Jurisdiction should have such an association, and should let it
do the work for the subordinate Lodges. California has just such an Association
in the city of San Francisco, but it does not rnmove the Inconvenience that often

the distance necessary to be present at the meetings of ~uch a body. A better plan
in our opinion wonld be to authorize the inste.Jling o!Hccr to confer the degree. Not·
withstanding the fact that our Grand Lodge requires the conferring thereof prior to
installation, we are individually led by our observation to consider it a useless
thlng,-not even an ornament.
We would like, did space permit, to notice many more of the sensible observa·
tions in this excellent report, bat we have already exceeded the limit.

Grand Master LYMAN KLAPP, of Rhode Island, thus alluded to the great BoAN·
lllRGES :I sometimes fear we are apt to look at ST. JoHN, the Evangelist, as an effeminate
character. I think we most frequently regard him as the beloved disciple, because it
11 in that language of the Master that we realize how His great heart went out to the
heart of such a man as ST. JOHN, and took him to His breast as the beloved disciple;
or possibly we think of him as the divine, the theologian. But he was a son of thun·
der; a more impetuous man never lived than ST. JOHN; a man with all the passions
ot manhood ; a man of the highest culture ; a man who made his mark upon the age
lo which he lived, and which has come down to us through the ages all along. He
was a great man; he was a type of men, and it was because of this that I believe the
Master himself recognized in BT. JOHN a type of humanity. That was why He took
him to himself and His bosom as the beloved disciple. It was necessary that the im·
petuous and impulsive and ardent mau should be brought under the teaching of the
Master, in order to become the disciple whom we recognize as the beloved or the
divine. I feel that much is due to his intluence. We revere BT. JOHN, the Baptist,
with his rugged life, his coarse raiment and hard fare. We recognize in him the
type of a rugged man. But it is in ST. JOHN , the Evangelist, that we recognize the
highest type of manhood. So we as Freemasons believe, unconsciously it may be;
but I think we ought more to study, and to realize more than we do, the character
of our patron Saint, whose memory we are celebrating to-night.
We regret that we have not the space for many of the excellent sentiments ex·
preBBed on this happy occasion. We believe in these pleasant reunions ; they unite
the brethren more firmly in the bonds of friendship and brotherly love. When the
festive and Instructive are properly combined, permanent good must result, goodtellowship Is strengthened, and more thorough knowledge of our rights and duties as
Ha.sons is inculcated.

California for 1884 receives full and fraternal notice. Bro. BARKLEY takes excep.. •
tioo to the decision of Grand Master HrNEB, to the effect that, in the absence of the
Master and Wardens of a Lodge, it cannot be opened for any purpose, even for the
burial of a brother. The decision is in accord with the Constitution of our Grand
Lodge, and Bro. BINES is not a believer io prerogatives. We regard the Master,
and, in his absence, the Wardens, according to rank, as the executive officers of a
Lodge ; and we deem it unwise that any other parties, for any purpose, should be
empowered to exercise their functions. It is extremely unlikely that on any occa·
slon all thre'e of these officers would be absent; but should they be, It would be hazardous to entrust the duties of the Master's position to irresponsible parties.
Bro. BABKLEY also excepts to the decision of Bro. HINlllB, in reference to objection
to advancement. Our Grand Lodge recognizes the right of objection, bot does not
believe that a candidate, after he has been made a Mason, shall be stopped lo his
search tor farther light by the Interposition of a single veto. When the candidate has
been made a Mason, he occupies a very different position from that which he held as a
profane. As an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft, he has rights which, by the
demands of justice, should be recognized. lf objection is made to bis advancement,
that objection should b e! examined by a proper committee, and the validity of the
objection be determined by the Lodge. Io tbe case presented by Bro. BARKLEY, it
was the duty of the brother knowing the charact er of the party to have preferred
charges against him. A. party who had committed so flagrant an offense as the
seduction of a brother Master Mason's daughter, should not be permitted to be
stopped from advancing only; he should be Ignominiously expelled from the Order•
and the party knowing that suoh a wrong had been committed by a brother, falls
very far short of his duty in n eglecting or declining to make such offense known.
The "patent process " which Bro. ABELL applies to the Lodges in order "to
bring them up to time " in the payment of their· Grand Lodge dues, and the making
of proper reports, is constant reminder and persistency. It is not always inability,

This is sufficient commendation, for :Missouri's Grand Secretary, whether in one

persuaded to believe that the appointment and reports of these committees have

predilection for the applicant.

The Graatl Master complains of a lack of uniformity In the work of the Lodges,

adoption of the same by the Lodges compulsory. This latter can be accomplished
quite readily, as in our Jurisdiction, by refusing to allow the Masters of the Lodges

officer empowered to grant It, to the effect that snch Master is proflclenl in the work
as adopted by the Grand Lodge. Dispensations had been issued during the year for

The Grand Master represents the law of the Jurisdiction to be in a lamentable
condition, the various rulings and decision~ being left in a promiscuous and chaotic
state. This is true of other Jarisdictions. There has not that attention been given
to the matter of systematizing the Grand Lodge decisions in any of the Grand Juris·
dictions which its importance merits. An attempt has been made in our own Juris·
diction, by one of our most capable Grand Masters, to prepare a proper digest of
Masonic law; but we have found the work to be of comparRtively little aid to those
who most need help. We suggest that the labors of our Committees on Jurisprudence
and Grievances would be immeasurably lightened if a digest were prepared that
would contain the laws of the Jurisdiction properly classified and indexed. Masters
of Lodges do not have the time, many have not the inclination, and few have the op·
portunity to search. through many great tomes for that whioh they most need. The
opinions of Grand Master WEl!PLE on this point are eminently appropriate, and his
suggestions are timely. His recommendations upon other matters are equally proper,
and indicate that it has been a study with him to do something worthy of his position
for the benefit of the Craft in general, and of his own Jurisdiction in particular. The
following is so apropos that we give it place:That the rule requiring Masters to cause to be read in open Lodge, the oonstitu·
tion, rules, decisions and proceedings of the Grand Lodge, be so emphasized as to
make it obligatory, taking no excuse for its not being done. This would help the
Grand Master, as each one will find that nine-tenths of the questions asked are already
answered in the law, and all that is necessary Is to read.
Our Masters seem in too many cases to think that the chief dnty imposed npon
them is that of conferring degrees. We take it that the novitiate should be Instructed
in the fundamental principles and in the general matters of Masonic law; yet such is
not the case. When the candidate has been conducted through the routine of his
Initiation, he l.s generally left without any further instruction than that whloh, by his
own nnaided efforts, he is enabled by observation to pick up. As much attention
should be directed to the ~erfeoting of the ashlars as to the selection of them.

The Grand Lodge funds are in such a flourishing condition that the Grand

The Grand Orator, Bro. CHARLES J. PHELPS, delivered a well prepared oration
before the Grand Lodge, in which he essays to discuss the propositions-What constituted speculative Masonry in the time of SOLOHON, and how the union between
operative and speculative Masonry was then consummated.? We confess that after
a thorough reading of this oration we have been unable to learn from it what its
author thinks about either proposition. We have not been able to read in the his·
tory of Masonry, or to learn from any portion of the traditions thereof, that there
was in the time of SOLOHON any union between operative and speculative Masonry.
We are not a believer in the transcendental nonsense that Freemasonry originated
in the days of SOLOMON, and we are of the opinion that Grand Lodge orators might
find topics for discussion of more practical benefit to the brethren than the mythical and fanciful antiquity of our institution.
To the query, "Can an appeal to the Grand Lodire be taken from the decision
of the Grand Master?" the Committee on Jurisprudence answered in the negative.
At the instance of the Grand Secretary, a committee of five well-informed
Masons was appointed to consider the problem of non-affiliation, and how it may
be lessened. This is a problem that it seems impossible to properly solve, and it is
one that has claimed the attemtion of both Grand and subordinate J;..odges for
many years. We hope the Nebraska Committee may meet with success in their
attempt a.t its solution, but fear that the outcome of their labors will be that which
has characterized all similar attempts in the past. The entire abrogation of affiliation fees, and earnest work upon the part of the brethren, are about the only
means that will result in any decrease of the evil.
The Committee on Foreign Correspondence reported that they deemed it unsafe to reoommend the recognition of the Grand Lodges of Lower California and

On favorable report of the Committee on Ways and Means, the ~nm of $150
was appropriated for the purpose of enaMing the Grand Secretary, or such committee as might be appointed by the Grand Lodge, to codify the laws thereof.
Our observation leads us to the conclusion that such action was very wise. One
of the greatest difficultie~ that the Masters ef our Lodges have to encounter is
that of determining, from 1volumiuous proceedings, what the law in any particular
case may be. So many resolutio,ns and decisions have been enacted and subsequently repealed, that, by the time one has examined the proceedings, he generally
finds himself in a maze of confusion. Simplification and codification of the laws
would tend greatly to obviate the necessity for applying to the Grand Master for
his decision upon questions often previously adjudicated.

The Address of the Grand Master is an excellent business document. After welcoming the members of the Grand Lodge, he says:On the sixteenth day of January, A. L. 5865, that Convention met in the city of
Virginia, and by the Oonstitntion which was then framed and adopted, that city became and has ever since, until the present time, continued to be the place of our

Speaking of the condition of the Craft, the Grand Master says:During the past year our numbers have slightly decreased, yet our general con·
dition is one of healthy and vigorous prosperity. This might seem paradoxical, yet
nevertheless it is true. It is not in num hers alone a true prosperity consists, but In
the material which constitutes those numbers that we are to look for our continued
welfare and success; and though we may not have increased numerically, this at
least may in part be ascrib,ed to a more jealous scrutiny at the ballot·box of that
material offered for our choice or rejection, wherewith to rear the edifice of Free·
masonry. That our numbers are a few less is no particular cause of discouragement.
From my knowledge of the Oraft, of its workings during the past year, from the
hopeful and intelligent countenances I see around me, I think I am fully warranted
In saying that the Fraternity in this State was never in better condition than at
present.
·
Relations with other Grand Lodges, except in the case of Utah, were harmonious.
In our review of Utah we have adverted to the misunderstanding that has, for the
time, disturbed the cordiality heretofore existing between these Grand Bodies. We
have, after reading the statement of the Grand Master of Nevada, no modification
to make upon the opinion we express under Utah.
The Grand Master experiences pleasure in approving the changes in the By-Law1
of severe.I Lodges reducing the dues from one dollar to fifty cents per month; whilst
with some feelings of deprecation he approved changes in the By-Laws of other
Lodges reducing the fees for degrees from sixty and one hundred dollars to fifty. It
occurs to us that it should be a cause for rejoicing that in the mutations of time the
Lodges have so prospered that they are able to reduce both entrance fees and
monthly dues. Tempora mutan.tur et nos mutamui· in illis. The times were in Cal·
lfornia, and in Nevada, too, when $50 "sings" were lying around loose. Those
"halcyon" days have passed, and there is now a higher estimate placed upon the
dollar, because the dollar is not so easily obtainable. Masonry is not supposed to
estimate men by any other standard than that of moral worth, and there is no gainsaying the fact that high entrance fees are a barrier to the admission of those who
would be the instruments of honor as well as of aid to our Order. The revenues of
a Lodge are mainly derivable from monthly dues. We are not of those who believe

Under Alabama Bro. HA!iUlOND, commenting upon the report of the committee in reference to " prerogatives," very rightly says :It occurs to us that it is better for a Grand J,odge at once to grapple with the

The following relative to the Grand Lodge of South Australia is in accord with the
opinions held by our own Grand Lodge :The question of the formation of a Grand Lodge in Son th Anstre.lfe. presents soma
difficulty. Last year we admitted that the Grand Lodge of Victoria might be regularly formed, but we declined to say that it had exclusive possession of the Territory
of that Province while a majority of the regularly constituted Lodges did not 1ubmlt
to it. A principle has been generally recognized by Masonic authorities on thl1 continent that three subordinate Lodges could form a Grand Lodge, This Is good enough
law when the parent Grand Lodges offer no opposition, where often there are no
more than three Lodges, and where the prevailing idea Is that a Grand Lodge shalt
at once be formed and grow up as one of the institutions of a new Territory or State.
But the case Is materially altered when the rule is applied to countries or oolonte1 In
which there is a largej number of Lodges. It seems an absurdity that In a ooantry
where there are say twenty Lodges three of these should be able to set op a Grand
Lodge and declare all the other Lodges clandestine if they do not subml• to lta
authority. l:!ome modification of the rule is necessary which will protect tbe right.
of, perhaps, the majority. The formation of our own Grand Lodge was, I think, oon·
sented to at the outset by three-fourths or more of the Lodges in the province.
Fourteen dispensations had been granted daring the year ; among others, two to
bury deoeasea brethren I

Committee on Relations with Forelg.n Grand Lodges recommended the adoption of a

The Report on Correspondenoe was presented by the Chairman, Bro. J.t11B8 A.
NORTON. It Is an interesting review of forty-nine Grand Lodges, including California
for 1884. Copious extracts are made from the Address of Grand Master HINlliB j
also from the report of Bro. SHAEFFER, and from that of the Committee on Jurl1prudence,
Bro. NORTON remarks that It seems that Masonic burial is not considered a matter
of courtesy among the brethren of California. We respond that the burial of Masons
belonging to and paying dues to Lodges In other Grand Jurisdictions, as well as to
Masons belonging to Lodges in our own Jurisdiction, iB religiously attended to; but
we believe that Lodges to whom the deceased brethren have been paylna duu
should foot the bills. If some of our brethren of the older Jurisdictions could have
the experience that California brethren have had since the very first settlement of
the State, they would, doubtless, modify their views in this partloular. They mlaht
conolude, in suoh a case, that true charity sometimes begins at home. California 11
peculiarly circumstanced, and San Francisco and many other of our towns are peon•
liarly situated. It might be well for New Jersey and some other Jurisdiction• to try
a little of the experiences that the brethren of California have bad in the la1t thirty·
tlve years. It Is all very nice to talk abont charity and courtesy, but when Lod1e1,
like individuals, are bearing burdens that are breaking their backs, It Is time that
they rai~e their voices against the imposition of still greater ones. Calitornia wlll
never close her hand or her heart against the calls of charity. The admlnlatratlon1 of
relief to those who are abundantly able to refund, or to the members of Lodaea that
are able so to do, are very different things. Grand Master HINES was right when he
said that the mere force of Masonic comity and a sense of right and justice ou1ht to
secure prompt payment of such bills ; but there are too many cases where Muonlc
comity or the other attributes are either lost sight of or purposely Ignored, Loda••
that complain about the matter of refunding, ought to have a little of our experience
in this matter; then, perhaps, the pictnre would present a dUfereut aspect. We
don't believe that the Lodges of California are morally bound to pBnunu themaelvea
in relief to those whose Lodges are able to administer the required aid. We are
willing to leave the estimate of California's courtesy and charity to those who have
seen both. We believe that there ought to be a way to compel Lodgea to relmburae
others for aid rendered to their membership, if they are able to do 10. Lod11e1 have
no right to make members and turn them over for support to other Lod111. When·
ever a Lodge has become so poor that it itself needs charity, It ouaht to 1urrender
its warrant, and thus stop its liabilities.
But we must close our review, which we do with the remark that we hope to 1ee
the brethren of New Jersey enjoy their Centennial, and then enter upon another
with Increased zeal and still brighter prospect,

MOST WORSHIPFUL-I am sorry that every Freemason of North Carolina was not
there. It would have given all a broader view of our ancient and honorable Fraternity, the strength and beauty of which we cannot estimate. It claims no undue
Influence in political 111fairs ; it sets up no sectarian claims ; it demandd a belief in 11
Supreme God ; it concedes the right to worship Him according to the dictates of
one's own conscience ; it teaches obedience to law and country; it spreads the cement of brotherly love and friendship; ft bestows its charity silently, surely, effectively. It is worthy of our devotion. Will you bear with me 11 little, while I give
7ou the opinion of the immortal WASHINGTON, who was made 11 Master Mason
while 11 minor, under the authority of the Grand Lodge of Scotland, August 4, 1753?
I have gathered his sayings from the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of the District
of Columbia.
Writing to the Grand Lodge of South Carolina, May, 1791, he said: "that he
recognized with pleasure his relations to the brethren whose principles lead to purity
of morals and beneficence of act.fon." In 1793, to the Grand Lodj[e of Massachusetts:
"that it is pleasing to know that the milder virtues of the heart are highly resrected
by the Society whose liberal principles are founded on the immutable laws o troth
1md justice." To King David's Lodge, of Rhode Island: " Masonry promotes pr!·
vate virtue and public prosperity." To the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts In April,
l 798: "My attachment to the Society will dispose me always to contribute my best
endeavors to preserve the honor and interest of the Craft." In November, 1799, to
the Grand Lodge of Maryland: "The principles and doctrines of Freemasonry are
founded in benevolence and to be exercised for the good of mankind."
Such Is the testimony of tho man whose monument, In the language of G~and
Master PA.BOB, " towers above all other monuments, as he towered above all other
men.''

The queatioo-" Can an accuser, on the trial of a brother for unmasonic conduct,
or any other charge, appeal from the decision of a Lodge on a general verdict of not
aunty? "-having been refer~ed to the Committee OD Jurisprudence, the majority
thereof decided that he could not. Such decision is not In accord with the law of
our Grand Lodge. The subordinate Lodge Is regarded as the creature of the Grand
Lodge, and~ acts In trials merely as the agent of the Grand Lodge. We think the
report of the minority of the committee WllB correct, and should have been sustained.

The Grand Lodge was convened for the purpose of laying the corner-stone of
the Poat-office and Custom-house. We have alluded to this ceremony because our

[Oot. 12,

attention was arrested by the Address of the Grand Master-scarcely two pagea
long, but oonta!ning food for much thought. We make no apology for quoting the
following:Modern progress is usually reckoned to have begun with the invention of prin'"
ing; an undoubted means of transmitting the result of steady research. All honor to
GUTENB&BG wh.:i invented, and to CAXTON who brought the invention to the knowledge of our countrymen. But the printed book or sheet is but the coal in the
mine-power in a latent state ; to discharge its destined duty it must be taken from
its hiding-place and be brought in contact with other elements. So with the printed
matter; to render it powerful it must be cironlated and placed before' the mass of
men freely and promptly. Printing, therefore, really never developed its full power
till RowLANI> HILL devised the present system of cheap postage.
The post-office is our great enlightener, carrying almost to every man's do or the
product of the thought and study of the moat gifted and moat industrious men.
As Masons we seek li~ht, the light of knowledge ; and not merely for ourselve.r.
for we are no benefit society, reserving all our energies to help those only who be·
long to tbe Fraternity; our scope is wide, wide as earth-we desire to inculcate
principles of truth and progress that will benefit the whole human race.
The postal system is a wondrous agent, not merely for the ~pread of knowledge,
but for the maintenance of good and kindly feelings. Consider, from our .own
knowledge and experience, the purport of the vast majority of letters that pass
through the mails. That there are business letters of an unpleasant nature to the
recipient is unfortunately but too true ; but for one letter disagreeable in ita pur·
port, are there not hundreds which perpetuate and promote, not merely kindly feel·
mgs, bot harmony and love? How anxiously the letters of the absent are waited
for, and the pleasure far exceeding the sorrow (which we cannot eliminate from
earthly matters,) which our letters in the main bring to us.
Brotherly love and relief are of a certainty stimulated by our correspondence
reaching us in such a simple and economical way from all parts of the earth through
our mail system. And truth, the old proverb tells us, is great and will prevail ; but
it is only through the light which publicity affords, that what is unreal ls exposed,
that falsehood is pot to shame, and that truth is established ; and publicity is mainlf
attained through the ready circulation of that great power of to-day- the news.paper. The world owes much to the press, but the press would never have obtained its power without our mail system. Tbus, the service of our postal organization cultivates the wishes we desire to inculcate; and as our Fraternity bas ne.ver
hesitated to assist at the foundation of temples dedicated to the worship of God, or
institutions for imparting knowledge to man, it seemed but appropriate that a build·
Ing ~estlned to the service of distributing and spreading this knowledge throughout
the community should be recognized as a fitting object for the labors of the Orafta fellow·worker in the cause of light and love.

Our Black-Book excites his "Yankee curiosity" sufficiently to lead to the question, "wh~t is the Black Book and its purpose? Will Bro. HILL throw a little lighi
upon this (to us) DARK subject?" In Bro. HILL'S stead we answer thst the BlaokBook is not a black book; it may be of. any color. It iB a book provided for our
subordinate Lodges In which the Secretary must record, upon pages alphabetically
arranged the full name or names of all those rejected for the degrees, expelled, eus·
pended, ~r restored by any of the Lodges, so far as he shall receive any notice
thereof. When applicants are rejected, or when member~ are expelled, suspended
or restored by any Lodge, notice of such action ie communicated to the Grand
Secretary; and every two months that officer. transmits a circular to the several
subordinate Lodges notifying them of all rejections, expulsions, suspensions, or restorations. This circular must be read in the Lodges, and then transcribed In this
Black-Book for the convenience of Committees of Investigation, of the Tyler, and of
the Lodge.

Now, It is supposed, that persons elected as Masters of Lodges are, at least,
possessed of ordinary Intelligence, and are capable of reading; Constitutions are
aupposed to be written In plain English ; every Lodge is likely to have in It one or
more Past Masters. If such IJe the case, we are impelled to the conclusion that
Masters of Lodges, who importune Grand :Masters for decisions upon questions
fully answered by reference to the fundamental law, or that have been frequently
dechled by previous Grand Masters, are culpably careless. Almost all Grand
Masters report that most of the questions presented to them are such as have been previously determined, or that can be determined by reference to the Constitution or to
the proceedings of their Grand Lodges. Masters should take the trouble, if trouble
It be, to inform themselves. "What are Masters for'' if it be notto acquire light and
furnish It to those of their Lodges who need It? Masters are, or owght to be, teach·
era ; and no one should aspire to a position, the duties of which he is incapable of
discharging.

Under Arkansas, Bro. CHADWIOK endo1·ses the views of Bro. DonGB in reference
to dispensing with the ballot by unanimous consent, and thinks "there is too much of
this parliamentary law." Now it may be from our obtuseness, but we fr1mkly confess
that we are unable to see wherein the dispensing with the ballot by unanimous consent
can result in any harm. The fact is, neither Bro. CHADWICK nor Bro. Donas states this
matter aright. The ballot is not dispensed with, but the Lodge by unan·i mous con·
sent agrees that the ballot shall be cast by some one named, for the particular person.
Members frequently know the sentlm"ents of other memhers in regard to whom they
desire to elect to a certain position, and the further fact that the sentiment of the
members seems to be unanimous in favor of Ruch party. Wh11.t harm then can arise
from a vote to test whether such sentimeotisunanimous or not. It infringes no right
helonglng to any member, and m many of our Lodges, large in numbers, the mere
saving of time is a great consideration. Besides it is a just method of extending due
commendation to worth and efficiency. The ballot is employed in but very few
instances in Masonic Lodges other than in electing candidates or officers. In the former
the ballot is always bad; in the latter case it may often occur that there is but one
person desiring a particular office, or bot one whom the membership desire. In such
cases we see no harm that can originate from dispensing with the ballot on the part
of the whole Lodge, and permitting it to be cast by some one nRmed for that purpose.

I bave heard some well-intentioned Masons talk about the beauty of the Oraft as
a non-religious organization, but these excellent brethren can hardly be accused of
any very intimate acquaintance with our history, or any undue famili arity with the
teachings of the Craft. Wheu they say " oon·religlou~," they simply mean " nou·
donominatiooal.'' Bot this loose method of speaking frequently oreates a wrong
lmpreRsion on the Masonic as well as the non-Masonic hearer, and helps to irive coun·
tonance to some of the calumnies which have been uttered againBt us. To be non·
religious would rtiqulre us fir•t of a.II to e xtloiruisb one of our three great lights,
namely, the volume of the Sacred Law, and to attempt ans thing of that sort would
be to divorce oul'Selves from 'the essential life uf genuina Freemasonry, whiuh, if
•erlously attempted, would rend the Craft from floor to celling, and if any of the
l'ral{ments survived the disruption, it would survive as a chaotic mass, without prin·
olple and without cohesive force of any kind . Extinguish "the Lamp of God," and
you have at once a darkness that may be folt-a morality that rests upon no basis,
l\nd that cannot be illustrated by any symbol. (I,oud applause.) The world has
never been, and we have no reason to suppose that it ever will be. without it> doubt..
era, its unbelievers and its skeptice. They exist with regard to 1111 progreBB, they
oombe.t every movement for moral or social reform. Io regard to Masonry the non·
believers and the skeptics are as legion ; they outnumber us on all sides, and yet
their unbelief and their skepticism prove nothing. Divine revelation fares no better,
and those who are waiting for the skeptic to pot away hie skepticism, or the fool to
pot away bis folly, are likely to leave the world very little better than they found it,
and themselves not improved in any respect. What Is needed, therefore, is not a
oeaseles8 wrangle about our conceptions of the Infinite and Eternal, the natural and
anpernatural, but a principle of love and hope that shBll help us by r egular steps
along life's rugged pathway until such time as the "lower lights" on the earthly
altar shall have merged into the dazzling glories of that Eternal light which be.th no
Hhadows.

RHODE ISLAND.

The pamphlet before us contains the proceedings of an Emergent Communication, held on the twenty-first day of June, 1884, for the purpose of attending the
funeral of Bro. PHILIP B. BOURN, a Paet Deputy Grand Master of the Grand
Lodge ; of the Semi-Annual Communication, held on the seventeenth day of N ovem·
ber, 1884; and of the .Annual Communication, held in the city of Providence on
the eighteenth day of May, 1885. This was the ninety.fifth .Annual Communication.
The M . •• W. ·. LYMAN CLAPP, Grand Master, presided, theR. ·. w. ·.EDWIN BAKER
being Grand Secretary. Thirty-one Lodges were represented.
We commend the expedition manifested in the dispatch of business in this
Grand Lodge, none of the Communications having occupied more than one day.
The .Address of the Grand Master is a brief business paper. He had visited many
of the Lodges, and had found them in a most satisfactory condition. He repre,
sents that "never in the history of this Grand Lodge has there been more real
prosperity or a greater degree of peace and harmony, not only among the members.
of individual Lodges, but between the Lodges in the Jurisdiction, than at the present time."
No decisions are reported. The attendance of members at the Semi-annual Com·
munication had been greater than that of any previous one. This is accounted
for by the fact .that the custom prevails of having a grand good time,-banQuet
and post prand1al-after the labors of the session have terminated. The Grand
Master believes "that the spirit of harmony then manifested will ceme~t more
closely the bonds of brotherhood throughout the jurisdiction." Great attention
seems to be given, in this Jurisdiction, to the building up of the membership in a
thorough knowledge of the true principles of Masonry, and the importance of the
exercise of true brotherly feeling. Saint John'B Lodge, No. 1, of Providence, had
some time since inaugurated the custom of having, from time to time, lectures and .
addresses upon various Masonic subjects for the instruction of its members.
Other Lodges had followed this excellent example. We cordially endorse such
work. Knowledge of the principles, and encouragement to exemplify them, will
do much more to add strength to our Fraternity than any increase of numbers.
God commands blessing upon such as dwell together in unity,-unityof sentiment
and unity of feeling and action.
'
The reports of the several District Deputy Grand Masters, and of the Grand
Treasurer and Grand Secretary, confirm the statements of the Grand Master.
'!.'here is no Report on Correspondence. The Committee asked further time to
report upon communications from other Grand Lodges. The proceedings contain
nothing of a general character, the business beini;r purely local.
There are in the Juriediction thirty-five working Lodges, h1ning a membership
of three thousand five hundred and ninety-seven. The Grand Master and Grand
Secretary were both re-elected.

UTAH.

The fifteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Utah WllB held in
the city of Salt Lake, commencing on the nineteenth day of January, 1886,-the
M." w. ·. PARLEY LYCURGUS WILLIAMS, Grand Master, presiding, and the R."
CHRISTOPHER DIEHL being Grand Secretary. All the eight chartered Lodgee of
the Jurisdiction were represented.
In his Address, the Grand l\j:aRter alludes to many topics of general 118 well as
of local interest. After congratulating the Grand Lodge upon the favorable auspices under which it had aBBembled, and the reasonable degree of proeperity enjoyed, he says :While the disquietude that has so long characterized so large a portion of the
people of Utah has been intensified during the year, we may, I think, reasonably
conclude it is due to the fact that more than the usual progress has been made
wward the removal of the causes which produce it. In the meantime Masonry has
looked on with serenity, and, true to her teachings, has given her moral support to
the enforcement of the laws, and the maintenance of the civil institutions of our
country.
The Grand Master takes occasion to warn the Grand Lodge against hasty legis·
lation. He is strongly opposed to the abolishment of the office of Deputy Grand
Master, and does not favor biennial sessions of the Grand Lodge. We think he is
right on both propositions. The following suits us, and shows clearly that Grand
Master WILLIAMS has a very proper conception of the purview of the powers and
duties of a Grand Master; and that he is not a believer in the "prerogative"
doctrine:In this connection I desire to express my conviction that our laws are not 118
rigidly enforced as they should be, and that there is a notion far too prevalent
among the brethren, that for the slightest cause, or to subserve a peraonal convenience, the Grand Master not only can, but ought to set aside or abrogate for the
time being, by his dispensation, any provision of the Constitution or By-Laws of
the Grand Lodge which may be in the way of obtaining a desired end. My opinion is that the Grand M11Bter, as such, is as much bound to observe and ohey the
Htatutes enacted by the Grand Lodge, as the subordinate officers and members of
the Fraternity. It is his especial duty to see those laws executed, and therefore
Hhould not himself set examples of their violation.
An unfortunate controversy has arisen between the Grand Lodge of Utah and
that of Nevada, in reference to the case of one M. D. FoLll:Y, It appears that this
party, whilst a resident of Nevada, presented his petition for the degrees to Wasatch
Lodge, No. 1, of Utah, and was elected and received the degrees therein. When
the facts became known to the Grand Master of Nevada, he, in a very courteous
and fraternal manner, complained to the Grand MaBter of Utah of the invasion of
the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of Nevada by W asatch Lodge. A
lengthy correspondence ensued, but the matter was not adjusted to the satisfaction
of the Grand Lodge of Nevada, and the Grand Master of Nevada directed charges
to be preferred against FOLll:Y in Eureka Lodge, No. 16, and upon trial he was
acquitted. An appeal being taken to the Grand Lodge of Nevada, that body
adopted resolutions expelling FOLll:Y, and notifying the Grand Lodge of Utah that
all Masonic intercourse with Wasatch Lodge and its members was interdicted until
the final settlement of the case to the satisfaction of the Grand Lodge of Nevada.
Thus the matter now stands. It further appears that FoLll:Y had been three times

There are many good things in this excellent report which, did space permit,
we would be pleased to notice. We cannot close, however, without expressing our
most hearty concurrence in the opinions of Bro. DIEHL on the evils of polygamy,
as well a.s those relative to the Solomonic origin of Ma.sonry. Under Oregon, he
thus expresses himself :King SOLOMON and the laws he gave may have been wise and good in his times,
but for the nineteenth century they are altogether too tyrannical. They won't def
at all for the Sons of Light. Come to think historical datas over, we don't believe
he ever made laws for them. He was a rich King, and his money builded the
Temple of Jerusalem, and, nothing better being known to the builder's guilds of
the middle ages, they used it as a •Yinbol in their Lodge work, and it waR keft a1
such at the reor~anization of Masonry, 1717, in England. In the tragedy o the
third degree, Kmg SOLOMON appears to great advantage, but, we ask, is that
tragedy historically or biblically correct? It is not. It is a beautiful poem, and
teaches excellent Masonic lessons, less<ms so valuable that nothing better could be
substituted. Even a SHAKESPEARE could not improve it, and for time and eternity
shall it remain a part of the Masonic work. But all that does not in the lea.st raise
our ideas of the historical King SOLOMON, who is set up as our lawgiver and whom.
we shall imitate. There is something fascinating about these old traditions, it is
true; they are surrounded with a sort of halo that is charming for many, but the
searcher wants the pure gold. It may take half of a lifetime to get rid of the mist,
but when once free from it, one feels that there iR more in life than the dream of
ancient glories or fictitious traditions. It is the present that counts, and the work
we do for the future. 'Ve look upon speculative Masonry as the great lever on the
wheel of advancement, and he who is a part of that lever finds his reward by be·
holding the onward march of the human race. To him the present and future is
all, the past nothing. If Masonry had nothing to show to the living generation
except its age, no matter how glonous that may'have been, it would not be worth
while to spend one single hour for it. Life is altogether too abort to waste even an
hour.

WEST VIRGINIA.

If we may judge from the Report of the Committee on Returns in this Grand
L odge, we should conclude that it would be immensely wise to appoint a Congress
of Instructors, qualified to teach Masters and Secretaries of Lodges the proper
method of discharging some of the more essential duties of their positions. We
are not a little surprised at the number of inaccuracies reported. It has always
appeared strange to us why complaint has so often to be made by Grand Secretaries
on this score, even when the law is so plain that he who runs might read. It is explainable on the i.rround only of superlative ignorance or inexcusable carelessne88.

The Address of the Grand Master is very brief, and contains nothing of general
interest further than the statement of the pleasan.t facts that prosperity and harmony have dwelt within the borders of the Jurisdiction, that no stain had been left
on its escutcheon, and that blessed peace reigned everywhere.
A number ~f Special Oommunications for various ceremonial purposes had
been held. Among other decisions we note the following :Quuticm..-A Master Mason suspended for non-payment of dues seeking restor·
ation, and there not being two-third votes favorable, should the money be returned
to him, or is it the property of the Lodge?
.Anawer.-He l1einl!' suspended for the non-payment of dues, and there being no
other charges against him, the money should be returned. If there are any other
charges against him than the non-payment of dues, they should be preferred in
writing, and proceeded with in regular form.
Doubtless the Grand Master decided in accordance with the law of the jurisdiction, but we think-justice being one of the cardinal tenets of Masonry-that Masons everywhere should place the seal of condemnation upon such a law. We see
neither justice nor charity in such a regulati,.n, and believe that when the duell ,
were paid the brother was entitled to the restoration of all his privileges as a member.
Th~ Grand Secretary, Bro. LONG, concludes his report with the declaration of
his intention to retire from the position in which, for fourteen years, he has so well
served the Grand L odge.
Tbe reports of the Grand Lecturer and District Deputies show that comparatively lit.tle work ha.cl been done during the year. This the Grand Lecturer considers as the result of the financial condition of the country, and not of any decadence in the pride 9r interest of the brethren.
The Committee on Correspondence presented a special report assigning reasons
for its failure to mo.ke a rei)ort proper, and suggesting the formation of a Masonic Congress for the United States which should have power to scrutinize the
character of Grand Bodies making application for recognition, and also to prescribe
rules that might enable a Mason in good standing in his own country, to visit upon
terms of equality any Masonic Lodge in the world. The idea appears to us
utopian. A little care and a little less haste upon the part of Grand Lodges to
recognize other Grand Bodies is the surest way. .As to individual Masons, if they
wish to be recognized as such, let them learn more thoroughly the work of the
Order, and they will meet with little difficulty in being recognized, and in being
enabled to visit upon terms of equality anywhere.

Just before the closing of the Grand Lodge, a brief but very excellent address
was delivered by the Grand Orator, Pe.st Grand Master JAMES H. HAYFORD, upon the progress of the world during the last fifty years, and its effects upon Masonry. After recounting some of the most wonderful advances in the arts and
sciences, Bro. HAYFORD says:And with all these improvements and inventions have grown up among men
new habits and new tastes. Men think and act, and the world and everything
in it move with lightning speed. Although we have annihilated time and space,
and turned night into day, "Freemasonry still survives, 11 but it don't keep up with
the times. Masonry is the most conservative thing on earth, and the world he.a no
use now for conservatism. It has always been our boast, and one of the especial
features of attraction of our " Ancient and Honorable Institution," that it mvtr
changes. It is not in the power of any man, or body of men, to make any innovations in Masonry. Nations may rise and fall, partieR and creeds may pass away,
even the Word of God- the great and sacred Light- may be "revised" and broug!!.t
down to modern times and· mod11rn language, but Masonry abideth forever. He
that should add to or take from it a word would be anath£ma maranathll.
Masonry is a symbolic exposition of great fundamental truths, and truth never
changes. The world has great need of that conservatism and of that institution which
will aid man in maintaining "in their fullest splendor 11 those truly Masonio ornaments, Brother'ty Love, Relief and Truth. In the rush and hurry of life, in the great
progress of art and science, man is apt to lose sight of those things which tend most
to enable him to Ii ve life aright, and to fit him for the life which Masonry and the
"11;reat and sacred Light 11 of Masonry teach us is to be, The world "in its pursuit
of wee.Ith and pursuit of knowledge," it is true, needs Masonry; but it does not
need Masonry "in just so far as Masonry can oonduoe to the acquisition of theae
two ends. 11 It has need of Ma.eonry for "a more noble and glorious purpose "-the
promulgation and conservation of those 11;reat truths, the observance of which fits
man for the exercise and the enjoyment of life in the upper a11d better sanctuary,
It is because Ma.eonry bas exaotly filled, and continues to fill, one of the greateet of
human wants. that it remaine, as it has done in all the years of its existence, con-.
servative.
Wyoming believes in the prerogative of the Grand Master to make Masone at
eight ; California does not, and we think California is right. The world does move;
in many of the non-e8sentials Masonry ha.e moved, and will in all thln11s move even
with the spirit of the age. Wyoming ought to move, and consign this dogma to
the place to which, aceording to the more advanced idea.e of truth and right, it properly belongs.

FOREIGN GRAND BODIES.
BELGIUM.

GRAND ORIENT OF BELGIUM,-Our Grand Secretary informs us that the latest
Bulletin of this Gran'.! Body received by him is the second fascicule of that publication for the years 1883-84. Among its contents we find the Encyclical Letter
of Pope LEO XIII against Freemasonry, which i• criticised as being "distingui~hed
by a collection of calumnies and untruths which should be sufficient to open the
eyes of members of our Order to the dogma of Papal infallibility"; two excellent
papers upon Masonic Precepts and the Principles of Freemasonry ; aml a number
of reviews and notices of sundry Grand Lodges and other Masonic Bodies in
Europe, Asia, Australia, and America.
California is mentioned as a Jurisdiction held in high consideration. Sundrf
decisions of our Grand Master are quoted with approval, and notice is given to
that portion of the Report of our Grand Secretary which (as usual,) announced that
all our Lodges had made complete returns and paid their annual dues in full.
Our Grand Lodge has in its library the bound volumes of the Bulletin du
<hand Orient de Be/,gique complete, from its commencement in 1874 to and including
the year 1884, with the exception of the publication for 1883. At the last advices
received the Ser.·. Bro. HENRI BERGE was National Grand Master, and Bro. HENRI
TAVERNE was Grand Secretary.

MEXICO

In our last report we presented a brief review of the history of Freemuonry in
the Republic of Me~co, and of its condition at the date thereof, Later advices
indicate that the aotibn of the Supreme Council, in unconditionally surrendering
jurisdiction over the Symbolic Lodges, was wisely conceived, and that its legitimate result has been to give an impetua to Masonry in that country which could
not have been accomplished in many years under the old system. The meJilbers of
the Symbolic Lodges now feel that they are, in truth, Free and Accepted Masona;
that they are no longer under the government of a Body, to the treasury of which
they were obliged to contribute without the privilege of being represented In its
councils; and that they are no more to have laws for their government, in the framing

Grand ./;od,ge of Oalifornia.

1886.J

631

of which they had no voice. Grand Lodges, on the American system, have been
formed in several of the States, the subordinates of which are rapidly increasing
and giving evidence of a. zeal and enthusiasm which is indicative of present and
future prosperity. Having heretofore, as b~fore stated, given a general history of
Masonry in Mexico, we11ow proceed to review briefly the proceedings of such of the
newly formed Grand Lodges therein as have transmitted their publications to the
office of our Grand Secretary.
FEDERAL DIBTRIOT,-The "Grand Lodge of the Federal District of the United
States of Mexico," which was organized on the twenty.third day of June, 1883,
does not publish its proceedings annually, in pamphlet form, but all its tranaactions
and the acts of all its officials a.re printed monthly in its official organ-La Gran
Logia-& periodical edited and published by Bro. CARLOS K. Ruiz, the flrRt Gra.nd
Master of that Grand Lodge, by its authority. Of this publication our Grand Bee·
retary has furnished us with a complete series from its first number, i11ued on
the tifteenth day of July, 1883, to that published on the fifteenth day of Ootober
of the current year. These pamphlets, together with the papers and documenta
mentioned in our Grand Secretary's Report, furnish a compreben1lve hl1tory of
this Grand Body from its organization to the date last above mentioned, The
Grand Lodge of the Federal District appears to have been recognized by a number
of Grand Lodg011 with which we are in communication, and has heretofore appealed to the Grand Lodge ef California for recognition and the establi1hment of
fraternal relations; but, owing to the somewhat complicated nature of Mucmio
affairs in Mexico generally, and the absence of sufficiently satisfactory lnforma•
tion, this recognition has been thus far delayed. It is now believed that all doubta
as to the legality of its formation and the permanency of its establi1hment hno
been removed, and that, at the present Communication of our Grand Lodge,
recognition will be extended and an exchange of Representatives be provided for.
The Grand Lodge of the Federal District complains bitterly of the action of
the Grand Lodge of Missouri in chartering and maintaining a subordinate Lodre
within the jurisdiction of the former. In this connection, the Grand Secretary
of the Federal District says: "Our Grand Lodge has done its best to obtain ju1tloe,
by using every conciliatory, prudent, and fraternal means in its power to avoid the
conflict which must now ensue between the Grand Lodge of MiBSourl and that of
the Federal District, which sees its jurisdiction invaded and Its rlgbta trodden
upon by the former." The Grand Secretary further states that the Grand Lodge
of Missouri has persistently refused to take notice of, or respond to, any of the
many communications sent thereto upon the subject, and hae continued to Ignore
every protest sent to her by the Grand Lodge of the Federal District. In view of
these facts, after exha.usting every effort to preserve harmony, that Grand Body,
at a Communication held on the fourth day of January, 1886, adopted the follow·
ing resolutions :lit. The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Federal District
(United States of Mexico,) does protest before the Masonic world in the most solemn manner, having th e right in her favor, 9.1rainst the invaeion of its jurisdiction
by the Grand Lodge of Missouri, which has permitted 2'oltec Lodge to work in this
Orient under its obedience.
2d. 2'oltec Lodge is hereby declared irregular and in rebellion, inasmuch aa it
has not submitted t o the authori_~ of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Federal District, (United States of Mexico,) which is here the only
lawful Masonic power for the l!'overnment of the Fratermty.
3d. No Lodge in this jurisdiction shall, until otherwise ordered, admit to ita
meetingR any member of any Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
Missouri, nor shall aid or relief be granted to such Masons if in distress or want.

Masonry in Peru has placed in charge of its destinies the eminent brother
General CESAR CANEVARO a most worthy Mason and one of the most distinguished
citizens of the Republic. It is a hat>PY choice, and one which we consider indicates
the most flatterinQ; pro•pects for the future of the Grand Lodue of Peru. The
elevation of Bro. CANEVARO to the Grand Mastership has been greeted by the entire Fraternity with significant demonstrations of joy, because they have reason to
expect activity, prudence and progress, when they see the gavel in the hands of
one who stands at the head of enlightenment and patriotism. We are certain that,
wherever the news is received of the event which to-day we celebrate, the exalta·
tion to the supreme government of the Craft of one of our most sympathetic public
men will be greeted with the utmost satisfaction. As a Mason and as a citizen,
the M. ', W. ·. Bro. CAN&VARO may be l!resented with pride as chief of an institution which aspires to be the school of virtue and patriotism, and is called to assume
so important a part in the movement to regenerate our customs both public and
private.
The Grand Master made a brief address after his installatifln, returning thanks
to the brethren for the high honor conferred upon him, and promising to use his
best efforts to advance the interests of the Craft. If he uses his moral forces in
the cause of Masonry as valiantly as he wielded his physical weapons in the cause
of his country, he will indeed be a brave 1tnd noble leader.
The R.-. W.·. Bro. J. ARTTJRO Eoo-.A.GUIBRE was agl\in elected and installed as
Grand Secretary. The announcement is made that the Lodge SteUa d'Italia, hithorto maintained under the Jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of Italy, had succumbed t o the force of circumstances and gone out of existence. The Bevista saysIts existence as regular Lodge ignored by the Grand Lodge of Peru, and de·
prived of all communication with the Lodges of this jurisdiction, the Lodge Stella
d'If,alia muri6 fa!ta de atmoafera querupirar. (Literally, died for la.ck of atmosphere
· to breathe.)
This violation of the Jurisdiction of the Grand Locige of Peru by the Grand
Orient of Italy, has been the cause of no little unpleasantness, and we conlfl'atulate our Peruvian brethren upon the disappearance of the disturbing element,
On the twenty-fifth day of March, 1886, the Grand L odge of Peru celebrated
the anniversary of its organization by a grand public assembly, and a concert and
ball. The Temple was beautifully decorated with flags, flowers and evergreens,
and every preparation was made for the comfort and pleasure of the numerous
guests. The Grand Master opened the proceedings with an eloquent discourse,
in which he stated the object of the reunion to be the commemoration of the establishment of the Grand Lodge of Peru, and extended a cordial welcome to those
who had honored the occasio" with their presence, addret!ljing himself especially
to the ladies. Following the Grand Master, eloquent and interesting addresses
were delivered bv Bros. I. LA PUENT& and A UGUSTIN Soro. A poem by Bro. J.
B. FUENTES closed the literary exercises. After this came the somewhat novel
ceremony of the Adoption of a Luveton .(Louveteau or Lewia) by the Grand Lodge.
The ritual of this ceremonial is given in full, and is almost identiclll with that
used by our Parfai,te Uwion Lo~ge on several similar occasions in this city. We
infer from the description that the celebration must have been in the highest degree
interesting and enjoyable, and we trust that our brethren of Peru may have many
happy recurrences of their pleasant anniversary.
The Freemasons of Peru, in common with other classes of her citizens, appear
to be profoundly exercised over the gradual reappearance of that most unwelcome
visitation, the disciples of IGNATIUS LoYCiLA, and are loudly calling upon the
government to enforce the law of 1855, which expelled these religious enthusiasts
from the soil of Peru. The B~vista is filled with scathing articles upon the Jesuits
and the alleged enormities committed by them; and, if one-half that is said of them
be true, we do not wonder at the strenuous opposition made to their return. It is

CONCLUSION,

Once more our t ask is completed. W e reach the end with feelings of pleasure
somewhat mingled with those of regret·-pleasure in the fact that our weary brain
will secure its needed rest-regret that we must leave the companionship of those
with whom we have passed so many pleasant and profitable hours. We m~ke no
pretension as no expert,-and shall feel entirely satisfied if we have succe~ded m our.
effort to interest and inform. Our opinion of the magnitude and the importance
of the work imposed upon the Correspondent of a Grand L odge ~as recei~ed addi·
tional strength, as has that of our inability to do justice t o all the mterests mvolved.
We h9.Ve endeavored to abbreviate as much as poBBible, and, hence, have been compelled to pass many things that we would like to have 'llOticed. 'Ve are pleased to
be able to represent that the year has been one of fair progress-financial ~nd otherwise. Harmony and prosperity have prevailed, and our noble Order is ready to
enter upon another year with increased interest and efficiency.
All which is respectfully submitted, for the committee, by
JAMES WRIGHT ANDERSON,

Chairm11in.

Bro. JAMES W. ANDERSON presented the following preamble and
resolution, which were unanimously adopted:WHEREAS, 1t has been made known to us that the afflicting hand of disease
has been laid upon our beloved brother, Pa.st Grand Master LEONIDAS E PRATT,
thereby depriving him of the pleasure, always so greatly enjoyed by him, of meetinir his brethren of the Grand Lodge, and denying them, not only the gratifica•
tion afforded by his presence, but the benefit of his wise counsel and useful labor:
therefore be itResolved, That the Grand Master and Past Grand Masters N . GREENE CURTIS
and WILLIAM C. BELCHER be and are requested to visit Brother PRATT, and, on
behalf of the Grand Lodge, to express to him the sincere sympathy of its members
for his affliction, and their earnest hope that he may soon be restored l() health
and the companionship of the brethren to whom he has made himself so greatly
endeared.

Bro. WILLIAM A. DAVIES, from the special committee to whfoh had
been referred the Address of the Grand Master, presented the following report:To the M. •• W. '. Grand Lodge of Calif<Yrnia:-

M.·: W.·.

Once more we are permitted by the Great Ruler of events to greet our
Grand Master, and, in accordance with our time-honored usage, to usemDld in
Annual Oc•mmunication for the purpose of enacting such · new legislation as the
growing wisdom of this progressive age may demand, and of reviewing and passing
upon the various questions submitted to our executive head during the recess of
this Grand Body.
In our Grand Master's Address we are reminded of the uncertainty of human
life by his fraternal notice of the death of one of the pioneers of Masonry in this
our Western home; and, recognizing our obligation as MMons to pay due honor to
the memory of the dead, as well as to protect and cherish the living, we pause in
the performance of the especial duty assigned us, to tender our tribute of fraternal
regard to the memory of a good man. Masonry honors the memory of tbe faithful
brother and laments his departure, but its votaries find consolation in a belief in
the a-oodness of God and the immortality of the soul.
Your committee recommend that so much of the Grand Master's Address as
relates to the arrest of the charter of Santa Clara Lodgo, No. 34; to the issue of a
dispensation to act upon the petition of a candidate for the degrees, without reference to a committee; to sundry questions propounded to the Grand Master, and hie
answers thereto ; to a certain proposed amendment to the by-laws of Excdai,or
Lod15'e, No. 166; to charges preferred against the late Master of Sacramenf.-0 Lodge,
No. 40; and to an examination of the '!Janner of trials in t.his jurisdiction; be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence:
·
That so much thereof as relates to the constituting of the Lodges chartered at
the last Annual Communication, and to the issue of dispensations for the formation
of new Lodges durinl{ the year, be referred to the Committee on Charters:
That so much thereof as relates to proposed amendments to the by-laws of
Lodges, be referred to the Co1I1mittee on By-Laws of Lodges; and
That so mttch thereof as relates to the distress at Charleston, South Carolina,
be referred to the Committee on Finances.
Your committee are in accord with the Grand Master in his opinions rea'arding
the effects of the growing tendency to interpose technical obstructions in the administration of Masonic discipline, with its inevitable result-the hindrance, if not the
absolute defeat, of justice. To those who are conversant with the many difficulties
to be met with in the trial of charges preferred before a Lodge located far away

1886.J

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

641

from the main thoroughfares of our Jurisdiction, we need advance no argument to
obtain a ready response to the declaration t hat, in all cases where it is evident that
an honest endeavor bas been made to administer substantial justice, the well-meant
ttforts of the brethren should not be set at naught because of an act of omission,
referring merely to the mode of conducting the inquiry. We have forms of procedure for the trial of all offences against our law, and it is well to observe all those
forms; but in no case should the omission of a requirement, which omission would
not be prejudicial to the rights of the Lodge or the accused, be permitted to
Interfere with the honestly determined judgment of a Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons.
And now, brethren, before closing this report, let us give you salutation. As a
Grand Lodge we have been wonderfully preserved. We are here to-day in the full
flush of vigorous manhood-for have we not with us our first Grand Master T It is
true that, for some of us, the frosts of advancing years would seem to eay, "but
a little longer and then-." And even now, while we write these closing words,
there comes to us the sorrowful tidings that one who has long borne with us the joys
and sorrows of this familv of ours, lies seriously ill at his home in this city. Let
llB remember him in his time of trial, and may God, in his mer cy, grant us his
companionship for many seasons yet during our journey.hence.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM A. DAVIES, }
JAOOB H . NBFF,
BENJAMIN F. THOMAS,
Committee.
THOMAS G. LAMBERT,
THOMAS FLINT, JR.,

Bro. ALVAH R. CoNKLIN, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the following reports :To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of Cali/O'Nlia:-

Your committee, to whom were referred sundry transcripts of trial-records
wherein no appeal has been taken, have attentively examined the said transcript.
and find that, in each case, the proceedings conform to the regulations of the Grand
Lodge, and that the dfltermina.tions reached by the Commissions in the several
cases are fully justified by the evidence.
It is peculiarly gratifying to your committee to be able to express their commendation of the excellent manner in which the records, submitted at this Uommunication, come before them. With but few exceptions the course of procedure by
th11 commissioners has been strictly legal and has conformed with exactness to the
requirements of our laws regulating trials. The transcripts a.re neatly prepared
and are creditable in every way. It shows that the lesson, endeavored to be taught
by your committee at the last Annual Communication, was well and kindly
received by the aubordiqate Lodges, has been profit.able, and has accomplished the
end desired- that of du& observance of our established forms of procedure .and the
proper administration of justice in accordance with our Constitution.
The tranar.ripts aho~e refer~ed to relate to .cases from the following named

w.·.

MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGE:There is something sublime in the thought that behind the ages, in the gloom of
the unremembered pa.st, in the very boyhood of man, there was a Society whose
principles were founded upon the equal rights of man, a.nd that the time of the
creation of this society ca.n not be marked by any historical event. Conspicuous
among the traditions of Masonry is the belief that it existed before any records of
profane history, before SoORArEB taught his sublime philosophy, before DEMOSTHH:NH:S thundered his orations a.gainat PHILIP of Macedon, before Rome existed,
and long before the Christian Era erected a new mile-atone on the highway of
nations.
In Masonry the old and the new are blended, the monarchial government of the
patriarchs and the freedpm of modern republics are made to haraonize together,
and the lesdona of the r~mote ages serve to abed new fo:ht t.hroug~ the gloaming ~f
the present. The quaint rituals of our Order and the faith which one Mason is
taught to have in another, are lessons which intlicate in a most marked d6gree the
simple character of those who lived in the early period of man's existence; and
these must have received their inspiration from the patriarchal age.
The old and the new differ in this, that the richer people become, and the more
enlightened they are, the more doubting and commercial are their instincts. A
warm heart does not often go with great buain.eas intellectual development, as business knowledge is principally the knowledge of dollars. In this age, man believes
what he sees more than what he is told. These facts would seem to carry on their ,

Grand Lodge of Oaliforni.a.
