face, if none others existed, the proof ef the antiquity of •ur Order; but its antiquity
does not alone inspire our veneration; it is not the number of its yea.rs, but ita
deeds, whioh we most admire.
Indeed, it matters but little whether Masonry existed onlyla few hundred years
ago, or before the pyramids, for we do believe that it eJ:isted before books were
printed, before gunpowder was invented, and before America. was discovered or
steamboats dreamed of. We know that railroads, telegraphs, teleph1mea, and
steam engines were not thought of when Masonry was being exemplified ever a
irreat portion of the world. vre knew that new nations have been created and old
ones have pa.seed away; that new and marvelous inventions have been made, and
that the world's history has been written and re-written over and over again since
Masonry was first taught to man ; yet the principles of Masonry are but little
chan&'ed, because time can not destroy truth, and because the calla of humanity
and the emotions of the human heart are the ea.me to-day as always, These are
like the inspirations of religion, or the love we have for hame and kindred.
.Although our rituals are uncha.ngeli, Masonry has progressed, Masons have
learned aomethiog daring the recent past. Masonry has a.dva.noed with the tide of
events and progressed with the march of human intelligence. It ha.a been a learner
and a teacher among men, but it ha.a learned only in its business relations with the
outside world. Its spirit, its sonl, is the same a.a of old; and, whether we note its
lessons in practical Muoory as exemplified in the construction of King SOLO.MON'S
Temple, or its sublimer leBBona in human charity and Christian benevolence, everywhere, and in all ages, it ha.a been an educator.
To-day it is the same irra.nd old Order a.a it was at the beginning. Its great &l\'0
has not broug'ht with it decrepitude or nurtured the seeds of decay, for it survives
now on what it d<tea to-day, It carves out its own history a.a fa.st as the fteeting
present passes by. We must admit that it is a human organizatien, with many
human frailties, and not destitute of human faults ; that it makes mistakes and
corrects them; but the mistakes our Order makes a.re but the proof of our human·
iJ;y, The remedies we afford come from the inspirations of a. Divine Providence,
and these represent the generous, the charitable side of man.
If we are to believe tradition, there i11 a peculiar romance about the early organ·
iza.tion of GUr Order. It ca.me inte existence in the far East, amid the grandest
specimens of God's handiwitrk, and in a.n age of faith that reached even beyond
the skies. It was craliled under the fostering ca.re vf the Patriarchs, and the sacred
precepts of prophecy and religion formed the corner-atone of the edifice. Yet Masonry acknowled1res no sect but the human race, no religion but that taught in the
Bible, whose Goo was the Goo of ABRAHAM, I sAAO and JAOOB. In the early
times Masonry wa.s a peace-offering to the world, and indeed in war it has been a.
conspicuous mel!Senger of peaae. In peace it has been the advance-guard in the
march of human freedom. Founded upon inspired religion and controlled by law,
it a.cknowledires alike its duty to religion, good order, and . relflllar government,
Though enry Lodge is a little republic, yet it ftourishes under the shades of monarchies, and a.mid the benign inftuenoea of the most perfect democracy, for the
whole human family is its children, and the whole world its home.
It is especially suited to the practioal charities of every-day Me, for ostentation
finds no place in Maeonry. Though it is a. humaa organization and conforms to
the customs of the peoples of all land.a, yet its creed is, and ever has been, to "do
unto others a.a ye w1mld they should do unto you." Its lessons give hope and
courage to the poor and ignorant, and lowers the pride of the rich and the envious.
Whatever else may be said of it, it is a. great leveler of men, but it seeks the highe11t plane for its level, and on that plane all are equal.

Procoodings of the

[Oct. 13,

, True, we •a re sometimes wearied with its plain and oft-repeated lessons &a
heard in the .Lodge-room, as we become annoyed at the rays of the blazing sun;
but, like the sun, this Order gives hope and life to all the world. No man can be
a iOOd Mason who is not a patriot, and true to his country, yet Masonry has
no national pride, no distinct nationality. There is no boundary line that marks
the limit of its usefulness, and the whole earth is its home. Still, each Juris,
diction is within some national authority which Masonry is bound t<> obey.
This is true because the language of Masonry is univer&Jal; it speaks in every
tongue and is known in every land. The most benighted and most ignorant of
men can understand its gieat truths and appreciate them. Its very simplicity is
its greatest strength, for it is intended for all men and all ages, past and to come.
It has been well said that Masonry has been the most remarkable and the most
illustrious organization ever known in hi.story, because it has brought, and still
brings, into one family and under one control all classes of people, from the prince
down to the humblest cottager. It makes no distinction of place, and confers no
honor except for real merit, for, after all, its only glory is the good it does, '
We often expect too much of Masonry, and we always expect too much of Masons. ¥aeons are human beings, and Masonry can only make the Mason the best
of his kind. The Masonic Order, therefore, cannot be any better than the men
who compose its membership; but Masonry never made a man worse, and it has
made many men better than they would have otherwise been. It is true that Ma·
sonry is not intended to remedy all the ills of life, nor does it give without receiving, for its charities are not and cannot be uni venal. Necessarily they are limited
to those who come within the scope of Masonic knowledie. To say that Masons,
even in the distribution of their charities, ~ake mistakes, is only to admit that
they are human, and subject to the same errors that other human beings are; and,
though we do make mistakes, we correct them without undue punishment vr
disgrace.
A Mason should never belittle the great character of the Craft by boldly defending those who possess neither character nor honor of their own, for the chai;acter of Masonry as an Institution is judged by the character of the men composing
it. We do not expect to build a house except upon a firm foundation, but when
the house is so built we would support its tottering walls against every blast that
beats against it. Masonry does not defend crime or criminals, nor does it seek to
hide them from the penalties which the law vf the land imposes upon them; for
the influence of Masonry should always be directed towards every good cause in •
the Order or out of it, as the Masonic character is a good character and can only
be maintained by good works.
It therefore becomes all-impor~ant for us to judge well of the Qharacter vf
those we admit into our Lodges. It is, perhaps, too frequent a thing that we in·
crease the membership thereof by admitting into our ranks those who are ill-fitted
to come among us; but we should not use the black-ball to keep a good man out
of the Order. Absalute justice is a living principle of Masonry. It is most impvrtant to guard agains' proselyting. It is not +mly important, but it is a direct
violation of Masonic usagrs to ask any one to become a member of our Order. Let
those who wish to know us, seek QB, and they will find what we are. Once let it be
known that we are not trying tlJ outnumber other associations, or to excel them in
popularity, and good men will seek admission to the Craft, and bad men will avoid
us. It is the best men we want, not the most. The great mistakl), after all, is
that we are trying to popularize Masonry toll rnuch. By this I mean that we try
sometimes to make everybody like us ourselv~ and like the Institution of Masonry, when, ilil fact, we shoqld only seek to deserve every good man's esteem and
not to expect his praise.

Masonry is, howeVlr, the most important social institution for still another
reason-it organizes the moral forces of the people. It occupie1 a plane different
from· that of the churches, (though it gives strength to them,) because it has no
reliiious creed. Its services in the field of politics are no less important, (though
it has no politics and belongs to no party,) because it teaches respect to orianiz~li
iOvernment a.nd obedience to law, and because every Lodge-room is a little republic where each brother is taught that he is a unit in the grea.t organization of
which he is a member, and in which he may rise step by step to the highest position
in its gift. Thus a laudable ambition is encouraged in the minds of the young,
which reaches it~ full fruition in advancing years.
And so, too, in the Lodge-room the impetuosity of youth is softened by the
milder counsels of age and experienoe. The old and the young in the Lodge,
are on an even plane, equal in their rights ; and yet every member has to earn his
reward by loni and faithful service. Promotion in our Order is not often a matter
of accident, and never should be gained by social position or electioneering devices.
It comes as the breath of Heaven comes, to strengthen and invigorate, not to
weaken or destroy. Masonry holds out to every good man a higher and loftier
aim in life than that afforded by the reward which comes of gratified ambition. It
gives every member the opportunity to benefit his fellow-men. The consciousne1111
of duty performed; the belief that one has lived with a purpose, and that purpose
a noble one; that he has made bright spots along the pathway of others; that ha
has given to the poor and cared for the sick ; that he has buried the dead and
made glad the bee.rt of the stranger ; are among the higher aims and loftier pur·
poses of Masons and Masonry. Whatever else we leave undone, these mUBt be
done. Failing in these, we fail in all the best and noblest purposes of the Order.

Your committee, to whom was referred the petition of JOHN NICHOLAS BAIL·
HACHE for restoration to the rill'hts a.nit privileges of Masonry, from which he was
suspended by SotfY!!ome Lodge, No. 123, on the twenty-ninth day of October, 1881,
find that the netice required to be given by Section Ii, of Article V, Part VI, of
the Constitution, was not thus given. That section provides that, in a case of suspension for unmaeonic conduct, should the application for restoration be refused by
the Lodge, as was the fact in this case, application for restoration may then be
made to the Grand Lodge; provided that notice, in writing, be given to the Lodge
of such intended application, not Iese than forty, days preceding the Annual Communication.
Your committee understand this requirement, as to time, to be mandatory, and
the notice in this case, having been served upon the eleventh day of September,
1886, but thirty-one days before the commencement of this Communication, was
not given within the time prescribed by the law, and the petitioner is therefore
precluded from receiving a favorable report thereon from your committee. With
these facts before them they can only report the followinll' resolution for adoption:Ruolved, That the petition of.JOHN NICHOLAS BAILHAOHE, f$r restoration to the
rights and privileges of M'yisonry, be dismissed.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the trial-record of A Uuraa
Lodge, No. 248, suspending GAMALIEL FULLENWEIDER HARRIS from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry on the seventeenth day of April, 1886, have examined
the same and find that the proceedings were properly conducted and that the infliction of the punishment of suspension was fully warranted by the facts adduced
in evidence. The Commission, however, in affixing the penalty of suspension, lim·
ited it to a period of twelve months. For this limitation there is not only no warrant In our Constitution, but there is a positive prohibition, as Section 3, Article
V, Part VI, thereof, presci;ibes that all sentences of suspension shall be for an indefinite period. The limited time of suspension thus adjudged by the Commission
In their sentence is simply surplusage, and should so be treated. E xcept the portion fixing a limit to the period of suspension, this record is approved, and your
committee offer the following resolution for adoption;.Re1ol.ed, That the transcript of the trial-record of AUuras Lodge, No. 248, and
the action of the Commission thereof in suspending GAMALIEL FULLENWErDEB
HARRIS from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and are hereby approved;
that the limitatien provided by said Commission1 that said suspension 'should be
for the period of twelYe D;lOnths, is unconstitutional and void; and that said
1entence of suspension be for an indefinite period.

Your committee, to whom was referred the tranacript flf the trial-record in the
oase of Bro. JOHN LAMBIE, who was suspended by Suiaun L odge, No. 55, on the
twenty·first day of November, 1885, from all the rights and privileges of Masonry,
from which action an appeal has been taken by him, have examined the proceedings therein and disapprove them.
The evidence in this case, both upon the part of the accuser and accused, is
composed to a great extent of letters which are unidentified, and which, even
though they were identified, would clearly be inaclmissible as evidence, being but
heanay. These letters, when offered by the aoouser, were admitted as proper evi-dence by the officer presiding over the Commiulon ; but, when the same character of
evidence was offered by the accused, some of the letters so produced by him were
admit ted, while others were rejected. In neither inatance were they admissible.
Other Elvidence consisted of a purely ez-pMte affidavit, taken lon1r prior to the trial
of tbe accused, without notice t o him, and having no semblance of a depo1itlon.
The record is defective, inasmuch as it does not show that the finding• of the
Commission were ever announced in the LC>dge and recorded thereiu aR ita judgment ; and the transcript of the proceedings of the Commiuion is not indor&ed as
approved by the Master, as is required by our twenty.fourth General Regulation.
After a full consideration of the testimony as it appears of record, and of the
additional evidence offered by the accused, which comes from Masons who rank
high in t he Fraternity here, as well as from members thereof from the Territory of
Arizona, of which the aooused is now a resident, going to show conclusively to the
minds of your committee that the accused is not amenable to the charge as preferred, they are constrained to offer t he following resol11tion and recommend its
adoption :.&aolved, That the proceedings and record of the Commission convened by Suiaun
Lodge, No. 55, which sentenced Bro. JOHN LAMBIE, on the twenty-first day of
November, 1885, to be suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be
and are hereby disapproved; and that the charge preferred therein be and is hereby
dismtssed.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of t he t rial-record in the
case of HENRY CLAY KELsEr, a member of Olay Lodge, No. 101, who was expelled
by Mountain Shade Lodge, No. 18, on the eleventh day of May, 1886, from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, and who has appealed from said action of that
L odge, have fully considered the same and report that they find the proceedings
regular, and that the judgment of the Commission was fully warranteli by the
evidence.
The charge against the accused was based upon and sustained by the certified
record of the Ori!B.inal Court of Sierra County, showing his conviction befflre said

656

Procwlings of the

[Oct. 14,

Court for the crime of which he had been informed against; and that is conclusive.
The appeal in this case claims that Mountain Sluuk Lodge, No. 18, had no juris·
diction over the person and offense of the accused, he being a member of another
Lodge within this State, and not a resident within the territorial jurisdiction of
Mountain Shade J,odge. This want of jurisdiction in the trial-Lodge is claimed by
a mere assertion set forth in the grounds of appeal, and is not supported by any
evidence.
The accused was a member of another than the trial-Lodge, but resided-at
least his offense was committed-within the jurisdiction of the Lodge in which
charges were preferred against him and by which he was tried; and there is no
evidence that his residence was at any other place than that where the crime waa
committed. The fact, therefore, that the Lod1re which tried him bad power so to
do is conclusive in the absence of any evidence to the contrary. This being the
case, charges could have been preferred against him in either his own Lodge, or in
the Lodge within whose jurisdiction he residsd. Either could take cognizance of
them. The appeal is not well taken, and your committee therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the appeal of HENRY CLAY KELSEY, of Olay Lodge, No. 101,
from tb.e jud1rment of Mountain Shade Lodge, No. 18, expelling him from all the
rights and pri•ileges af Masonry on the eleventh day of May, 1886, be dismissed,
and that the said judgment be and is hereby affirmed.
All which is respectfully submitted by
ALVAH R. CONKLIN, }

Bro. WILLIAM A. DAVIES, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports :To the M.-. W. •. Grwna Lodge of O<Uiforma ; -

The Committee on J urisprudenoe have examined the reported action of the
Grand Master in issuing dispensations for the formation of new Lodges ; in deputin~ certaia officers to constitute the Lodges to which charters had been granted
at the last Communication; in his authorizations· for the laying of corner-stones
and the dedication of Masonic Halls; in approving sundry amendments to the bylaws of certain L odges; and in granting a dispensation to ballot, without refeNnce,
to Live Oak Lodge, No. 61 ; and, as these are all matters vested in the discretion
of the Grand Master by the Constitution, th'ey have only to report that his action
has, in all respects, been in consonance with our law.
Your committee have had under consideration the proposed amendment to the
Constitution, offered by Bro. JOHN M. l.IULll:NDY, to strike out the words "one
dollar," in the second line of the second clause of Section 4, Article VIII, Part I,
and to insert in lieu thereof the words "seventy-five cents"; so that the clause
shall read-" F or each Master Mason borne upon its roll at the date of its annual
report, the sum of seventy-five cents."
It is respectfully suhmitted that your committee are still impressed with the
same convictions which governed their report upon the same proposition at the
Annual Communication in 1883. The result sought to be attained by this amendment is the reduction of the tax levied for the support of the Grand Lodge. The
amount received from this source during the last year was about $14,500. The
adoption of this amendment WGuld reduce that sum twenty-five per cent., and,
while seriously affecting our aggregate income, would afford but slight relief to th11
individual Lodies.
As they have said before, your committee are fully CQnvinced of the prepriety
of keeping our receipts at such a standard as will msure sufficient revenue for the
exercise of all such fraternal demands as may be made upon us at home or from
abroad. They fe'el ,that the adoption of this amendment would endanger such
standard of revenue ; and, fo view of our incre11Bing responsibilities, as evidenced by
the additional petitions at ithe present time for the generous bounty of this Grand
Lodge, they repeat their f~rmerly ~xpressed opinion and again recommend that
the proposed amendment be not adopted.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM C. Bll:LOHER,}

.

such as would entitle him to affiliate with the local Lodge, should he be restored.

At the last Annual Communication, the Masonic Board of Relief of the city of
Harysville presented certain papers complaining of a decision of the Grand Master
in a matter in controTersy between that Board and Nicolaus Lodge, No. 129, relative to certain expenses incurred in the burial of one E. M. BRONSON, The
decision complained of was based upon the following facts:On the eleventh day of January, 1884, Bro. BRONSON, a non-affiliated Ma10n, presented his dimit and application for membership to NicolauB Lodie, No. 129, and,
in accordance with the provisions of Sec. 8, Art. V, Part VI of our Constitution,
paid thereto a sum equivalent to six months' dues thereof. On the eighth day
of F ebruary, next following, his application was rejeoted. His payment .placed
him in good standing for six months thereafter, being until August eighth. On June
1ixth BRONSON pa.id another six months' dues to the Lodge, but did not again pre1ent or offer to presAnt any application for membership, being told by the Seoretary
of the Lodll'e that the simple payment would continue his good standing to January
eleventh, 1885. On September second, 1884, he died at Marysville, and was there·
after buried by the Masonic Board of Relief .,f that dty, not being at the time in
good standing, and, by reason thereof, not being lawfully entitled to Masonic burial.
But it fully appears from the papers submitted that, at the time of the payment
of six months' dues on .Tune sixth, BRONSON was distinctly informed by the Secre·
ta.ry of Nicoi,aua Lodge, No. 129, that his good st.anding would extend to the
eleventh January, 1885; and it further appears that that Secretary gave informa·
tion to the Board of Relief of Marysville to that effect. The funeral expen•e•
&mounted to seventy.five dollars, which sum was paid by the Board of Relief, and
that Board requested its re-payment by Nicolaus Lodge, No. 129. Application
being made by both parties to the then Grand Master, (the writer of this report,) he
decided that the Board of &lief was not entitled to have the sum refunded. This
decidion, by somti mistake or overai'l'ht of that Grand Master, foiled to appear in
hie Annual Address for the year 1885.
After a full consideration of the matter-viewing the facts in the light of the
1uperior wisdom and experience of other members o{ this committee-the writer
hereof is fully convinced, and agrees with them, that the decision of the then Grand
Master was erroneous and should be overrnled; and that NicolaUB Lodge, No. 129,
having, through the mistake or culpable negligence of its Secretary, caused the
11penditure, is responsible to the Masonic Board of Relief of the city of Mary11ville
for all sums properly expended by that Board in the burial of said BRONSON.

Our Constitution provides for the removal of Lodges and prescribes t~e proet!d·

resolution for that purpose will be offered at the next; then that, at the next,

members present; and thereafter that the action be approved by the Grand Lodge
or the Grand Master. This implies that there shall be presented to the Grand
Lodge o:r the Grand Master some good reasons for the removal ~sides the m~re
fact that a vote has been had,-something more than the bare recital ~hat a notice

In this case your committee have the simple fact that the res?lut1on, after 1mndry

The committee think that appro~al. should, except perhaps in rare instances, be withheld unlesR at least a clear maiori~y ~f al~ the members favor the remova1 Here it does not appear that such a mai.or.1ty did favor removal, or that any epepial benefit would accrue therefrom; and it 1s recommended

and should weigh well the meaning of every word used, as well a• the general purport of each section or subdivision; and the language used should be clear, and expre"8 our meaning exactly, and be incapable of any other meaning. We do not
think that any one of these preposed Regulations would stand the test of such a

The first relates to the formation of new Gra.nd Lodges, and declares that three
or more regularly constituted Lodges may, if they constitute a majority of all the
Lodges in "a territory,'' organize a Grand. Lodge, provided 11ll the Lodges in the
territory have been duly notified of the intended action.
Territory is a word of somewhat uncertain signification. The first definition
given by Mr. WKBBTll:R is-" The extent or compae&of land within the bounds or
belonging to the jurisdiction of any State, city or other body." If these reaolutiona
were limited to the United States of America, we might very properly understand
that the word "territory" was intended to mean and include a district of country
embraced within the well defined and fixed ooundaries of a State; and, as well, a
district of country belonging to the Federal Government, organized as a Territory,
the boundaries and extent of which are at all times subject to be changed at the
will of that Government. Applied to other countries, its meaning would be very
uncertain.
The second of these resolutionk relates to the rights and powers of a Grand
Lodge, when once legally constituted in a new territory, and declares that such
new Grand Lodge is sovereign over the whole of that territory, and that all the

A Grand Lodge has been established in the Territory of Utah, and, as the rfsolution deolares, is sovereign Gver the whole of that territory. SuppoRe that, at its

In the United State~ the law appears to be settled that three or more Lodges,
if they conotitute a majority of all the Lodges in any State or organized Territory,
and if all the Lodges therein have been properly notitied in regard to the proposed action, may form a Grand Lodge; that such Grand Lo:lge, when formed, is
entitled to have and maintain exclusive jurisdiction within such State or Terri·
tory; and that any Lodge within its jnrisdiction, refusing to yield obedience to it,
would by such refusal render itself irregular. But we do not understand that
this rule of exclusive jurisdictional right is a fundamental rule or has been uni;
versally accepted, or that it ever has been accepted or reeognized by all or any of
the Grand Lodges of Europe.
England, Scotland, and Ireland constitute one government, yet in that government there are three Grand Lodges-that of England, established in 1717; that of
Ireland, established in 1728; and that of Scotland, esta.blished in 1736; all which
exercise concurrent jurisdiction and have established subordinate Lodges and Pro.
vincial or District Grand Lodges in the Provinces and Dependencies of the British
Empire.
In Germany there are three Grand Lodges having their seats at Berlin, and
these exercise concurrent jurisdiction.
In France there ie a Grand Orient, practicing what is called the French Rite,
and a Supreme C()uncil, practicin11 the Scottish Rite; an<l these exercise concurrent jurisdiction in the Republic and its Poseeeeions.
Yet in Great Britain, Germany, and France these Grand Bodies have, for a
long series of years, in the exercise of their concurrent jurisdiction worked harmoniously, and we are r.ot advised that any claim to exclusive jurisdiction haeever
been made by them or ~ny of them.
Whenever a Grand ~odge has been established in any of the Provincea of the
British Empire, the Gr&nd Lodges of England, Scotland, and Ireland have refused
to recognize the newly establish;ed Grand Lodge, except upon the condition that
their subordinate Lodges should be allowed to maintain their allegiance and continue work under their old warrants or charters without molestation so long as they
should desire so to do. So it was in the ca.see of the Grand Lodge of Canada and
the other Grand Lodges in the Dominion of Canada; and so it was in the case of
the Grand Lodges of the Australian Oolonies.

The preamble assumes that full and exclusive jurisdiction over every Lodge of
Masons located within its territory passes at once as a fundamental right to any
new Grand Lodge upon its formation, and that any Lodge in such territory, which
refuses to recognize and surrender to the authority of the new Grand Lodge, is
necessarily in rebellion to the constituted authorities, and that it is only just that
its members should be excluded from all assemblies of, and from all intercourse
with, good Masons everywhere.
As we have said in our report on the pending contention between the Grand
Lodges of England and of Quebec, this claim of im!Dediate and exclusive jurisdiction over all or!<"anizations of Ancient Craft MaRons in the territory over which a
newly established Grand Lodge assumes jurisdiction, is not a fundamental right at
all, and has never received the universal or general assent or approval of the governing bodies of Masonry iii the world; but is altogether recent, and is largely, if
not wholly, the outgrowth of the peculiar condition and political relations of our
American States to one another and to the General Government.
The real parties to the contest are the Grand Lodge of England and the Grand'
Lodge of Quebec, and it would seem to us that, if the matter at issue were of Ruch
serious moment that other Grand Lodges ought to engage actively in it, their blows
should be aimed at the principal and not at the subordinates.
The relations 'llf Grand Lodges are in many respects like those of independent
nations. If France and Germany, for some real or fancied cause, engage in war
with each other, it does not follow that the United States, because they have
entered into and continued treaty relations with one or both, should actinly engage
on one side or the other. Notwithstanding the pendency of the conflict, our Government may continue to maintain the most friendly relations with both. So when
a contest arises between two Grand Lodges with which our Grand Lodge maiatains friendly relations, we think that the latter may properly continue its friendly
relations with both. The recognition of one Grand Lodge by another does not
imply that the Grand Lodge extending the recognition approves of all the claims
asserted by the one thus recognized, nor that it will enter actively, or at all, into
any controvel"!y that may arise in regard to such claims.
This Grand Lodge has entered into, and for many yeard maintained, relations
of amity with the Grand Lodge of England and with the Grand Lodge of Quebec,
and we do not think that the existing difficulty between those two should interrupt
or in any way interfere with those relations.

But we do not understand upon what foundation this new Grand Lodge, with
its thirteen constituent Lodges, could in 1881, declare the Spanish Peninsula unoccupied territory, even for a Grand Lodge of Symbolic Masonry; an<l that it might
rightfully assume exclusive authority and control over all Lodges of the Ancient
Craft, when there were in that territory at the time more than three hundred
active Lodges of Master Masons under the obedience of the three Grand Orients
which we have named. At that time the Gran I.Qgi,a Simb61ica, constituent of the
Grande Oriente de Espaiiw., and of which Bro. J UAN ANTONIO PEREZ was Grand
Master, .had under its obedience more than one hundred and thirty Lodges; and
the Grand Lodge of the Gran Oriente Nacional more than one hundred and fifty, of
which one, Matriteuse, No. 1, dated its organization as early as 1728, and claimed
to be one of the Lodges established in Madrid by the Grand Lodge of England
when under the Grand Mastership of U>rd COLERAINE. Spain was certainly not
unoccupied territory in 1881, and the claim of the new Grand Lodge to exclusive
jurisdiction is without any foundation. 'l'he most earnest advocate of Grand Lodge
sovereignty and exclusive jurisdiction could not uphold such a claim.
We do not mean to say that, because only a small fraction of the Lodges in the
territory participated in the formation of the new Grand Lodge, its formation was
necessarily irregular; for it appears that all those J,odges were working under
charters from a fo~·eign Jurisdi~tion, aild it may be were practicing the York Rite,
or some regular rite other than the Scottish Rite; and if the new body were formed
only to preside over and .w ork in that rite, it might be in all respects independent
of those Grand Orients and not necessarily in conflict at all witb them or their subordinates; and In such case they might, and, for anything that we can see, ought
to be willing to welcome the new Body and enter into friendly relations with it.
There is no reason in the nature of things why all those Grand Bodies might not
work as harmoniously as do the three Grand Lodges in Berlin, each respecting the
rights of the others. But an assertion of a right to exclusiva. control is a declaration that all others must surren<ler to its authority or bti,declared irregular.

On the twenty-fifth day of June, 1883, the Grand Lodge of the Federal District
of the United States of Mexico was organized at the city of Mexico. Your com·
mittee have before them and have carefully examined the proceedings of the Con·
vention by which that Grand Lodge was organized, its constitution and statutes,
and the reports of its proceedings as published in its official organ, La Gran
LQgi,a, a journal under the editorial management of Bro. CARLOS KOCH Rurz, the
first Grand Master of the Grand Lodge named.
The new Grand Lodge claims jurisdiction only over the three symbolic degrees
and within the territory of the Federal District. The Supreme Council of the 33•
has formally relinquished to it all control over those degrees, and has thus made
it what it professes to be-an independent Grand Lodge. By its Constitution It
asserts absolute jurisdiction over all Lodges of Master Masons, and over the three
degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft, and Master Mason, within the territory of the Federal District. It complains, therefore, that the Grand Lodge of
Misso1ui has not recognized its authority, but has permitted the Lodge " Tolttc,
No. 520," upon its register, located in the city of Mexico, to continue to work under
its obedience. This it .terms an invasion of its jurisdiction. It also complains of
a like invasion by the Grand Lodge of Hamburg.
The Lodges in regard tQ which these complaints are made were chartered and
established in the city of Mexico prior t o the organization of this new Grand J,odge.
As your committee have had frequent occasion to say, they do not understand that
it is an established law, or a universally recognized rule, that a Grand Lodge which
has rightfully established a subordinate Lodge, as the Grand Lodge of Missouri

established its Tottec Lodge in the city of Mexico, must, upon the organization of a
new Grand Lodge asserting jurisdiction over the territory within which such Lodge
is located, immediately compel its subordin•te to transfer its allegiance to that
new Grand Lodge or surrender its charter. But, on the contrary, they do understand the rule in such casea, elsewhere than in the U oited States of America, to
be that the parent Grand Lodge may of right permit, and is in duty bound to permit, its subordinate to continue its work and its allegiance, and to sustain it in the
n1aintenance of that allegiance, so long as it shall desire to continue its work under
its oric:rinal charter. It.is a matter of comity to permit the subordinate to transfer its allegiance, if it choose dO to do; but the Grand Lodge which should
abandon a subordinate in such a case, would prove recreant to a solemn duty which
it assumed when it granted the charter, and which it ought faithfully to perform.
Your committee need not discuss the proposition here, but it is proper that it
should be mentioned, in order that it may not be supposed that, in extending recognition to the Grand Lodge of the Federal District of Mexico and entering into
friendly relations therewith, the Grand Lodge of California assents to all the
claims preferred by that new Grand Lodge in respect to exclusive jurisdiction, or
that it will necessarily or probably sever its friendly relations with the Grana
Lodge of Missouri should that body pera;at in sustaining its Lodge ToUec in the
city of Mexico.
Thia Grand Lodge extends recognition when a new Grand Lodge has been regularly formed, and seems to have been established upon the firm basis of the
landmarks of Masonry and to have given promise of permanent usefulness; and
it enters into fraternal relations therewith because it would cultivate friendship and
maintain the most cordial correspondence with all legitimate governing bodies of
Masons and with all Lodges and Masons in obedience to them; but it by no
means deems it a duty to become a party to their controversies.
In this case your committee recommend the recognition of the Grand Lodge of
the Federal District because they find, upon a careful examination of its constitution, statutes and proceedings, and the proceedings of the convention which established it, that it was regularly formed and has adopted and declared the landmarks
of Masonry as its fundamental law, and because it shows that it 1s, and gives
promise that it will continue to be, permanent and useful. They therefore offer
the following resolution and recommP.nd its adoption:ReBolved, That the Grand Lodge of California recegnizes the •· Gran L6gia de
Libres y Aceptadoa Masonea de! Distrito Federal" of the United States of Mexico
as a just and legally formed Grand Lorlge, and cordially accepts its proposal for the
establishment of friendly relations and an interchange of Representatives.

MosT WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER, BRETHREN, ANlJ FRIENDS:A ·great sorrow overshadows the Masonic Fraternity of this Jurisdiction,
Its beloved Past Grand Master, LEONIDAS E. PRATT, is dead. No, not dead, but
gone before-gone to the reward which a busy and useful life, spent not for self
alone, well merited; a reward higher than life's honors can bestow, higher than
the highest ambitions can attain; a reward which glvea the weary crafhman, after
years of toil and sorro~, an eternal, blissful re~t. He Is not dead, though his soul
has left its tenement of clay, for he lives in the hearts and affections of his brethren,
who "knew him but to love him, who named him but to prai11." JI 11 noble
deeds of pure beneficence, his always active yet unobtruaive charity, hi1 genorou•
and kindly disposition, will ever remain green in the memory of hl1 brethren of the
Craft he so much loved.
We are here to-day to mingle our serrow with that of the bereaved widow and
fatherless eons iii this their hour of affliction and desolation; to atte•t onr love
and esteem for the friend now gone:; to pay a last sad tribute to the departed
brother who was so near to our hearts in life, and whom in death we now •<>
greatly mourn.
One short year ago Bro. PRATT stood where I now stand, and, from the depth•
of his great, warm, tender heart-alas! now stilled-and with a tongue ever
eloquent and affecting, paid fitting tribute to the memory of a deoeaaed officer
of this Grand. Lodge; and to-day, it is my sorrowful privilege to place upon hie bier
this chaplet of immortelles, not for myself only, but for the entire Fraternity, a.a
a memento that our love f&r him was great while living, and that hie memory will
ever be enshrined in our hearts as it is now embalmed with our tears. But worda
are weak, and they can but faintly give voice to the eloquence of a grief which
vainly attempts a fitting utterance.
At five o'clock on the morning of the twenty-fifth day of October, 1886, at hlH
residence in the city of San Francisco, surrounded by hie irrief·etricken family and
sympathizing friends, at that hour when night threw back her mantle to welcvme
the coming day, when all nature was hushed ' in early morninir's deep repo1e,
the spirit of our beloved brother took its eternal flight to that unknown le.all
whither our fathers have gone before us. In the full posaeBBion of all hl1 fe.culti11 1
paialesely, calmly, he met the Angel of Death ; and our faith in God, our hope of
immortality, gives UB the blessed assurance th~t the toiJ-worn craftsman haa found
eternal rest.
"Our love will dream, our faith will tru1t,
Since He who knows our needs ta Ju1t,
That somehow, somewhere, meet we mn1t.
Alas for him who never sees
The stars shine throu;rh his oypreH tr~e;
Who, hopeless, lays his dead away,
Nor looks to see the breaking day
Across the mournful marble• play;
Who hath not learned, In hours of faith,
The truth, to flesh and eeaee unknown,
That Life is ever Lord of Death,
And Love can never loae its own."
Brother PRATT was born in Pompey, Onondaga County, in the State of New
York, on the twenty-ninth day of AuguHt, 1833. While yet a youth the wondrous

tales of treaRure, which turned countless eyes to the new El Dorado, had reached
his eastern home, and m 1855 we find him a resident of the Golden State. After
some experience in the mines he fixed 'his dwelling-place in Sierra County, where
he en!j'aged in the practice of the law. Equipped with· a broad legal and general
learning, and spurred on by an ardent love of his profession and a noble ambition
to auooeed, he early won distinction. In 1860, being then twenty-seven years 11f
aye, he was elected District Attgrney of the county. His successful administration of the affaira of that office found a grateful appreciation by his fellow citizens,
and he wu soon promoted to the higher station of Dietrict Judre. At the expiration of hie term of that office he refused a re-nomination therefor, and was called to
a different sphere of action. In 1865 he was elected to the Senate of the State,
where be served with a fidelity to the interests of hie constituents, and an ability
no a legislator, which made him an honored and conspicuous member of that body.
In 1868 he removed to San Francisco, where he returned to the actiTe duties of his
pr.>feeaion, and where, in 1881, he was elected District Attorney of the City and
Uounty.
A.a a lawyer, he was learned in his profession and true to eTery trust reposed in
him; of unyielding integrity and unswerving fi!ielity; e.-er actuated by a high
•ense of propriety and dignity; and, in the heat of forensic debate, never for~etting
the courtesies of a gentleman. As a Judge, he was courtly, impartial, firm, just,
yet merciful. As a Senator, he was wise in counsel, bold in action, and fearless in
debate; true to his constituents and loyal to his country.
For the first time we were brought personally together in the State Senate in
1867. There I formed for him a warm and most sincere attachment. Na.ture
had lavishly endowed him with noble qualities 'of both head and heart which
rendered him dear to all who knew and appreciated his many gifts. He was brilliant, earnest, RCh3larly, eloquent-a born genL!eman and orator.
He was a learned and zealous Mason. Feeling deeply the reeponsibilitie11 of the
Order in its relations to men, his conduct was a living exemplification of its sublime
teachings. As an evidence of the high appreciation in which he was held by his
brethren of the Mystic Tie, h~ was thrice elected Master of Mountain Shade Lodge,
No. 18; was Grand Orator of the Grand Lodl!'e in 1865; and in 1867 was elected
Junior Graod Warden. The ability displayed in the discharge of these high duties
won him still more exalted honors. In 1868 he was elected Deputy Grand Master;
and the following year he was called to preside over the destinies of the Craft as
its Grand Master, the highest dignity within its gift, and an honor which should
only be conferred, as in our brother's case, upon one well skilled, true and trusty,
and learned in the law, literature and traditions of the Order.
He was elected to this high office for four consecutive yea.rs, from 1869 to 1872.
As our Grand Master he not only inculcated, but by example illustrated, those noble Masonic virtlftls, brotherly love, relief and truth: love to GGd and our fellowmen; relief to suffering humanity in whatever form it might be found; and truth,
that divine attribute which is the foundation of every virtue, which comes from
the Creator and sheds blessings upon His creatures, aud which is more lasting
than time, more durable than ~arth.
Our brother was kind, gentle and good; guileless as a child and tender.hearted a1
a woman; and his charity was only circumscribed by the limit of his means.
Wherever and whenever suffering was presented to him, he asked no question&,
but gave; and his benevolence.was prompt, active, and without ostentation. The
poverty of the hungry, homeless wayfarer touched his tender heart and generous
nature; and his soul went out in boundless charity and infinite tenderness to poor
frail humanity. Want and misery, in any form or from any cause, found in him a

teachings of our Order, by administering comfort and consolation to the sorrowing,
lifting up the downfallen, and inspiring all with hope and oonfidence. The poor,
the friendless, the orphan, the widow, may indeed weep, for they have lost a friend.
Their tears will be a nobler offering to his memory than the most eloquent words
of eulogy. The good that he has done ia not, cannot, be buried with him. It
remains as a halo around his name, to make him remembered as long as charity
exists, not a mere abstract, but a living, glorious reality.
He has gone from us forever. We shall miss from tbeae ha.II~ the well-known
form-the cheerful smile-the cordial, fraternal greeting' of our departed brother.
His voice, ringing out in eloquent strain•, when right was to be dPfond11d or wrong

Master, as follows:..__
Once more, my brethren, have we a•sembled to perform the last sad and solemn
duties to the dead. The mournful notes which betoken the departure of a spirit
from its earthly tabernacle have again alarmed our outer door, and another baa
been taken to swell the numbers in that 1.1nknown land whither our fathers hue
gone before WI·
Our brother has reached the end of life. The brittle thread which bound him
to earth has been severed, and the liberated spirit has winged its flight to the un·
known world. The silver cord is loosed; the golden bowl is broken; the pitcher is
broken at the fountain; and the wheel is broken at the cistern. The dust has re·
turned to the earth as it was; and the spirit has returned to God who "'ave it•
While we deplore the loss of our beloved brother, and pay this fraternal tribute
to his memory, let us not forget, my brethren, that we, too, are mortal; that our
bodies, now so strong an<! vigorous, mnst ere long, like his, become tenants of the
narrow grave; and that our spirits, too, like his, must return to the God thatepake
them into existence. " Man that is born of woman ie of few days, and full of
trouble. He cometh forth as a flower, and is cut down; he fleeth also as a shadow,

to be forgotten.
Seeing then, my brethren, that life is so uncerta.in, and that all earthly purauits are vain, let us no longer postpone the all-important concern of preparing for
eternity; but let us embrace the present moment, while time and opportumty are
offered, to provide against that great change when •all the pomps and pleasures of
this fleeting world will pall upon the sense, and the recollection of a virtuous and
well-spent life will yield the only comfort and ccmsolation. Thus we shall not,
unprepared, be hurried into the presence of that all-wise and powerful .Tudll'e, to
whom the secrets of all hearts are known ; and on the great day of reckoning we
shall be ready t.o give a good account of our stewardship while here on earth.

favor of that Eternal Being whose goodness and power know no bounds; that, on
the arrival of the momentous hour when the fading taper of human life shall faintly

This lamb-skin, or white apron, i1 an emblem of innocence and the peauliar
badge of a Mason. It is more ancient than the Golden Fleece or Roman Eagle ;
and, when worthily worn, more honorable than Star or Garter, or any other Order
which earthly power can confer. This emblem I now deposit in the grave of our
deceased brother. ( Droppi,11{1 it upon the coffin,) By this act we are reminded of the
uoi versa! dominion of Death. The arm of Friendship cannot oppose the King of
Terrors; the shield of Fraternal LoYe cannot protect his victim ; nor can the
charms of Innocence avert his fatal touch. All, all must die. This grave, that
coffin, and this circle of mourninir friend1, remind u1 that we, too, are mortal, a.nd
that ere long our bodies, also, shall moulder into du1t. How important then it i1
for us to know that our !Wdeemer liveth, and that be 1hall 1tand at the latter day
upon the earth !

Taking th~ sprig of ~cacia in his hand, he oontinuedThis Evergreen, which once marked the temporary reetlng-pla.oe of one illu1trious in Masonic history, is an emblem of. our enduring faith In the immortality
-0f the soul. By it we are reminded that we have an imperieha.ble part within ua
which shall sunive the grave, and which will never, never die. By it we a.re ad·
monished that, though like our brother, whose remains now lie before u1, we too 1hllll
eoon be clothed in the habiliments of death, and be deposited In the silent tomb;
yet, through the loving goodness of our Supreme Grand Master, we may confidently
hope that, like this evergreen, our souls will hereafter flourish in eternal 1prinr.

The choir then sang the beautiful and appropriate ohant-Tllg Will
-Oe Done-and the Grand Master proceeded with the service, as follows :From time immemorial it has been the custom among the Fraternity of Fi'0f'
and Accepted Masons, at the request of a brother, to accompany his remain• to the
place of interment, and there to deposit them with the solemn formalitie1 of the
Craft.
In conformity to this usage, and in accordance with the duty which we ow11 to
<>ur departed brother, whose lose we now most deeply do deplore, we have a11um ·
bled in the character of Masons to offer up to his memory, before the wctrld, the
last eatl tribute of our affection ; thereby demonstrating the sincerity of our past
t>eteem for him, and our steady attachment to the prinoiplea of our beloYed Order.
The great Creator having been pleased, in His infinite wisdom, to remove our
brother from the cares and troubles of this transitory life, thus severing another
link in the fraternal chain by which we are bound tog~ther-let ~s, who survive
him, be yet more strongly cemented by the ties of brotherly love; that, during the
brief space allotted to us here, we may wisely and usefully employ our time, and,
in the reciprocal intercourse of kind and friendly acts, mutually promo~e the welfare and happiness of each other.
Unto the grave we have consigned the body of our deceased brother-earth to
earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust ;-there to remain until the last trump Rhall
1ound on the resurrection morn. We can trustingly leave him in the bands of a

The Grand Ohaplain then repeated the following prayer:Almighty and Eternal God-in whom we live, and move, and have our being~
and before whom all man must appear at the J udgmont-day to render an account.
of their deeds while in this life-we, who are daily exposed to the flying shafts of
death, and who now surround the grave of one who has fallen in our midst, do most
humbly beseech Thee to impress deeply on our minds the solemnities of this day~
and to grant that their remembrance may be the means of turning our thought.
from the fleeting vanitip,e of the present world to the lasting glories of the world
to come. Let us continually be reminded of the frail tenure by which we hold our
earthly existence; that in the midst of life we are in death; and that, however
upright may have been our walk, and however lll]uare our conduct, we must all submit as victims to the great destroyer, and endure the bumbling level of the tomb.
Grant us Thy divine assistance, 0 most merciful God, to redeem our mis-spent
time; and, in the discharge of the important duties which Thou hast assigned us.
in the erection of our moral editice, give unto us wi8dom to direct us, Btrength to
aupport us, and the beauty of holineBB to adorn our la.bore and render them acceptable in Thy sight. And, when our wwk on earth is done, and our bodies shall g<>
down to mingle with their kindred dust, may our immortal souls, freed from their
cumbrous clay, be received into Thy keeping, to rest forever in that spiritual
house, not made with hands, eternal in the Heavens. Amen!
Rupon11e. So mote it be !

again uito newness of life, and expand, in immortal beauty, in re:Ums beyond the
skies. Until then, dear brother, until then, farewell l
